The groaning tr6incher there ye fill, . Your hurdles like a distant hill; -Your pin wad help to mend a mill In time o' need. - While through your pores the de' s distil • Like amber bead. His knife see rustic labour dight, And cut you up wi' ready slight, Trenching your gushing-entrails bright , _ Like ony ditch; And then, oh what a glorious sight, - Warm-reekin', rich!

Then horn for horn they stretch and strive, Deil tak the hindmost, en they drive, Tills' their weel-swali'd kytes belyve Are bent like drums; -7 Then auld guidinan, insist like to rill's, _:- "Bethankit !" hums. Is there that owre is French rival, Or o/io that wad stew a sow, Or fricasse -wad mak her spew MT perfect scunner, Looks dawn wi' sneering, scorrete view On sic a dinner! Poor devil see him owre his trash, As feckless as a withered rash, His spindle-shank a guid whip-lash, Thsnieve a nit; Through bloody flood oz. field to dash, O 116 vi unfit...!

Only what we have wrought in ear characters during life can we take away with us. at is what, is done and suffered in the bone, that has the profoundest interest for us. Is it not plain that'not in senates, or courts, or chambers of commerce, but in the dwelling-house must the true character and hope of -the time be consulted? The Lacedemonians applied their minds to no learning but what was useful, and would not suffer the profes- sor of any speculative sciences to live in their govern. ment, lest, by their disputations and empty.notions, they should deprave the true excellency of virtue. Avery short fat volunteer with a huge -"busby" or helmet was going along when a passer-by heard twq street gamins chaffing him. " What do you charge a quart for your milk here ?" asked a man, as he put his head in at the door of a milk shep. " Fourpence, was the reply. "Ain't you got any for threepence-halfpenny ?" " No, ' said the proprietor; "but," he added, "we can soon make you some.' ".:A lady had the following epitaph placed en her hus- band's tombstone: "Here reposes my beloved husband; he died of a misprint." The wife had not observed a misprint in her cookery book, and had quietly used lib. of,cayenne pepper instead of loz., and the poor man -died in consequence. The wisdom of the ancients, as to the government of r life, was no more than certain precepts what to do, and whatynot ; and men were much better in that simpieity ; for as they came to be more learned they grew less care- ful of being good. Plain and open virtue is now turned into a dark and intricate science, and we are taught to dispute rather than to live. The spelling-class was up. The word "rebutter" passed all around; none could tell the definition. At last little Joe P—, near the foot of the class, called out, "I can tell, sir I" "'What is it," said I. "It means," said he, "to butter on both sides. Re' signifies a repe- tition; and if you butter it again, you must certainly butter it on the other side !" A young lady being addressed by a gentleman older than herself, observed to him that the only objections _she had to a union with him was the probability of his dying before her, and leaving her to the sorrows of widowhood. To which he made the apt and delicately complimentary reply, "Blessed is the man who bath a virtitoes wife, for the number of his days shall be double." TIEREHIPENNY '"ESQUIRES."-Discussion sometimes arises (says Truth) nowadays as to the precise value of the title "Esquire." It is generally agreed that its use should; not, if possible, be allowed to ally gentleman worth, say, less than ten shillings a week unless he be an office-boy, or otherwise "professionally" engaged. It has, however, been reserved for the press to fix the exact worth of .the title. A journal published in the teem of Burnham, a popular resort on the Somersetshire ,ast, has the following note at the head of its "List of Vi itors":—" The word 'Esq.' .charged 3d., prepaid." THE SLANDER Boox.—A gentleman states that he once saw the title slander book" printed on the binding of a small ledger. On examining it he found that the vari- cius members of the household were charged s 6 much apiece for each slander. He was informed that this plan of fining for slander originated with a good young girl, with a view to prevent evil-speaking and its conse- ..cpu-noeq She observed the wretched effects ,of it in families and neighbourhoods, what great fires were kindled by it, what sweet fountains embittered by it, . and she hit upon this expedient to knock the evil thing on the head. When anyone was speaking ill of another before Peter the Great, he would say, "Well, but has he not a bright side? It is easy to splash mud; but I would rather help a man to keep his coat clean?' A CANINE MEMBER OF THE LIVERPOOL POLICE Foxes —The Liverpool dock police belonging to the south division of the city boast of a canine member who goes by_tbe cognomen of " Sergeant Jack." As showing the sagacity of: their unpaid companion we may mention i that he s known by and is acquainted with every police- manland inspector on the line of docks from the Cus- tomtHouse to the docks at the extreme south end. The dog hos been in the force for about ten years, and re- gularly- attends the " mustef," going on and off duty. As soon as the policemen fall in "Sergeant Jack," after eyeing them alternately, listens for the word of com- mand from the inspector, namely, "Right turn; quick march," then gives a barkand is soon lost sight of. He then , roceecis a little farther on, and meets another "mus- ter." During the- periods- between on and off duty "Jack" frequents the policemen's huts and gets his food from them gratis. The South Docks police, with whom ho is acquainted, do their duty Without any interference by "Jack," but should a stranger come on the beat " Jack" walks round him and inspects him as an inspect- - lag rave, would do. "Sergeant Jack" has only been &f duty once in his-ten years of servitude, and he was AO mucirmissed that the majority of policemen off duty belonging to the South-end Docks division went in search of him. Re was ultimately found in the posses- sion of a "dog Lawler," who had evidently stolen him to sell, him again, not because of his value, but ap- parently for his notoriety. OFFICIAL AGRICULTURAL RETURNS. The following is a summary of the introductory re- port to the Agricultural Returns, 1884, so far as they relate to,the United Kingdom. The land under cultiva- tion of all kinds of crops, bare fallow, and grass amounted for Great Britain to 32,465,00dacre5, an in- crease of about 81,000 acres, chiefly in permanent pas- ture. England has an additional cultivated area of 49,400 acres; Wales, 9,550 acres; and Scotland, 21,750 acres. There is an increase in the area under wheat and a decrease in that under barley and oats, the changes in these crops being in the opposite direction to that of the preceding year. The total area returned under wheat is this year 2,677,000 acres, an increase of nearly 64,000 acres over 1883, is was then remarked upon as being the smallest recorded. It is nearly a million of acres less than in 1874.

Ma. FRODDE AND CARLYLE.—lncomparably the most curious and interesting part of Mr. Froude's book is that which contains his own personal recollections of Carlyle. The earliest of them go back as far as 1848, but for the last seventeen year of his life Mr. Froude was to him as a son—a son as affectionate and dutiful as ever the old

man was blest with. In the earlier parts of the book Mr. Fronde has found it necessary, in order to give a true picture, to set forth many letters and journals which exhibit Carlyle in a light half pathetic, _balf ludicrous: In his lifetime he was often represenod as being not only the prophet and apostle of stbength, but as being himself the strongest of the strong, a stern, impressive rugged Calvinist, the worthy successor of stalwart ancestors— something between a Jewish prophet and one of Crom- well's Ironsides. This notion Mr. Froude's biography effectually dispels. Mr. Froude says:—" Robust, consti- tutional strength, which is half of it insensibility, was not among the gifts which Nature had bestowed on Car- lyle. His strength was moral. It lay in an unalterable resolution to do what was right and to speak what was true." Elsewhere he says :—"Nature had made him weak, passionate, complaining, dyspeptic in body, and sensitive in spirit, lonely, irritable, and morbid. He bes came what he was by his mral rectitude of principle, by a conscientious resolution to do right, which never failed him in serious things from his earliest years, and, though it could not change his temperament, was the inflexible guide of his conduct." Mr. Froude's personal ' recollection of him will enable everyone to understand the sort of genius which gave him an influence all but unexampled over his contemporaries. LMr. Froude says: —" His conversation when we wer's. alone together was even more surprising to me (than his kindness). I had been accustomed to hear him impatient of contradiction, extravagantly exaggerative, overbearing opposition, with bursts of scornful humour. In private I found him impatient of nothing but being bored; gentle, quiet, tolerant, sadly humoured, but never i//-humoured ; ironi- cal, but without the savageness, and when speaking of others always scrupulously just. He talked more of things than of persons, and on every variety of subject. He had read more miscellaneously than any man I have ever known. His memory was extraordinary, and a Universal curiosity had led him to inform himself "minutely about matters which I might have supposed that he had never heard of. With English literature he was as familiar as Macaulay was. French and German and Italian he knew infinitely better than Macaulay."

As regards barley, the area in 1884 was 2,168,000 acres a decrease of 123,000 acres. Oats covered 2,915,000 acres, showing a decrease of 60,000 acres. Rye was sown on 3,700 acres less than in 1883. Beans and peas show but little variation. For all corn crops in Great Britain' the total area was 8,484,700 acres, a decrease of 133,900 acres, or 1.5 per cent, from that of 1883, and 946,700 acres, or 10'0 per cent. less than in 1874. Of the area under green crops, about 565,000 acres were planted with potatoes. This is greater than 1883 by 21,600 acres, and has only been once exceeded. Turnips and swedes were sown on 2,027,600 acres, as compared with 2,028,900 in 1883. For mange's the acreage was less than last year by 2,500 acres, but vetches, lucerne, and other green crops unenumerated have increased by 14,000 acres. Sugar beet which comes under this head- ing is returned as occupying 812 acres, of which 643 acres are in Suffolk. :f Altogether the total area of green crops was 3,487,700 acres, an increase of 33,000 acres over last year's figures. The growth of flax is still diminishing, the acreage hav- ing been only 2,200 acres, less than a fourth of 1874. Extension of the cultivation of hops in England has been maintained, there appearing a further increase of 1,200 acres. The quantity of land annually in bare fallow necessarily varies greatly, according to the weather at the sowing season, and the result is seen in a further de- crease in Great Britain from 778,000 acres in 1883, to 749,000 acres in 1884. Clover, sainfoin, and grasses under rotation covered 4,381,000 acres or 14,500 acres less than in 188,3. The extension of permanent pasture is again remarkable, amounting to an increase of 225,000 acres over 1683, and bringing thelotal area up, to 15,290,000 acre's. The area under arable land on the other hand is this year less by 144,000 acres, about 17,175,000 acres being returned as compared with 17,319,000 acres in 1883. Yo'd see her mek to t' trap, pop her foot on to t' fost step to gooa deawn, on then like a blast o' leetenin hoo'd vanish, on ther'd be sich a crash o' pots! Eh, dear o' me, but ther wor sich werk ! We used to put sand on sometimes; well, thad wer trodden off directly on happen some soup, or some broth shed on steps i' t' place on id, un then deawn they popped! Aw cluttered deawn two or three times misel un mom dud t' wife, on of course ho allus blamed me for id. But as id happened ther wer never .nobry seriously hurt. Aw dar say t' lasses would hey some black place abeawt urn some- where. Aw'd hed this shop oppen abeawt two months when aw geed id i' my heyd as a gas oven would be a grand thing. Aw kept hearin feet one on then another say heaw handy they wor fellow med up mi mind as aw'd buy one, on sooa as id wod be up to mark aw spent welly twenty peawnd on id. Id cost mo o'er two peawnd to hey id coupled to t' meter. Neaw fa o as my wife has a good deal moor sense then me hoo hes'nd as much courage; nowe nod by a lot; un when we geet thad gas stove ther wor sich runnin. Yo see when yo torn ony o' t' burners off ay a gas stove they gooa eawt wi' a bit of a explosion. Well, for two or three days t' wife, every time as boo turned one off on heerd this pop as id med boo dud a bit of a dart as if th' heawse wer cumin deawn, on id took her a tooathry days to ged ony bit like used to id; in fact, hoo never geet as boo could torn one off beawt winkle un puttin her hands at front of her face. THE ANDALUSIAN. One of the least known, but certainly not one of the least valuable of the Spanish family is the Andalusian. In somkparts of the country there are what is known as the "Blue" Spanish, and these are very nearly allied to the Andalusians of the present day. There are also birds known as the." White" Spanish, but the latter are either sports from the blues, or White Minorcas. But both the Blue Spanish and the Whites are highly valued where they are kept, and we have often, wondered that they have not became popular. They are very heavy layers, of large white eggs, are hardy, and either in a suburban garden or on a farm thrive equally well. Whether there are any in this district we cannot tell, but if so the owner of Ahem will doubtless be ready to bear out our remarks regarding them. But it is not with either the Blue or the White Spanish that we wish now specially to deal, except so far as the former is connected with the Andalusian. This and the Minorca with the Leghorn and the Black Spanish all form part of the Spanish family, and are each and everyone cousin of the others. The origin of the.Anda- Inman cannot be traced with any certainty, but it has been known and recognised In this country for about forty years, but during that period it has never ad- vanced to the position of a popular variety. The first birds brought over were some blue and speckled fowls, • imported from Xeres de la Frontera, in Andalusia and several importations; of the blue variety took place at subsequent dates. But it is very evident that neither of these colours are very numerous, even in the district of • the peninsula from whence the name of this variety is derived. By careful breeding the present Andalusian has been obtained, but, there would appear to be little doubt Lthat frequeut crosses with other varieties have been made, for perhaps no other breed is characterised by greater irregularity in the produce. Almost every colour of Spanish—black, white, blue and speckled— will come out of one hatching, and the drawback from an exhibition point of view is the difficulty in obtaining birds which will pass the present standard. But the frequency of the darker birds would show that the Min- orca has been used,pretty freely of late years. On this account it is very difficult indeed to obtain specimens of the blue variety, but still they are to he found in some places. The shape and general appearance of the Andalusians are very much that of the Spanish, namely, with large and deep head, tall single comb, well serrated, and tong, fine wattles; long neck covered with hackles; light active body, broad in front and tapering to the tall; the back being round; closely tucked wings; round and well forward breast; clean legs ; tail in the cock high and sweeping, and the whole carriage very upright. The colour of the best specimens is a deep blue breast, and the rest of the plumage a deep slate blue, with a lacing of darker colour, .save in the cock, when the hackle, saddle, and sickle should be a rich glossy black or deep purple. These characteristics, with the dark horn beak, the bright orange or red eye, the red face, comb and wattles, neat white ear lobe, and dark leaden-blue legs, make the variety very pleasing in appearance. It will be seen from this description that the white face which forms so striking a point in the Black Spanish, is not heretre-produced, and we are glad that it is so. But probably this last-named breed has been used for cross- ing with the Andalusian, for a very difficult thing to avoid is the white on the face, and there is such a de- cided tendency to this that in two or three years, if en- couraged, the faces would be entirely white. But it ought to be sternly repressed, and as far as possible we do this. A bird with any white on the face ought not to be bred from at all. If Andalusian breeders would keep the true type before them, try and obtain a few good fresh birds from Spain and abstain from crossing, they would soon very materially improve the quality of their stocks, and add to the success of the breed. Andalusians are essentially a laying fowl, and in this respect are equal to the best of the Spanish family, which as a family are by far the best of all fowls as layers. They lay ilarge eggs perhaps scarcely so large as the Black Spanish, but not much less, and the num- ber of eggs produced is very large, often reaching from 150 to 180;per year, if ti good kind is procured. They are not sitters as a rule, but, like nearly all the non- sitting varieties, occasionally a hen is found to tare up her maternal duties. They bear confinement very well indeed, and yet are equally suitable for wide ranges. There is just Zone exception to their bearing confine- ment well, and that is they do not like a damp place. For such a:run as this—if it were not possible to alter it —we think the Minorca had better be chosen. They are hardy—naturally hardy—but where there has been cros- sing with the Black Spanish, we sometimes find the slow feathering of the latter partially reproduced. This is not so in the pure-bred fowls, as they feather well;grow rapidly as chickens, and bear cold as adults capitally. Of course, such large combed birds are very apt to get caught during severe frosts, but this can be prevented if properly housed. Andalusians are not noted as table fowls, but the y..ung birds are 14. no means to be de- spised, and there is a fair amount of meat on adult fowls of this breed. one of the Spanish family can claim much merit in this way,for their special excel- lencies are in the direction of egg laying. We can cor- dially recommend this breed to any who wish for eggs most of all, whether farmer, fancier, cottager, or suburban resident. We do not say that „nit is charac- terised by any great beauty„but then its eggs make up in this respect, and it is hardy and precocious—two qualities which will be its great recommendation. In our opinion it shares with the Minorca and the Leghorn the right to claim the premier Positions as laying fowls. SEASONABLE HINTS. The high:winds and cold rains of the past few days have warned us that the fine weather can be reckoned on no longer. 'We may have many fine days yet, but cannot presume upon.thein. Birds will need to be fed a little better if the supply of eggs his to be at all main- tained, for they are getting scarcer and dearer, and an egg is now worth double what it was a veryfew weeks ago. What is perhaps the next matter of importance after proper food is exercise, and, if there is not un- limited space, we should remove all the cocks and small pens and throw all the hens together until the time for making up the breeding pens arrives. This is, of course, where the various breeds are kept separate. Exercise keeps birds in condition as does nothing else, and they are hardier and stronger for it in every way. A good plan is to have a loose heap of dry earth or Sand, in which the corn is buried daily. The work entailed in searching out this corn gives a great deal of exercise to the fowls, to their great benefit.

div.head: LIBERALISM IN MID-CHESHIRE.
div.p: LIBERALISM IN MID-CHESHIRE.

MEETING AT LYMM. A meeting of Liberal electars and non-electors of Lymm and Grappenhall polling districts was held on Monday even- ing at the Assembly-room at the Plough Hotel, Lymm, to bear addresses by the Liberal candilates for the division. Mr. W. Long (Thel avail ) presided, and amongst those present were—Messrs. T. Rigby and I. S. Leadam, candidates ; G. W. Latham (Bowdon), T. W. Killick (Altrincham), J. Rylands, J.P. (Thelwali), E. Brewtnall (Thelwall), F. Roberts (Warrington), A. Patterson (Altrincham), C. Broad- bent, J.P. (Latchford), Milne (Sale); and J. A. Swanwick, D. Boyd, R. Dutton, J. Swanwick, Cameron, Welford, and Hudson (Lymm). A letter was read from Mr. G. C. Dew- burst, Beechwood, regretting his inability to be present. The CHAIRMAN said that the chief object of the meeting was to evince that in that division of Mid-Cheshire they were not behind their countrymen in the agitation for the exten- sion of the franchise to rural householders. Tney must show that they would do their utmost in support of the will of the people, and would withstand the dotninacy of party or class against the universal wish of the people. The Tories, who at first denied the existence of a universal cry for the franchise, now admitted it, but wanted to tie up Redistribu- tion with the Franchise. The Liberals also desired redis- tribution, but should not those who admittedly had a right to the franchise have a voice in the distribution of political p3wer ? (Heir, hear.) When Mr. Gladstone—(cheers)—on his way to Midlothian spoke at Warrington, he said that he wished to get the opinion of his own constituents, but in Scotland he found the enthusiasm so great that he said " You want this franchise and I atilt do my best to get it for you." They must endeavour to obtain their purpose in a legitimate manner, and if then they failed they would know who were the parties responsible for any breach of order. They had present that evening their two candidates, Mr. Leadarn and Mr. Rigby, who would address them. He was glad that in Mr. Rigby they had a gentleman who stood so well with the agricultural classes. (Applause.) Mr. BOYD (Lymm) proposed the first resolution-se" That this meeting of the inhabitants of the Lymm and Grappen- hall polling districts strongly approves the determination of the Government to pass the Franchise Bill, protests against the conduct of the House of Lords in rejecting it, and urges the Government to submit t) no dictation from the Peers." The time was coming, he said, when all who were entitled to a vote would be in possession of it. He congratulatedthe Liberals of Lymm on having assembled in such numbers to consider the question. (Applause.) Mr. Banwrseee (Thelweit), seo3nded the resoldtion. He thought that the fact that they were not at present repre- sented in Parliameot by Mr. Leadam was due to the sha- dows that were passed over that part of the county from a neighbouring large house, and to its ramifying influence. He was sure that wilts increased enfranchisement there would be a different tale to tell. (Cheers.) The reform bill that followed the burning of Nottingham Castle and the thrill of feeling that then aroused the people was the greatest sham ever foisted upon the country. It merely gave a larger number of people to elect the same members, and that was a game that the Tories wished to play over again. The crisis was at hand, the probability was that the House of Lords would reject the Franchise Bill, and then the people must stand manfully by the Government. Mr. Glad- stone, as did Earl Grey on a former occasion, would then have to ask for a sufficient number of Liberal peers to pass the measure, or he must. resign. If the latter, a general election would follow, and be had not the fear entertained by some as to the result. He believed that the enthusiasm ot the coarnry would so stand by the Liberal candidates when the election came that they would have a gain of at least sixty seats that Mr. Gladstone would return to power by the will of the nation, and that the bill would then pass without difficulty. (Cheers). Mr. &nein who rose to support the resolution, said that he was conscious that he was attempting an arduous task in appearing as an advocate of Liberal principles in the pre- sence of so many gentlemen who had long been the advo- cates of these principles in that part of the county and had proved their fidelity to them, but he was impelled to attempt the advocacy of those principles by the faith that he had in them and by his desire to conduce to their growth generally, and more particularly in the minds of the agricultural clas- ses. He heard the other day of a speech that had a good be- ginning and a good ending, but it's great fault was that it had too much middle. No such complaint should be pos- sible in regard to the subject they were then considering. Their minds were made up and they were ready, without the preliminary of long speeches. A singular fact was that although both parties were agreed upon the necessity of the measure no progress was made. The ostensible reason was the opposition or the House of Lords, but he feared that there WAS opposition somewhere else. If the minority in the House of Commons sincerely desired the pessicg of the bill and the representation of the people generally they bad only to add their voices to the majority and the opposition of the Lords would vanish like the morning mist before the rising sun. A further excuse for delay or prevention of the measure was that there was a difficulty on a point of pro- cedure. Bring in a Redistribution Bill, it was:said, and debate them as parts of one measure, which was tantamount to say- log "Add a more complicated measure to one that is less difficult, and then we will pass it. Alone, the Franchise Bill might be passed, but couple with it the difficulties that might arise on the matter of redistribution, it would be im- possible to presume that the two could together pass. He did not say that the House of Lords was blameless, but it had kept well within its legal riehts in suspending the bill, and he could well believe that in the majority of cases its , members in their own minds thought themselves well within their expedient rights. The House of Lords was by no means perfect. It would be improved in moral character by the elimination of some of its members—(laughter)—by a better training of some inadministrative sections and by the more just distribution of its highest honours to proved capacities. But the House of Lords should not so much be made the scapegrace for the sin of others. The burden of the guilt lay at the door of those Conservative members of the House of Commons, who had given their influence and votes against the measure becoming law. The House of Lords had done wrong in not regard:tag the voice of the majority, had thus provoked the criticism of the coun- try, and in due time would have to reap what it bad sown. He did not desire the abolition of that House—it might dis- charge functions profitable to good government—but it was not meet that the Government should submit to its dictation. The Government was the chosen administration of the Queen and the people and it was theirs to do their duty. As a farmer he should like to see more security of tenure and more encouragement given to enterprising cultivation than now existed, or was generally recognised. The pop- ulation was daily growing and the land being constantly reduced. The land too, was not being improved as it might be by the education of farmers' sons, who were destined to be farmers, or by the perfect security of capital invested in it, or by Government provision of capital for its cultivation by advances, as some years ago they gave to owners where- with to improve their estates and buildings. There were also questions of local taxation, railway rates, and others, that affected the farmer and through him the labourer in which legislative action might be taken with advantage both to them and the country. The county of Cheshire contained 11,000 tenants entitled to vote, there were over 705,000 acres of land, which, on an average of 50 acres to one oc- cupier, left 14.000 tenants. The land of the kingdom comprised 47,000,000 acres, which,on the same division. gave 910,000 tenants or voters, among whom five only were heard in the discussion of the administration of laws bear- ing directly or indirectly upon their interests. He hoped he might plead for their support on the ground that he knew something of such questions, and of the necessity there was for more adequate representation of the interest with which REMARKABLE DISAPPEARANCE! his life had been generally connected. Mr. Rmorns, J.P., expressed his gratification at bearing the two candidates for the division. A short time since he met with a description of a Conservative, and it was so clever that he could not forget it—" A. Conservative has no knowledge of the past, no appreciation of the present, and no plans for the future." They would appreciate that say- ing when he told them that it was one of the late Earl Beaconsfield's. (Laughter.) lie presumed Earl Beaconsfield said it before he was a Tory himself, but if they read the speeches of Conservatives they would find an illustration of that saying. Re hoped that Mr. Leadam and Mr. RigbY would be returned as members for Mid-Cheshire. _

div.head: COTTAGE GARDENING.
div.p: COTTAGE GARDENING.

CELERY.—The crop of this general favourite esculent is in good order this season in most localities, and where' it received an abundant supply of water when the weather was dry, in the early stage of its growth, the heads are of enormous size. We see that the celery fly has been at work in some gardens, as several of the leaves look brown and withery. Many growers are as yet quite ignorant of the cause of the pale yellowish' patches that appear on the foliage of the celery during the summer months, and increase in number till the end of September, when most of. the patches will be brown. If, on their first appearance, a leaf is examined, it will be found that the patches have the appearance of a small bladder, in which is enclosed the larvae of the Tephrilis Onopordinus, which punctures the leaves and deposits its eggs. They, in course of time, are hatched; and we all at once see these small bladders or blisters, which are the result of the larvte, separating the epidermis from the paunchyma, where it continues to feed by enlarging its possession. It ultimately, emerges, having become almost a winged insect, to breed an addi- tional colony, for we believe one will lay some hundreds of eggs in the course of the season. As we may now expect frost sufficiently severe to injure the celery, it will be as well to take the necessary steps to protect it. If some of the centre leaves of the heads are damaged by frost ever so slightly decay sets in, and continues to descend till it reaches the roots. At present sufficient protection may be given by packing the soil first with the hands round eaph plant, and afterwards pack up more soil against it with the spade. Instead of leaving the space between the trenches as hard as the move- ments of human feet can make it, we make a practice of forking or digging it up after every operation, and we discover that it is much more friable, and better suited for packing next to the plants. When it is intended to preserve celery as long as it can reasonably be expected to do so, the tops of the ridges on each side should be left slanting, so as to throw off the rain. Pnoxr GARDEN.—BuIbs are so cheap as to be within the reach of those with limited means to secure a few. They are all very beautiful and flowering. As they grow at a time of the year when there is very little else, they ought to find space in every garden. They have all been found to thrive as well in the town garden as in the country. To make the best of all bulbous plants, such as Snowdrops, Tulips, and Crocuses, they should be planted in patches and not frittered away by planting two or three here and there, as, by so doing, the effect that they would otherwise produce is destroyed. If we had only a dozen snowdops we would plant them at even".distances, tin a space six inches in diameter, and the planter should arrange them first by placing one in the centre and the others in two rows round it. Of tulips, five would occupy such a space, and we would only have those of the later kind in the group, though there can be no serious objection to a mixture of red and white, but the mixing of shades will be most dis- appointing. Crocuses look well as an edging to a border if three or four rows of distinct colours are planted, and the same.larrangement may be carried out in a round bed that may occupy the centre of the garden. But in all other .instances we would group them by placing seven ;or nine in a space six inches in diameter. The spaces between can, at the proper time, be planted with Geraniums, Zinnias, Asters, Stocks, and Lobelias for summer decoration. The Crocuses and Snowdrops being much'smaller than the Tulips, should occupy, a position as near the outer edge of the bed or border as possible. Associated with the Tulip for a background, we may place the: Jonquil, single and double; also Polyanthus Narcissus, and St. Brunos Lily, as well as some of thZ tall-growing Scillas, of which the common Blue Bell may be taken' as a type. All the above die:down during the season, and the summer flowering plants already named cover the ground as the dead tops of the bulbs are being moved. THE WlNDOW—Tulips are almost as easily cultivated in the window as the Hyacinth; the soil that suits the one will: do for the other. The number of bulbs in a 61n. pot may be at least five, which is the size generally used in private gardens for general decoration. In pot- ting these the] bulbs are so covered with soil that they are scarcely seen. If the soil is placed in the pot loosely up to the rim, and the bottom slightly tapped on the potting table, and the bulbs thrust in, followed by another tap or two, the operation may be safd to be complete. •In some instances, perhaps, a little more soil may be required, so as to effectually cover the bulbs. The Crocus is net a very satisfactory pot plant, and seems to object to too much confinement. Gardeners even cannot induce it to flower indoors very little earlier than it does outside in warm localities, and its flowering season is so short in pots that it scarcely repays for the trouble. Polyanthus Narcissus may be successfully grown in pots, and its sweet-scented flowers will be highly appreciated. The bulbs of this are usually thrust half way into the soil, and the latter is pressed rather firm.

The Conservatives said to the farmer, "Our opposition the franchise is in your interest. Unless we can keep the franchise from extension you, the farmers, will be swamped, and be of no account to the people who are in your emefieYe most." And then to the agricultural labourer they say, "We are fighting for your benefit. Our fear is lest your interest eLee!'l be swamie d by the lute-eels of the unfran- chised inhabitants of the-towns, and mei', we cell check that danger we think it very much better that you should go without the franchise altogether." (Laughter.) He (Mr. Leadam) asked farmers not to be misled by language of that kind, but to remember that until manufacturers wer.er backed up by the votes of the artisans in the towns their interests were neglected in the same way that the interests of the farmers How are. They might depend upon it that they would never get their interests adcqiately represented and looked after until they had the labourers at their back to support them at the polling booth. (Cheers.) The resolution was then carded unanimously. Mr. LATHAM, who was received with cheers, proposed the second resolution. It was "That this meeting welcomes the candidature of Messrs. Leadam and Rigby, and pledges it- self to do its utmost to secure their election for Mid-Che- shire at the next general election." The issues of the time, he said, were great, there was much political work to .be done, and it would be necessary to have a Liberal majoritY in the House of Commons. He asked them to return the Liberal instead of the Tory caneidates. He humonrousll compared the Tories to dolls, and urged them to get out of the doll stage into the man stage. He held that a Tory could not get rid of his creed, but in the hatred he had for popular government, his hostility to progress and reform, his subordinatini the people's will to class intelests and pie' judices, in his willingness to spend the people's money rd shed the people's blood in order to get up a false prestige, was the same yesterday, to-day, and for ever. (Cheers.) Having severely criticised the action of the Upper House in relation to the Franchise Bill. Mr. Latham said that they admitted the House of Lords as a party, but if that House and the House of Commons clashed the weaker body must go, and that body was the House of Lords. He would not go into the question of the final destination of the House.of Lords, and would only say that it was their duty to resist its claims in this world, whatever might be it claims in the next. (Laughter and applause.) Mr. Klemm (chairman of the Executive Committee) seconded the resoletien. He said that at the election of 18S0 Liberals were returned pledged to extend household franchise to the counties and to support other measures which had not yet been secured; and he claimed that the cause was to be found in the obstruction of certain mem- bers, notably, Mr. Whartou, Mr. Bartlett, and Lord R. Churchill. • With an extended franchise and a redistribu- tion by which each member represented a certain number of voters, he believed it would be impossible for these ob- structionists to find seats in the House of Commons. appealed for the support of the electors of the division ln favour of the two Liberal candidates. _ .

div.head: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
div.p: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.

HOUSE OF LORDS —Morener. The Lord Chancellor took the chair at 12-25. There was a good attendance of peers, and the Prince of Wales was in his place on the cross benches. The Duke of Wellington, Lord Clifden, and Lord Petre (a Roman Catholic priest) took their seats on succeeding to the, peerage. Lord Sydney, Lord Steward, brought down the Queen's reply to the address of their lordships in answer to ,the Royal Speech. THE REPORTED FALL OF KHARTOUM—Lord Gaetiviretz, 'replying to Lord Salisbury, stated that there was no truth in the report that the Khedive had sent telegrams to the 'Queen and the Prince of Wales informing her Majesty and his Royal Highness that he had received news of the fall of Khartoum. While the Government were not in a position to say positively that Khartoum had not fallen, they had no reason to believe that it had. LORD WOLSELEY'S Ixerarcerroem —LIMA SALISBURY criticised the instructions to Lord Wolseley. He held that, according to all precedent, any instructions given to that gallant general ought to have come from the Govern- ment direct and not from Sir E. Baring, and that those which had been given were highly objectionable, not merely in form, but in substance also. They resolved themselves into this summary—that the policy of rescue and retire confined itself entirely to the rescue of the two men who lad gone te rescue the gaerisons, and that the policy of res- cuing the garrisons had been abandoned.—Lord GRANVILLE denied that the form adopted in this case was not in ac- cordance with precedent. The instructions had been drawn up by Lord Northbrook in consultation with Sir E Baring and Lard Wolseley, but they were submitted to and considered by the Government, who took upon themselves all responsibility in connection with those instructions. His reading on them Was that they authorised Lord Wolselev by military means to enable the Egyptian garrison to evacuate Khartoum, and that, consequently, they did not nply the abandonment of that garrison.—Lord DUNRAVEN contended that the Government incurred obligations in respect of the Egyptian garrisons when they compelled the Khe- dive to abandon the Soudan.—Lord Ellenborough observed that General Gordon had been very unfairly treated in having all his important requests refused by the Govern- ment. NEW BILLS-Lord BRAMWELL presented bills dealing with summary jurisdiction and the law of evidence, and the , measures were read a first time. THE ELECIION OF REPRESENTATIVE PEERS. Lordl WATENEY intimated that on Tuesday of next week he would call attention to the mode of electing representa- tive peers for Ireland and Scotland, and move a resolu- tion. Their Lerdships adjourned at 4-55. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—MoeneAr, The Speaker took the chair at four o'clock. Mr. Campbell-Bannerman, Chief Sec-etary for Ireland, took his seat for Stirling burghs on his re-election. BOLTON.—Mr. CAMPBELL•BANNERMAN informed Mr. Healy that it had been determined to remove the suspen- sion of Bolton, who had arranged matters with his creditors. —Mr. IlEarar made a violent protest, and was called to order by the SPEAKER. THE REPORTED FALL OF KHARTOI73I.—STATEMENT BY LORD BARTINOTON —Sir S. NORTHCOTE asked if the Government have received any intelligence from Khartoum or from Egypt respecting the fall of Khartoum or the posi- tion of General Gordon.—The Marquis of HARTINGTON : My right hon. friend has asked me to answer this question. So far as we are aware there is absolutely no foundation for the rumour that has been circulated as to the fall of Khar- toum or the capture of General Gordon. (Cheers.) That rumour appears to have originated at Cairo, and we have re- ceived absolutely no confirmation of it. The latest intelli- gence, I believe, that we have received arrived late on the night of the 31st October. It was a telegram from Sir E. Baring, who said :—" Wilson telegraphs Kabbabide Arab has brought news that the Mandi's troops attacked Gordon's post at Omdurman, opposite Khartoum, a few days ago, and were repulsed. I also heir that hostile Arabs are numerous at Gabara, on the Debbah-Khartoum road. I think these reports are likely to be correct." Sir E. Baring says that he gave the substance of this to Reuter's agency to correct re- ports about the fall of Khartoum, which is without founda- tion as far as I am aware. That is the latest intelligence we have from Dongola. The Urider-Secretary for Foreign Affairs has telegraphed to-day to ask Sir E. Baring whether he can give any explanation of the reports that have been spread at Cairo, but no answer has been received. I have received a direct contradiction of the statement in this morning's Times that telegrams had been sent by the Khe- dive to the Queen and the Prince of Wales giving .an ac- count of the fall of Khartoum. (Cheers.) MORE OBSTRTCTION.—THE PREMIER'S PROTEST.

div.head: ACTION OF THE SPEAKER.
div.p: ACTION OF THE SPEAKER.

The adjourned debate on the Address was resumed by Mr. SEXTON, who moved a fourth amendment, calling for a more-impartial adminstration of the criminal law in Ire- land, especially with regard to the composition of juries. In support of it Mr. Sexton inveighed energetically against jury packing, which, he maintained, bad reduced trial by jury in Ireland to a farce, and enabled the Government to punish the innocent when they could not get at the guilty, or even when they could. He referred to the circumstances of the Maamtrasna murders and to the recent trials in Dublin, in regard to both of which he contended that the Government had contrived to pervert the course of justice. Mr. O'BRIEN seconded the amendment in a speech cf a similar strain, asserting that the Government had murdered innocent men and had screened the guilty. Mr. TREVELYAN, who were received with cheers and with counter-cheers from the Irish members, justified the action of the Government in changing the venue of the trial of cases of agrarian crime on the ground that Parliament had given the Irish Executive in their discretion power to do so under the Crimes Act of 1882. The answer to the charge of partiality against the juries was that their verdicts had been discriminating. ("Oh.") The average et acquittals or of disagreement on the part of the juries in these trials was equal to the average of verdicts in England or Scotland. The right hon. gentleman was proceeding to show that French's letter, which he characterised as an odious produc- tion, only proved that the Government had discharged their duty in the matter with zeal and ability, when he was again interrupted by Mr. Healy. The SPEAKER Order, order. These interruptions are most unseemly, and it they are continued I shall be obliged to take notice of them. Mr. POWER, having remarked that in Ireland there was one law for the rich and one for the poor, protested against the Irish judgeships being given to Government partisans. Mr. BIGGAR charged the Government with packing juries for the purpose of convicting persons whether guilty or in- nocent, and inveighed against the partisanship of the Irish judges, being called to order by the Speaker. Mr. LEAMY contended that the present lawless state of Ireland was due to the policy of repression and coercion, which had been in ingurated by the Liberal party; and Mr. BARRY supported the amendment. Mr. MARom entered upon a long historical review of the persecution of the Catholics in Ireland, and was twice called to order by the SPEAKER. Mr. A. MOORE expressed the dissatisfaction largely felt by Roman Catholics at their frequent exclusion from juries. Mr. W. REDMOND animadverted on Mr. Bolton's restora- tion, which he attributed to Ministerial fears, and expected that Mr. French would shortly be set at liberty with a large sum of money in hie pocket to leave the country. Mr. PLUNKET vindicated the conduct of the Irish juries, and though he attributed much of the deplorable condi- tion of Ireland to the action of the present Government, he did not think they were liable to the censure now pro- posed. Mr. Kenny, Col. O'Beirne. and Mr. Deasy having sup- ported the amendment, The Soetcrroß-GENERAL for IRELAND replied categori- cally to the charges brought against the Government. He denied that the right of free speech had been interfered with in Ireland, and protested against the insinuarinn that the merchants of Dublin who had served as special jurymen had not honestly fulfilled their duties. , Mr. J. H. M'CARTHY moved the adjournment of the de- bate. (Cres of "No "and 'Divide.") Mr. PARNELL insisted that before the debate closed they ought to have an opportunity of hearing the new Chief Secretary. Mr. GeecereerE said be felt it his duty to offer a decided opposition to the motion for adjourning the debate. It was perfectly true that the present Chief Secretary had not entered into this debate, because he had no special respon- sibility for what hod occurred in Ireland up to the present time, and the Minister who was responsible and also the law advisers of the Crown had entered fully into the matter. No doubt the subject was important, but there were other im- portant subjects awaiting the decision of the House. (Cheers.) The prolongation of debates was being applied to an extent that threatened to be fatal to the dignity and efficiency of the House. (Renewed cheers.) They had already had eight cloys' discussion on the Address. Parlia- ment had been called together by the Crown for a Special purpose, and had been exhorted to give immediate attention to that purpose. It Was impossible for them as officers of the Crown not to assist in giving effect to that injunction, which he iselleved to be sustained by the feeling and voice of the nation. (Loud cheers.) Mr. HEALY said it might be the opinion of the Goverm- Ment that there were other subjects of great importance, but that was not his opinion. To him and his friends the lives and the liberties of their fellow-countrymen were of greater importance than the possession of a vote at quinquennial elections. (Vociferous cheering from Mr. Parnell and the other Irish members.) The SPEAKER: I must call the hen, member to order, and remind him that he must confine himself to the question before the House, which is the question of adjourn- ment. Mr. O'BRIEN: You want to get rid of us for the Franchise Bill.—Mr. HEALY proceed to argue that the question had not been fully discussed.—Mr. LEAMY complained that the Solicitor-General had not spoken earlier.—Mr. O'BRIEN referred at some length' to the Meamtrasna murders.—Mr. Ruseross I rise to order. Are these remarks in order? (Cheers.)—Mr. O'BRIEN: I am obliged to the hon. gentle- man, who has not yet discovered himself to fame. The SPEAKER : The hon. member must confine himself to the motion for adjournment. He is not in order in travel- ling beyond it. (Cheers.) Mr. O'BRIEN: I was simply replying to the interrup- tion of the hon. member opposite, and endeavouring to show that your rule in Ireland has been a rule of corrup- tion. The SPEAKER: Order, order. That is not the question.

The question is the adjournment of the debate. (Loud cheers.) Mr. O'BRIEN: I am trying against a good many odds to show that the debate ought to be adjourned. The hon. member proceeded to refer to what he termed the tyranny which had characterised the proceedings of the Government. The SPEAKER: I have twice observed that the hon. mem- ber is irrelevant. I now call upon him to resume his seal. (Loud cheers.) Mr. SEXTON, who was greeted by those around him with uproarious cheers and cries of Tyrants" and " Cowards," commented on the speech which had been delivered earlier in the evening by Mr. Trevelyan. The SPEAKER: Order, order. The hon member is not now discussing the immediate question before the House, but is entering into debate and commenting on speeches delivered' during the last debate. Mr. SEXTON complained that the members of his party had had no opportunity of replying to the speech of the Solicitor-General. 1 The SPEAKER: it is my duty again to tell the hon. member--( Loud and continued cries of " Oh " and " Clo- sure " from Irish members.) I must aek the hon. members to be silent while I address the House. For the second time I tell the bon. member that he is not dealing with the point befsre the House. I must warn him that be has twice deviate! from the question, and if he should continue to do so it will be my painful duty to ask him to resume his seat. (Cheers). Mr. SEXTON: I thank you for your warning; but if you have your duties in the Chair every member of this House has also his duties to his constituents. (Loud cheers from the Parnellite members.) lam respectfully stating my reasons for adjourning the debate ; and if I again incur your censure I shall gladly welcome any penalty you may place upon me. Mr. W. Redmond and Mr. Biggar supported the motion for the adjournment, the latter being called to orler twice for wandering from the eubject.--Mt. Bury having spoken on tne same side, Mr. A. O'CoNtroß complained that Mr. Glad- stone had declared that the Crown enjoined upon the House to proceed with the Franchise Bill. Mr. GLADSTONE denied the use of the phrase "enjoined." The word "injunction " had escaped him in the course of his observations, and he should wish to withdraw it. (Hear, hear). The debate was continued by Mr. Kenny, Sir J. M‘Kenna, and Mr. Deasy, Mr. Deasy being at one point called to order for irrelevancy —Mr. WARTON, at half-past one, advised the Government to concede the request of the Irish members.— Mr. J. REDMOND claimed the right to see the Solicitor- General's speech in print, and said if the wish of the Irish members was not granted now it would be their duty to move another amendment to the Address, on which all would be able to speak next day. Mr. R. POWER having spoken of the vile and infamous policy of the Government, and of the new Chief Secretary's ignorance of Irish affairs, was twice called to order by the Speaker. Mr. CALLAN, who spoke for less than two minutes, was first called to order, and then told by the Speaker that he was trifling with the House, and directed to assume his seat. Mr. O'KELLY briefly appealed to the Government to give way in view of the uselessness of a struggle.—Mr. I'. P. O'Connor, Mr. M'Carthy, and Mr. Molloy supported the amendment.—Mr. GREY said some forcible method would be needed to close the debate before Irish members would sub- mit —Dr. Commas supported the amendment.—COl. NoLaN denounced the way in which the Irish members were threatened. The SPEAKER ruled his expression out of order.—Mr. MARIJM followed. His remarks were also ruled out of order as irrelevant.—The House divided—For the adjournment of the debate, 30; against, 118. Mr. GLADSTONE said the Government having protested by the division against the undue prolongation of the debate, he would new consent to its adjournment. On the motion of Mr. HEALY, it was then ad borne L The House rose at 2-40. HOUSE OF COMMONS—TUESDAY.

The Speaker took the chair shortly before 4-0. THE SKYE CROFTERS.—In rep'y to Dr. Cameron, Sir W. HARCOURT said he had had official communications from the justices and local authorites of Inverness informing him that in Skye the police had been attacked and overpowered. The duty of her Majesty's Government was clear to take measures, in conjunction with the local authorities, for the maintenance of order. (Hear, hear.) MR CHAMBERLAIN AND THE ASTON HIOTS.—In answer to Mr. Lewis, Mr. CHAMBERLAIN said the original sworn depositions quoted by him or read extenso in that House, in the debate on October 30th, were in his possession on that date. The whole of them had now been forwarded to the solicitors who had the conduct of proceedings. He added that some objection having been taken to some irregu- larity in these papers, he was informed that the whole of the statements had now been repeated in statutory declara- tions, and communications had been addressed to the Tory solicitors that these were at their service if they desired to found any proceedings upon them. (Hear, hear.) DEBATE ON THE ADDRESS. On the motion of Mr. GLADSTONE, the House agreed to give precedence to the Address for Wednesday and Thurs- day. The adjourned debate on Mr. Sexton's amendment to the Address in reply to the Queen's Speech was resumed by Mr. HEALY. The new Irish Secretary had, he contended, be- gun badly by announcing that the suspension of Mr. George Bolton was to be removed, Mr. Bolton being a man who had on more than one occasion received strong rebukes from Irish Judges for his treatment of his wife and his withhold- ing testimony in a murder case in Sligo. In conclusion, Mr. Healy dealt with Mr. French's letter, remarking that if the memoir of that individnal were not shortly published to the world, the inference he (Mr. Healy) should draw would be that French was to be paid £2OOOO out of the Secret Service Fund in order to purchase his silence. Mr. O'DoNNELL said he believed they were now entering on a new era and phase of what was known to British law as treasonable agitation. Lord LYMINOTON regretted that the Government had thought fit to retain the services of Mr. George Bolton. He hoped the Irish members would challenge Mr. Bolton's salary when the estimates were under consideration, and promised them a good share of support from that (the Liberal) side of the House.--Dr. Cueretnes thanked Lord Lymington for the modicum of sympathy be had extended to the Irish members.--Mr. CORSET strongly deprecated the system of jury packing, which he maintained had clearly been shown to prevail in Ireland.--Mr. O'KELLY animadverted on the course pursued by the Irish Govern- ment` in constantly setting aside Catholic jurors and in em- pannelling Orangemen.---Sir P. O'Bninte ridiculed the constant assertion by the Irish members that nothing had been done by the English Government for Ireland, and as- serted, on the contrary, that within his own time the whole condition of the country had been greatly changed for the better.---Mr. T. P. O'Corneon complained that no member of the Government had risen that evening to answer the statements of his hon. friend, and deprecated the silence of the new Chief Secretary. He accused the Government of having employed a female spy in the House last session. Sir Wet. flatworm., who stated that the silence of the Government was not due to disrespect but to the fact that they had left it to those charged with the administration of Irish affairs to answer the Irish members, urged in excuse for the reticence of the newly-appointed Chief Secretary, that he could not be expected to speak on matters that he had had as yet no means of becoming familiar with. In replying to the statement of Mr. O'Connor as to the em- ployment of female spies he said he had listened with the greatest interest 16 the hon. member's romantic narrative, and was of opinion that the literary faculty of the hon. gen- tleman had never been displayed to greater advantage. For his own part, and on behalf of his right hon. friend the late Chief Secretary, he could only say that beyond the fact of the receipt by the right hon. gentleman of of the mysterious £l5 which had been referred to by Mr. O'Connor they had never heard of the lady who was said to have paid it, nor of the transaction of which it was supposed to be the out- come.

Mr. JUSTIN MCCARTHY, referring to the charge against the Government of employing female spies, regretted that an accusation which was' at any rate, believed in Ireland, had been so lightly passed over.—Mr. REDMOND followed in the same strain. Mr. WARTON was unable to concur In the wholesale charges made against Irish juries ; and Mr. Car.rmsr, who cited a number of cases in which in asserted that jury pack- ink had been resorted to. Mr. Pansztr. rose amid cheers from the Iriah members. He maintained that the right of the Irish peasant to live free from the dread of imprisonment or even death, under a system which brought into play the evidence of informers and the establishment of a secret examination, was of far more importance than the pretended extension of a sham constitutial right to a section of the Irish people. The Government had failed in attempting to govern Ireland without such measures as the Crimes Act, a re-enactment of which measure was even now threatened, he could not say how such a proposal would be met, but he could assert that it would not only be a serious thing for Ireland, but a serious matter for England also. Ireland had now been governed under a united Parliament for 84 years, and he asked the Government whether they ceuld honestly say they were any nearer the end they had in view than at the beginning. (Irish cheers.) For the amendment, 34; agi!.'hst, 140.

div.head: SOUTH AFRICAN POLICY OF THE _GOVERNMENT.,
div.p: THE SOUTH AFRICAN POLICY OF THE _GOVERNMENT.,

Mr. GORST then moved a fresh amendment expressing regret that Her Majesty's Government should have assumed a formal protectorate over Bechuanaland without taking effectual precautions to prevent Montsioa from being con- quered by freebooters domiciled and organised in the Trans- vaal under the sanction of its government. The amend- ment further expressed regret that, after Her Majesty's Government had received full information of the forcible appropriation of Montsioa's land by the Rooi Grond free- booters, delay, greatly increasing the difficulties of any set- tlement, has been permitted to take place in announcing the intention of the Government to turn out the freebooters, by force if necessary, from the territory under Her Majesty's protection. The hon. member, in an able and temperate speech, supported this thesis by copious extracts from the latest Blue-Book. After some remarks from Mr. Ashley and Sir M. Hicks-Beach, Mr. CHAMBERLAIN summed up the South African policy of the Government in a sentence. "we are," he said, "determined at all hazards to use our whole strength if necessary to maintain the obligations we have undertaken. But in doing that we are also determined to proceed with the assent of our Colonial fellow subjects, and with that of the majority of the Dutch population." Mr. Gorst's amendment was withdrawn, and the Address was • agreed to. On the report stage, Mr. AsnuraD•Barrutrr

div.head: ExAMINEIL SATURDAY, NOVEMBER A, lBB4
div.p: THE ExAMINEIL SATURDAY, NOVEMBER A, lBB4
moved the adjournment till next day. The House adjour. ned at a qaarter to one. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WgnsEsnev.

The House was made at 1240. ORDER OF BUSINESS.—Mr. GLkDSONE immediately moved that the several stages of any bill relating to the re- presentation of the people should have precedence on every day for which they might be set down by the Government. —Sir Jona; Hee moved an amendment excepting Wednes- days from this arrangement.—Sir STAFFORD NORTHCOTE suggested that the Government should have priority for a fortnight only.—Mr. GLADSTONE suggested the whole of November; and the amendment having been withdrawn and a farther amendment negatived, the Premier's motion in this limited form was agreed to. BEEATE ON THE ADDRESS —On the report of the Ad- dress, Mr. BARTLETT moved an amendment praying Her Majesty to direct her Ministers toefficiently support General Gordon in establishing a stable and civilised Govetnment at Khartoum.—Lord E. FITZMAIIRICE Slid it was notorious that this point was pressed on General Gordon in the orig- inal instractions given to him, and from the despatohee re- ceived from Lord Wolseley they knew that the subject was occupying his Lordship's attention in a most remarkable degree. He (Lord Edward Fitzmaurice) thought it was not desirable that a discussion should ba raised on partial information, and he protested against the assumption that the Government only wished to ' withdraw as rapidly as possible from the Soudan.—Sir S. NORTHCOTE thought the instructions te Lord Wolseley were of the loosest kind, and though he did not regard that as an occasion for raising debate on the Egyptian question be did not regret that his hon. friend had introduced the subject.—After some further discussion the amendment Was negatived without a division,—Mr. BIGGAR attempted to raise another discussion on the administration of justice in Ireland, but the SPEAKER ruled him out of order, and the motion that the House do agree with the Committee in the answer to the Address was carried by 134 votes to 18 —The order for the second reading of the Franchise Bill was fixed for next day. THE IRISH POOR LAW.—MR. O'DONNELL SUSPENDED.— The second reading of the Poor Law Guardians (Ireland) Bill was moved by Mr. J. E. REDMOND; who hoped that the fact that the bill had not been printed would not be held to be a fatal objection.—Mr. ELTON, however, moved the ad- journment of the debate; and, after some di.cussion, Mr. CAMPBELL.BANNERMAN, while supporting the main pro- vision of the measure on behalf of the Government, said it was 'difficult to discuss the bill seeing that it woe not printed, and he felt bound to support the motion for the ad- journment of the debate.—Mr. SEXTON denounced "the policy of impeding the progress of the bill by an unworthy technicality."—Mr. O'DONNELL added his protest in terms which led the Speaker to call him to order, and as be per- sisted in addressing the House the SPEAKER first asked him to resume his seat for irrelevancy and then "named " him for disregarding the authority of the Chair.—The PREMIER thereupon moved that Mr. O'Donnell be suspended from the service of the House, and the motion was passed by 163 votes to 28. Mr. O'Doxlmr, then walked out of the House, crying out as he did so, "You are play- ing your expected part, M. le President." Mr. PARNELL accused the Chief Secretary of obstructing the bill under discussion. Mr. GLADSTONE said he should have been glad if the objection had not been taken, but he could not vote against it. On a division the votes were :—For the adjourn- ment, 130 ; against, 97. The debate was therefore adjourned, and the House adjourned at 5-30.

In the division upon Ml7.—O'Donnell's suspension, Sir R Wallace and one or two other Conservatives voted with the Parnellite members in the minority, as did Mr. O'Connor Power, but Dr. Lyons and other Irish members, together with Mr. Warton, voted in the majority with the Govern- ment.

HOUSE OF LORDS.—THOBSDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat upon the woolsack at a quarter past four o'clock. THE DEPRESSION OF TRADE PROPOSED COMMITTEE OF INCEDIRT.—The Earl of DDNRAVEN moved the appoint- ment of a Select Committee, to join with a Committee of the Commons to irquire in'o the condition of the trade and commerce of the country. Lord GRANVILLE opposed the motion. No doubt there was great suffering at pre- sent, but little evidence had been brought forward to show that trade was in the terrible state of depression alleged. The Earl of KIMBERLEY thought nothing cou'd be worse than to institute such an inquiry. The Earl of Harrowby and Lord Carnarvon having spoken, the Marquis of Sams- BURY said the doctrine of setting up countervailing duties as a weapon of defence was getting converts in every quar- ter of the House. He could see no harm in the inquiry, from which our fiscal system, if sound, would emerge the strorger.—The motion was ultimately withdrawn, and the House adjourned until Monday. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—THCRSDAY.

The Speaker took the chair at four o'clock. QU'ESTIONS.— Mr. MoNnErma informed Mr. S. Leighton that there was abundant testimony—and one of his witnes- ses was Mr. Birley, of Manehester—that when properly ap- plied the Education Code would not produce over-pressure. Mr. CAINE brought under the notice of the Attorney-General the electioneering handbill which was circulated in Scarborough last Sunday an- nouncing the capture of General Gordon. THE ATTORNEY•CrENERAL, after hearing an explanation from Sir T. Batesen, said be did not think any evasion of the law was intended, and he pointed out to Mr. Caine that the result of the erroneous statement had not been very disastrous to the Liberal party.
FOREIGN SEWS.
EGYPT ANO THE SC.I.UDA.N

- - A SENSATIONAL CANARD.--ATTACK BY TIE MARDI REPULSED. WED WOI,4ELEY AT DONGOLA. A highly sensational story was published by a Parisian paper on Saturday, and circulated throughout the kingdom on Monday. It was to the effect that the rumours stitch have been current for some days past alleging that General Gordon is a prisoner in the hands of the Mandi are true. An army of from IDO,OOO to 150000 id said to have surrounded Khartoum. Yishling to discontent amongst his garrison, Gordon, after being deserted by the greater portion al his force attempted to effect a junction with the relief expedi- tion:but only General Stewart succeeded in escaping the hostile Arabs, who everywhere lined the banke of the Niler and when, after reaching Berber. Gordon tried to return te Khartoum he was captured. The reference made by Lord Harlington to this canard will be seen in our Parliamentary news.

• ThrIIBEH (VOL DONGOLA). SllNDAY.—Crerdon attacked the rebels at Anderman who a notate or twelve vessel. includ- ing steamers. The engagement lasted 45 hours. _L 7ro antra 25,000 of the rebels, and they had four Krupp guns. One burst. They retreated, leaving enormous numbers of dead behind them. The fugitives retired to Markeat, but were retumlig with an additional force. Obeid was taken by the powerful Takata tribes, who are mortal enemies of thefts,- garas and the Mandi. The prestige•of the Mandi is waning in the country between here and Obeid, many merchants Passing through this place. The English forces will meet with no resistance in going to Khartoum, but if the rebels are not punished and intimidated for Colonel Stewart's mur- der they will close round in thousands from west, east, and eonth.—Daily News. DONGOLA, 817NDAY.—The Mabdi is reported to have been lately at Khartoum, and to have summoned General Gordon to surrender. The reply of the General was that he would hold Khartoum against the Mandi for 12 years. After re- ceiving this answer, it is stated that the Mandi retired south- wards for a distance of a day's journey. DONGOLA, MONDAY.—Lord Wolseley arrived by steamer this afternoon. He was received by Sir Herbert Stewart, Sir Charles Wilson, and a guard of honour of the Mounted Infantry, the Sussex Regiment, and the native troops. Major Slade informed the Mudir of the-arrival of Lord Wolseley, and o ,nducted him on board. Lord Wolseley subsequently visited the Madir at the Mudirie, the troops lining the roads. I returned to-day from Debbah for the occasion. The Mandi's forces are 30,000 strong, with 2,000 horsemen. When at Handak a messenger came from General Gordon to Abda Kad r, the distinguished Englishmen and soi-elistant Morocco merchant. His message was:—'• It will be very difficalt for you to come. Bagara everywhere between this place and Debbah:' Abdel Kadir sent back the messenger to procure a email boat to wait a little below Khartoum, paying 30 dollars. He purposes leaving in 20 days, or when he hears the boat is ready.—Daily News. Donaote, MONDAY.—Farther confirmation has been received here of the disaster to the steamer conveying the unfortunate Colonel Stewart. Colonel Stewart and some of his party were enticed on shore unarmed, and murdered. The whole party on the steamer numbered 54 persons, of whom 38 were killed. The prisoners and papers were sent to Berber. The Mandi's forces had been collecting around Khartoum, and the Mandi was again sent to General Gordon summoning him to surrender. General Gordon sent back the answer„" Not for ten years."—Standard. WADY HAMA, SATE:RD/Mt.—Eighty tons of provisions for the whale boats are being sent to Sarras daily. The Canadians are awaiting the arrival of more whale boats, having passed all those over the rapids which have already reached this place. A detachment of Engineers sailed to- day in whale boats from Gemai to Sarras, the journey occu- pying four hours. These are the first troops which have used the new boats.

WADY Haute, MONDAY.—Colonel Alleyne arrived at Dal to-day with his advanced force. The journey from Sarras was accomplished in three days and a half. All the boats carrying two and a half lons each made their way through the Cataracts without unloading. The Khedive's yacht Ferooz arrived here to•day with 120 men of the Guards' division of the Camel Corps, under the command of Colonel Rowley, and 18 whale boats, containing one company of the 2nd Battalion of the Essex Regiment. Cam, SATIIRDAY.—TWO despatches had been received from Major Kitchener, reporting that the rebels had made an attack upon Khartoum, but that Gesteral Gordon had made a sortie, had driven back the enemy, and had cap- tured a large quantity of corn. News to the same effect has been breught to Snakim by the son of a friendly shiekh a few days ago. General Wolseley has arrived at Dongola. Colonel Golborne, the correspondent of the Daily News, has died at Dongola. Sir Evelyn Baring has received the fol- lowing telegram from Sir Charles Wilson, dated Ambukol, Oct. 31st:—" Three men, when forty days' journey from Khartoum, saw Colonel Stewart's steamer wrecked near the Wady Garna Cataract. They saw Colonel Stewart, Mr. Power, and M. Herbin, French Consul at Khartoum, on board. General Gordon's steamer bad visited the province of Sennaar, when it had brought back 50,000 ardebs of grain." A confirmation of this Sennaar news has bean received via Suakim by the British authorities here. ALEXANDRIA, SATURDAY.—Messengers from Kabbish tribes report that the MaLdi had attacked Gordon', outposts at Anduraman, near Khartoum, and had been repulsed wftb. heavy loss ALEXANDRA, MONDAY.—Unconfirmed lIIInOIIIs are cur- rent here of a serious disaster to two officers aad a company of English soldiers beyond Dongola. THE REPORTED CAPTURE OF GORDON.—TELE- GRAM FROM LORD WOLSELEY.

Canto, TuEsnay.—ln reply to Sir Evelyn Baring's in- quiry concerning the truth of the rumours of the fall of Khartoum, Lord Wolseley has telegraphed from Dongola, under yesterday's date:—" Major Kitchener telegraphs to Sir Charles Wilson that he saw a certain Ibrahim Wadbeel, who recently arrived from the Arabs some distance south. This man reported that all WAS quiet, and that when General Gordon received our messenger be fired a salute and held a parade of troops. Both the British and Foreign Consuls at Khartoum were with Colonel Stewart. M. Nicola is sup- posed to have remained behind in the boat and to be there- fore site. A second telegram from Major Kitchener, dated Sunday, announces that Haji Abdallah has arrived from Wady Garna, and stated that a man from Shendy reported that the Mandi came with a strong force to Omdurman, and asked General Gordon to surrender. Gorden replied that he would hold Khartoum for 12 years. The Mandi then re- tired without lighting to Emmek, one days' journey south of Khartoum, and 12 hours' journey from the river He then gave out that be would not fight for another two months. Many of his followers left him. Sidel Hassan, who is an important personage, sent word from Kassala to General Gordon that he would soon come and help him. Sheikh Saila, son of Hameln Pasha Khalifa, has written a letter to the Robatat tribe, offering them peace if they will come in. Mahomed El Kheir is still the Mandi's Ameer at Berb,r, but the people are afraid of General Gordon. The read to Khar- toum ie not open, excepting by way of Metemneh, and there the Mabdi's men come in during the night." CAIRO, TITESDAY.—CoIoneI Freemantle wires that 400 rebels attacked the Suakim railway this morning. The Egyptian Cavalry pursued them fire miles and behaved well. One man was wounded.

DONGOLA, WEDNESDAY.—Lord Wolseley hag reviewed the Royal Sussex Regiment and the Mounted Infantry, and has expressed himself much pleased with the appearance of the troops. After the review a sham fight was held. The camels are rapidly becoming accustomed to military move- ments, and stand fire well

ADEN, Ocrouaa 22.—H.M.5. Philomel has captured a dhow with 150 slaves on board, which will be brought here.

SAIGON, WEDNESDAY.—The transport Saone is about CO sail for Kelung with all the war materill asked for by Admiral Ceurbet. SHANGHAI, TsunsnAv.—The Chinese Council of State has failed in its attempt to arrange a peaceable settlement with France It is reported that the Chinese Government has insisted upon Li Hung Chang's attendance at Pekin. THE CHOLERA. _
Moms, WEDNESDAY Nom—There have been 13 cases of cholera and six deaths here during the last twenty-four hours.

BizaraN, MONDAY.—The Congo Conference will be defi- nitely opened on the 15th mat, but the Plenipotentiaries will meet On the 13th List. for an informal preliminary discussicn. On the 19th inst. the actual deliberations of the Conference will commence, when Prince Bismarck will preside. THE GERMAN ELECTIONS.
