WINNIPEG, SUNDAY.—A mob of three thousanC persons has hanged and burned an effigy et Mr. Miller, Attorney- General of Manitoba, because he ordered a prisoner to be flogged who had attempted to escape Mr. Jolro Nor. quay, the Premier, has promised to, consider the demand for the dismissal of Mr. Miller, and to give an. rammer in two days. Great excitement pre7aile, and the traops have been called out, but no collision with the people has occurred.

Touowo, Subrnay.— The police force sent from here to Micidpienlerr were tiled at goon after landing. They charged the rioters, a number of whom they arrested. The police are now returning here, special corstables having been sworn in to preserve the peace at Michipicolen._

div.head: ERLECIIISE BILL.
div.p: THE ERLECIIISE BILL.

In moving the second reading of the Franchise Bill, Mr. GLADSTONE said the question had been fully discussed. and should the host le.motion which appeared on the paper some days ago be revived he thought it would be an abuse of the time and the patience of the House to discuss it in detail. It was known from the former declarations of the Govern- ment how entirely impossible it was for them to consent either to the union of the two subjects of the franchise and redistribution in a 'single bill or to their simultaneous treatment in two bills. The majority of the House would lose the control entirely were they to consent to either of these courses. After deprecating the interpretation which had been put by certain persons on his words of warning to the Peers, the right hon. gentleman said the franchise question was one of great simplicity, while the question of redistribution was one of great complexity. Any measure of redistribution that must give a hope of per- manent settlement must be a large one, and must give due consideration to the question of population as compared with that of elec- toral area. Further, it must be equitable and liberal as between the three great divisions of the country, and not of a needlessly complex character. Beyond this it ought to be just to the different classes of the community. There was, he held, much room for mutual sacrifice and arrangement. Many questions would arise as to what distinctions should be drawn as between the community and the individual, be- tween urban and rural populations, and so forth, but on many of these points regard ought to be had to the pries- pects of harmony and peace,and the prospect of creating a contented and satisfied feeling in the.community. It was, in his opinion, impossible to pass a measure of redistribu- tion that should not on the whole be favourable to the popular will. If it were true that there was a general desire for redistribution on the other side of the House that desire ought to be treated with due consideration, and the Government were in hopes that there would be a disposition in the House to enable the work to be done thoroughly. He believed that the more speedily it was accomplished the better would it be for the vast issues involved.—Mr. E. STANHOPE (iii the absence, through domestic affliction, of Lord It. Churchill) moved that in the opinion of the House ally measure purporting to provide for the batter representation of the people must be accompanied by provisions for a proper arrangement of electoral areas. He said he was unable to detect in the Premier's speech any symptom of a desire to meet the reasonable proposals of the Conservative party. In reply to the allegation that the country had decided against the Opposition, he said the only way of settlement provided by the constitution was an appeal to the constituencies, which the Liberal party desired to avoid. Mr. ECROYD seconded the amendment.—Mr. GORST thought that on a question of procedure, which this was in reality, the minority should yield to the majority. As to the introduction of a Redistribution Bill. the Government were as solemnly pledged on that point as they possibly could be, and if they wanted to manipulate seats for their own advantage it was a task they could not perform. To reject the bill would be making enemies of the new voters. —The debate, which was a very protracted one, was con- tinued by Mr. Arthur Arnold, the Lord Mayor, Mr. Grantham, Lord G. Hamilton, and Mr. Shield, &c., and on the motion of Sir R. Cnoss, it was adjourned.

The Bishop of MANCHESTER on Wednesday began his quadrennial visitation of the clergy of his diocese. In his charge--delivered after morning service at the Cathedral— his Lordship gave some interesting statistics of the progress of Church work in the diocese during the period of his episcopate, and also dwelt upon a variety of ecclesiastical topics. VICTORIA UNIVERSITY.—At a meeting of the Court of the Victoria University, held on Wednesday at the Owen's Col- lege, the application of the University College, Liverpool, to be admitted as a college in the University was discussed.— On the motion of Lord Winmarleigh, seconded by the Bis- hop of Manchester, the Court accepted the application of the University College, Liverpool. WIFE MURDER AT COLLYHURST.—An inquest was held on Wednesday on the body of Ellen Shaw, late of Dalton- street, Collyhurst, whose husband is in custody on a charge of having murdered her by strangulation. The evi- dence showed that the wife, who had periodical fits of drink- ing, was frequently subjected to ill-usage by her hus- band, against whom the jury returned a verdict of wilful murder. A MANCHESTER MANSLAUGHTER CASE.—At the Man- chester Assizes, on Wednesday, Charles Blanchfield, a shoemaker, aged 66, was indicted for the wilful murder of his wife, Dorinda, in Manchester, on 21st Aug. last. In the course of a quarrel the prisoner stabbed his wife with one of his knives, and she died in a few moments. The jury reduced the offence to manslaughter, and the prisoner was sentenced to 15 years' penal servitude. THE BOLTON MURDER.—At the Manchester Assizes, on I Tuesday, Kay Howarth, of Bolton, was indicted for the wilful murder of Richard Dugdale, commercial traveller. at Bolton, on October 3rd. The two men had been drinking together, and subsequently Dugdale was discovered mur- dered and robbed. Neat morning the prisoner was ap- prehended and was found in possession of the murdered man's property. He was found guilty and sentenced to death.

div.head: KILLED AND SEVERAL INJURED.
div.p: KILLED AND SEVERAL INJURED.

BOMBAY, SllNDAY.—Serious disturbances between the Arats and the police occurred at Hyderabad during the celebration of the Mohurrum Festival. Eleven of the police were killed, and several wounded. The Arabs looted the police stations and pillaged some houses, causing a panic in the city, were all the shops and houses were closed. The NizAm, with great promptitude, summoned troops from Golconda. The Arabs then dispersed, and order is now restored. A Council was subsequently held, at which the Nizain was present, and a committee of inquiry was ap- pointed. THE UNITED STATES.

div.head: NEW SOUTEI 'WALES.
div.p: NEW SOUTEI 'WALES.

SYDNEY, SATEDDAY.—Parliament was prorogued to-day, afters twelvemonths' session, which has been unprecedented for the number and importance of the measures passed. Lord Loftus, the Governor, announced that during the session 300 miles of new railway lines had been opened, making 1,600 miles now open for traffic, and that nearly 400 miles were in course of construction, besides 1,278 miles author. bed by Parliament. The revenue of the colony was in a flourishing condition, and the mining pros.pects were most satisfactory. His Excellency especially alluded to the discovery of numerous rich silver lodes in the north- western districts, and of a valuable diamond-bearing coun- try, as well as fresh fields of tin and copper.

div.head: PRESCOT.
div.p: PRESCOT.

DESERTION OF A FAMILY.-John Twohey was summoned at the Prescot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, for neglecting his family, whereby they became chargeable to the Prescot Union. Mr. S. H. Hartley (clerk to the Guardians) stated that the defendant's family were chargeable to the Union for about three months, and were relieved at a cost of £lO 4s. 6d. The man was apprehended in July last, but the I Guardians gave him an opportunity to pay the money and ' the case was adjourned for three months. Since then the man had only paid 18s , but the Guardians wished to give the man another chance of paying the difference.—The case was adjourned for a month. THEFT OF A RABBlT—Before Messrs. Earle and Willie, at the Prescot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, Henry Newton I and Thomas Brophy, two old offende,s, were charged with ' stealing a tame rabbit, value is, the property of Jas. Rylance. I Prosecutor keeps the Beehive beerhouse, Kemble-street, Prescot, and on the 24th ult. the two prisoners entered. They subsequently went into the back-yard where the rab- bit was kept, and on their return they had seme drink. They then went out, and shortly afterwards the rabbit was missed. The men were followed and were found in another I public-house with the rabbit in their possession.—The I prisoners alleged that they picked the rabbit up in the road- I way adjoining the Beehive beerhouse.—Newton, who had ! been 25 times previously cmvicted, was fined 20s. and costs, or in default 14 days imprisonment; and Brophy, who bad I 12 previous convictions recorded against him, was fined 10a. and costs, or 7 days imprsonment. PRESCOT BOARD.—The monthly meeting was ' held on Tuesday forenoon, when there were present : I Messrs. W. L. Evans (chairman), J. Leatherbarrow, Willis, E. Tyrer, H. Cross (clerk), W. Goldsworth (surveyor), and I W. Goldswortb, jun. (assistant surveyer).--The Bridge over the Railway at lrhiston.—Mr. Cross submitted an agreement between that Board and the London and North- Western Railway Company respecting the re-construction of Platt's Bridge at Wnieton. He explained that for the present the company were desirous only of erecting a tern. I porary bridge.—The Chairman said the Board should see the , rail way company did not use any temporary bridge as a per- I manent one, and the Board adopted the agreement.--The Expenditure.—The surveyor's statement of expenditure fer , the four weeks ending October 30th showed the following totals:—Bold, £l5 31; Knowsley, £6 14s : Rainhill, £8 16s 41 ; Whiston, £l3 63; team labour, £l2; new ma- terials. £25 3s id; incidentals, £3 3s 81; total, £B4 6s ld. —Claim against the Board.—The Clerk read another letter from Mr. Tyrer, solicitor, St. Helens, on behalf of Mr. Joseph Frith, farmer, Whiston, asking the Board to re- consider the claim for damage done to Mr. Frith's crops by the bursting of a sewer. The Board at one time admitted that damage had been done but for want of particulars they were unable to estimate the extent of the damage.—The Chairman expressed the opinion that the Board had never admitted their liability, although they had been quite will. lug to do something towards it with the Rural Sanitary Authority.—Mr. Leatherbarrow said they had given Mr. Frith to understand he might expect something.-The Chair- man said be had made two exorbitant claims.—After some further discussion, Mr. Leatberbarrow moved that the Board pay one-third of £lO towards the damage.—Mr. Tyrer seconded the motion, which was agreed to.--There was no other business of interest. PRESCOT LOCAL BOARD.—At the monthly meeting of this Board, on Wednesday evening, there were present— Messes. Spenceley (chairman), Fogg, Prest3n, Whitfield' Hatton, Goldsworth (surveyor). Cross (clerk), and Dickin- son (nui.ance inspector.)—A New Rate : On the motion of Mr. Fogg, seconded by Mr. Preston, it was resolved that the rate for the ensuing half year be la Oct in the £ Death at the Hospital : The medical officer's monthly re- port stated that there had been a death at the Netherfield- road hospital, and the funeral expenses amounted to 123. The health of the town was satisfactory. After some , conversation the Board resolved that the funeral expenses I account should be paid.—Alteration of a Street Name : Mr. James Berry, of Holly Bank, forwarded to the Board a me- meriel having reference to the naming of a road running from the Crown Hotel to the railway station. The memo- rialists suggested that the resolution passed at the last meeting of the Board naming the road Rigby-street should be rescinded, and Queen's-road or Cambridge-road sub- stituted as its name. They also suggested that the Board , should take steps for planting forest trees on eaeh side of the road, and thus improve the appearance of the principal I and main entrance to the town. Among the signatures to ! the requision were those of Mr. W. L. Evans, J.P., Rev. H. A. Macnaughton, Messrs. W. Tyrer, C. B. Jackson, dm A long discussion on the subject took place, Mr. Hatton ex- pressed the opinion that Rigby-street was as good a name as could be given to it.—Mr. Preston ultimately gave notice that at the next meeting he would move that the resolution naming the road Rigby-street be rescinded, and that the road he called Victoria-road.—The question of planting trees along the road TM left over for further consideration. Births and Deaths : The Registrar's monthly report showed that the deaths during the month of October had been Prescot 5, Eccleston 0; corresponding month last year ; Presoot 5, Eccleston 1; the death-rate being 9.34, against 112 in the earns month last year. The births were: Prescot 14, Eccleston 3, total 17; and the numbers were exactly the same in the corresponding month of last year.—This was the principal busineas. RURAL SANITARY- ATITHORTTY.—A meeting of the Pres- cot Rural Sanitary Authority was held at the Whiston Workhouse on Thursday forenoon, when there were present: Mr. J. Leatherbarrow (in the chair), the Rev. T. Chambers, Messrs. W. A. Meadows, J. B. Longton, W. Newsome, I'.l Eatock, and S. H. Hartley (clerk).—A. letter was read from the Local Government Board, dated the 11th ult., stating that with reference to the application of the Rural Sanitary Authority of the Prescot Union for sanction to borrow a loan of £1272 for the purchase of land as a site for the erec- tion of a hospital for infectious diseases; the Local Govern- ment Board would proceed to direct the local inquiry to be held on the subject by one of their inspectors. The inquiry would take place as soon as the other engagements of the inspectors would permit, and due notice of it would be given.—The Local Government Board wrote stating that with reference to the sewerage of Eccleston they wished to be informed what course the Rural Sanitary Authority had determined to adopt with regard to the question.—The Chairman remarked that instructions had been given to get in the quantities and prices, but they had not yet been re- ceived.—The Clerk stated a sketch and plan had been sent to the Local:Government Board, as had been requested.— The Medical Officer of Health (Dr. Hall) reported that the cases of diphtheria at Halewood were confined to one house. He mentioned in his last report that he suspected the water I to be the cause of the disease, and Dr. Campbell Brown's re- port of theemalysis justified him in that supposition. He had, therefore, to ask that orders might be at once sent to Mr. Neilson to supply a purer water. There bad been two isolated cases of fever in the district since his last report, but there was nettling special to report upon. Disinfection had been carried out in the usual way. The deaths returns were as follows: Bold, 00 per 1,000; Ditton, 0.7 ; Ecclesten, 2.5 ; Hale, 87 ; Halewood, 26; Knowsley, 16; Reinhill, 1-3; Speke, 00 ; Tarbock, 3 1 ; Whiston, 0 9 ; Windle, 2 1 Mr. John Twist (surveyor) reported that a sample of water from Neil's well at Halewood, the site of the late outbreak of diphtheria, has been sabmitted to Dr. C. Brown for analysis, and he reported it as being "very impure and not good for domestic use." The well was a shallow one, and might not be as fully protected from Soakage as it might be. —The Rev. T. Chambers drew attention to exaggerated re- ports which had appeared in the Liverpool papers with re- gard to the outbreak of diphtheria at Halewood, and ex- pressed the hope that the Frees would be more careful in future in regard to the insertion of such exaggerated state- ments.—This was the principal business.

THE PRINCE AND PRINCESS OF WALES arrived at Wy. combe shortly after six p.m. on Tuesday evening, and drove to Wycombe Abbey on a visit to Lord and Lady Carring• ton. The Royal visitors were enthusiastically welcomed, the town being on fete. The visit extends to Thursday evening. THE FENIAN CONSPIRACY.—Frederiolt J. Allen, clerk in the Freeman's Journal office, was remanded at Dublin on Monday, charged with being concerned in a treasonable conspiracy. The Crown has secured some documentary evidence in the handwriting of the prisoner, showing that the Fenian conspiracy is still active, having its head-quar- ters at Paris. In Dublin, on Tuesday, Allen was again re- mended charged with treason-felony. A difficulty has arisen in reference to obtaining a specimen of the acknowledged writing of the accused, in order to prove from it that the Paris documents were written by him,

div.head: NATIONAL LIBERAL CLUB. V.2I7NDATION STONE LAYING BY MR.
div.p: THE NATIONAL LIBERAL CLUB. V.2I7NDATION STONE LAYING BY MR.
GLADSTONE.

The foundation Mona Of the new premises about to le erect eel at the junction of Whitehell-p'ace and the Thames Embachment was laid by Mr. Glads'one on Tuesday, id the presence of street 3,000 persons, including many leading members et the Government and of both Houses of Parlia- ment. Theme, club, it is stated, will be the I trgest of the kind in the trerld, and when complete will, it is estimate, afford accommedation for 8,000 members. The proceedinge were presided weer by the Earl of Derby, who is chairman of the Building Chmpeny, which hes been formed for the special purpose of erecting the new club house. Mr. Glad- stone, on his arrivake was reteivel with great enthusiasm, as were the other members of the Government present. When the cheering heel, subsideir The CHAIRMAN said he believed that the building they had met to inaugrate would be not only an ornament to that part at London, brie would forma- a valuable headquar- ters for that great politicrie connection which they repre- sented, and which be believed was never stronger, more numerous, and more unite& (Cheers.) The want of a club of this iind had been Ring felt. They Lad already between 4,ooCsand 5,000 members, ie meetly resident in the country, and he had no doubewhen they opened their new building they would have the 8000• members it was esti- mated it wouldaccommodate. (Cheers.) Hlebelieved they were the largest institution of the kind in England, and perhaps in Europe. (Cheers.) He did not propose to de- tain them longer, except to say that he thought they were very much indebted to their opponents. (Laughter.) They had played the game for the Liberals better than they could have done it for themselves. (Hear, hear.) The only fault he could find with them was that their policy was too Radical for his taste. (Laughter and cheers.) They had got as institution which they declared they were devoted to, and yet the Conservative petty were prepared certaiely to weaken and possibly imperil it for the Bike of an imme- diate party gain, which would not be very considerable even if they secured it. (Cheers.) He concluded by call- ing upon the Prime Minister. Mr. GLADSTONE advanced to the stone,which having care- fully adjusted and laid, he, amid loud cheers, returned to his position on the right of the Chairman. He then said: —My Lord Derby, my lords, ladies, and gentlemen,—Yon have very highly honoured me by requesting me to lay the foundation stone of this club. (Cheers.) Speaking generally,l should say there conld not be a less interesting occasion than laying the foundation stone of a club in Lon- don; for, after all, what are the clubs of Lonaon ? I am afraid little else than mere temples of luxury and ease. (Hear, hear.) This, however, is a club of a very different character—(hear, hear);—a club that contemplates practical patriotic objects—(hear, bear) ;—a club which, as we have been told in most happy phrase, is to supply a 'political exchange" for the Liberals of this country. At this time in particular, but, indeed, at all times, it is a matter Of ex- treme interest to consider what must be the work and the function of such a club as this. It is obvious it is for the maintenance, for the interchange, for the propagation, for the consolidation of Liberal principles. (Cheers.) What, gentlemen, are Liberal principles, and what part have they played, and will they play, in the public life of this country? (Hear, hear.) Well, if we go back to the period before the great Reform Bill, when the principle of repro. sentation was but imperfectly developed, you find that there had been an almost unbroken term of fifty years of Tory Government, and the consequence was that our trade was crippled, our people were in many cases but half-fed, while our Criminal Code was so cruel as to be a disgrace to the world. (Hear, hear.) The access to institutions was bar- red and narrowed by religious tests, and, in fact, gentle- men,l should detain you too long were I to go over the dreary lists of all those abuses which have found for suc- ceeding Parliaments so much noble and necessary work. (Cheers.) Then, gentlemen, Came the Reform Hip, and I ask you to consider how great is the contrast between the history of the last half century and the half century that preceded. (Hear, hear.) But I measure, gentlemen, from the present day, and, speaking for a moment of the present,! join in the congratulations which the Chairman has offered you on the condition of the Liberal party. But I join also in his astonishment and seeming regret that the policy of his opponents has been what is called playing into our hands, but so playing into our hands as to carry the prospects and possibilities of change far beyond what we, as Ministers, have proposed or desired. (Cheers.) I will endeavour to supply one illustration. I take the case of the agricultural labourer. What is the agricultural labourer of this coutitry but a man belonging to a class which, beyond all other classes, is subjected to the influences that are termed and believed to be Conservative? He is the man on whose enfranchisement the Tory party, if it had really had the courage of its opinions, ought to have looked with warmth and favour. (Hear, hear.) But instead of that, by pronouncing through some of its members positive sentences of aversion and contempt for the political enfranchisement of those men, and in general by hampering and obstructing —we are not allowed to say rejecting, but by causing to fail —the bill for their enfranchisement, they have in the teeth of their own obvious party interests done everything they could, and! believe they have done it with no small effect, to drive the agricultural labourer into our arms openly. (Cheers.) Look at the foundation that the Liberal party has among the masses of the people. Its principles and its position are not like that undulating canvass which jest now severs us from the weather without. (Hear, hear.) They are like that solid and massive stone I which it has been permitted to me this day to I lay. (Cheers.) What has happened on the very spot where we stand. Whilst 550 artisans of London, representing what may be called, perhaps, the higher stratum of the skilled labourers of the country, chosen for their efficiency in their work, and chosen without the smallest reference to politics—amongst those 550 men arose, in connection with my own little worthy name, a de- sire to give some manifestation of their feelings in regard to the great.crisis of that day, and I am told that out ot those 550 much more than 500 have spontaneously tendered their subscriptions to show what are their convictions and their desires in respect to the progress and power of the Liberal party. Is it possible, gentlemen, for you to have a more signal and striking proof of the breadth, and the depth, and the solidity of those fenndations upon which, as a political power, ass factor in the public life of the nation, you have taken your stand and are prepared to do your work? (Cheers.) Gentlemen, the House of Commons, at this moment has connected with it, not a single, but a double work of reform. There is a reform without in the large and vast extension of the constituency which will add,l believe, so much to its ierength and the security of the country. (Cheers.) But there is also the not less important work of reform within—(cheers)—for that honourable Assembly, "the first deliberative assembly in the world," is now doomed to see its efficiency impaired and its dignity destroyed by the advantage which its own too generous rules have ena- bled individuals and sections to take, efli that the House I Itself has become the slave of these individuals and sections —(hear, hear,)—and nothing can relieve it of that slavery except a great and drastic change in the form of its proce- dure. (Cheers.) To every one of yen, gentlemen, hardly less than to the great question of the franchise and what is immediately connected with it,! commend the consideration of that subject which is not less pressing—(hear,hear)—than any constitutional question that has ever been brought before this country. (Cheers.) Well, now, we met nearly a fort- night ago, as we were told, "to consider the Franchise Bill." And yet, with the exception of a preliminary stage effected after midnight, we have not been permitted to touch that work. (Cries of "Shame.") We are still at the mercy of Mr. B and Mr. C, who moves upon the Address to the Crown his amendment, and his amendment, and no one can.tell even now when we shall be permitted, in con- sequence of this astounding condition of the rules of our procedure, and of that advantage now for the first time taken of them, to get to our proper work. (Cries of "Shame.") Never mind. It is most inconvenient, per- plexing, and,! might almost say, afflicting to many of those who have to attend on these weary nights—(hear, beer).— and to exhaust the time which must be passed through tilt we come to our proper business. But, I say, never mind. There is strength enough in this self-governing country— (cheers)—to rectify that, and all other mischiefs. All that is wanted is that it should become sufficiently notorious (Cheers.) Those who are now holding us back and forbid- ding us to do the work for which the Sovereign summoned us together, are doing their best to make the matter so deeply felt that, though they may somewhat postpone the applica- tion of the remedy, the security goes on strengthening from day to day that when that remedy comes it should be effec- tive—(cheers)— i and your representation n Parliament shall be restored ti something like its original power and dignity —(hear, hear)—and shall be put into a condition to do the business of the country. (Renewed cheering.) Now, gentle. men, as to the Liberal party. Just let me ask you to forecast what it is likely to be from an impartial consideration of what it has been. I am not now going to dwell upon dis- putable matters of opinion. I am going into the region of facts. I wish you to see what has been the position. of the party; during the last 50 years, and from that .position to form in your own minds an estimate of what will be its probable position during the fifty that are next to come. That is the answer to the question which I put to you— what is to be the work and the function of this club ? The function of this club is to ho to assist the working of the body by which, in the main, the great achievements .of the last fifty years have been accomplished, and to realise the promise that the near future holds out of cur longings and our expectations. Since the first Reform Bill,see what a change the introduction of a fuller application of the representa- tive principle has had. It has led to a period during which the general rule has not been Tory domination, bat Liberal pre- ponderance. Fifty-two years, gentlemen, have passed since the Reform Act. Fer 36 out of these 52 years Governments avowedly Liberal have been in power. That is a proportion of considerably more than two to one. Gentlemen,—That does not state the whole case, for Conservative Governments, through good sense or political expediency or otherwise, have often been the organs of Liberal opinions and the champions of Liberal measures. (Hear, hear.) Sixteen years have been nominally given to Toryism. But Sir Robert Peel was in power for a few months in 1834-5, and these few months were devoted to bringing before Parliament a series of measures distinctly liberal in their character. He was in power again from 1841 to 1846, and while I might quote many other instances, I stand simply upon this, that the whole history of that Government was a history of per- severing efforts to deal with what was the most crying afflic- tions of all to our interests, namely, the restrictive commer- cial system of the country, to relax our tariffs, to set free our trade, and finally to overthrow the lenge fabric of the Corn Laws. (Cheers.) In the same way the Conservative Government in 1866, which retainedpower for *years, was

Iphielly signalised as the Government which first propoun- ded the principle of household suffrage which we are now endeavouring to consunernale and to carry throughout the whole length and breadth of the country. Putting together the cue of these three • Governments, which occupied :wither eight years, and adding together these to the 3id years of tioYernments avowedly Liberal, that makes 44 oat of 52 years during which Liberal principles have been the dominating power guiding the legislation of the country. (Cheers.) Is H likely, gentlemen that that state of things which has marked the last half century will be altered in the half cestury to come ? (Cries of "No.") What era& it that brought in Liberal power and predominance? It was the acknowledgment of the repre- sentative system by the Reform Act, which to the full ' acknowledged the prixeiple, though the application wag partial. Well, but if the acknowledgment of that ptin- oiple brought in Liberal preponderence, leek you whether you auppose that the great extension of that principle, reducing it to something like universality and eonsie- tency, le likely or is not likely to give increased oppor- tunby /cr the application of Liberal prictiplee, and to. secure in all likelihood a not less marked Pre- ponderer:ma of Liberal power and Liberal administration in the Gcrearnment of the future? (Cheers.) It it there. gentlemen, that I say that we stand on the solid around of fact, not the ground of speculationeand looking back ta what hes happened during the lifetime of the oldeet among as, } will endeavour to anticipate upon that solid ground of fact,. and by the date which experience nupplies those future re- sults of which we can only say that they are still in ex- pectation, but that they are not beyond the reach ofm- tional and probable forecast. Then, again, I congratulate you who are for tong years to come the representatives of a great cause, for this cause, though it is defended and pro- moted by a partya is something much more than the cause- of a party—(cheers)—and there aaain I stand on the- ground, I think, cf -universal confession. Who denies tbat the legislation of the last half century has been in general Liberal legislationeand who denies that that Liberal legis- latien has been beneficial to the country at large. (Re- newed cheers.) Well then, gentlemen, in stedying the in- terests of your party you are studying wider and nobler in- terests. It has been given you to do this work on the part of the whole of your fellow-countrymen. (Cheers.) Cherish that noble idea. Endeavour to choose let attaining ycur great ends means which are marked not by, selfishness, but by breadth, foresight, and confidence in the greatness and high destinies of the empire, and take it to yourselves, for the highest of all honours, that to subserve those destinies, to have promoted them, as you and your preueceseors Lava promoted them, and to stand, in fact, upon go wide a ground is the object you will profess to yourselves, for, rely upon it, there is nothing that can render a political party so illustrious as to stand upon the ground, to defend the ground, to maintain it and keep it safe from every foe, the ground that belongs to the nation that has such national characteristics as natienal welfare and national happiness ior its great distinction. (Loud cheers.) Earl GRANVILLE said he was not quite clear in what capacity he was called upon to address them, but be- thought In that company he could not assume to represent the whole of the House of Lords, but only a large minority. the large t that in a party quest,on had ever there sup- ported Mr. Gladstonee policy up to the present time. He had no hesitation in saying that a very few months ago the Heave of Lords had a very fair share of respect and popu- larity amongst the people of this country. (Hear, hear.) He was not without hope that, notwithstanding an act of nnwisdom perpetrated last summer, and again threatened to be repeated, statemanship and common sense might put him in a position not very long hence to hold the same opinions in public with regard to that ancient institution. (Hear, hear.) Speaking as the Foreign Secretary, he might say that they had had to deal with many onerous legacies be- queathed to them by their predecessors which have taxed their powers to the greatest extent. 'Questions had risen in rapid succession in which every course they could adopt was open not only to plausible, but even reasonable objec- tion. These openings for criticism had been largely ex- ercised by their Conservative opponents, and they would no doubt have notioed how passionate was the love of the Conservative party as well for the Franchise Bill, if it was not overshadowed by their still greater love for redistribution. (A laugh.) During all this time they had heard regrets that Lord Beaconsfield and Lord Palmerston were not alive. He wished, in the face of this autumn session, Lord Beaconsfield could return, and he was sure that Lord Palmerston's foreign policy was condemned quite as severely as had been that of Mr. Gladstone's Government. (Hear, hear.) He did not comulain of the interest which people took in our outside relations. He did not complain of the Opposition. (Hear, hear.) But if they went beyond the legitimate limits of opposition for the sake of party, then he was sure it would be the aggressor who would lose, and not those against whom the attacks were directed. (Cheers.) The Marquis of HARTINGTON, in moving a vote of thanks to the Premier, said it was scarcely twelve hours since Mr. Gladstone was in his place and vainly attempted to induce the Irish members to believe that indiscriminate ravings were not the hest plan to secure that equality to Ireland which they professed to have so mach at heart. In a short time Mr. Gladstone would be again in his place, and he thought they would agree with him that some repose was needed by a man filling the not sinecure post of Premier and leader of the House of Commoas. It had been cynically said that this new club was to be the home of the caucus; and if that were so there would be nothing te regret in the fact, for if it were true that domicile had influence on the nature of the most savage animal, then it might so happen that the caucus would become civilised by its change from Birmingham to London, (Laughter.) Mr. CHAMBERLAIN seconded the resolution. From time to time, he said, the Liberal party had made an indignant protest, and the Lords had reluctantly given way, but now they were told they would stand firm and risk their position, and stake their existence on a throw. He confessed their proceedings filled him with hope and confidence—(cheers)— for if they were bent upon doing this they might yet see an advance which he had never dared to anticipate towards that real self-government upon which he believed depended the happiness and welfare of all classes in the community. (Cheers.)

The vote of thanks having been passed, Mr. GLInsToNz briefly replied. Sir WILLIAM Malcolm moved a vote of thanks to the Chairman, and said he claimed with the noble lord to be a moderate man, but it was exactly the moderate men in these days who had occasion to be alarmed at consequences of the violent measures of intemperate Tories. (Laughter and cheers.) Sir CHARLES DILRE secmded the motion, which was car- ried and badly acknowledged by the CHAIRMAN (Lord Derby. This concluded the business of the meeting, and Mr. Gladstone was subs.quently presented with an address from 55t) wotking.men on a neighbouring building. In replying, he said he hoped he would be able to bring the great contest in which they were engaged to a triumphant consummation by those constitutional methods which were traditional with the English people.
PANIC IN A GLA.SiIOW THEATRE. FOURTEEN PERSONS KILLED.

A panic, attended with most disastrous results, occurred on Saturday in the New Th,,atre, Glasgow, a building ca- pable of accommodating 5)) persms, in consequence of some one giving a false alarm of fire. Instantly the crowded audience rose to their feet arid rushed frantically to the doors, and in the terrible struggle which ensued fourteen persons, whose ages ranged from Id to 60, were either trampled to death or suff dotted, and fourteen were more less injured. The lessee of the theatre, Mr. McKay, and the aseistant managers, attempted in vain to allay the panic, which was somewhat increased by some men and boys jumping from the gallery into an acrobat's net stretched above the stalls. The gallery was reached by six flights of stairs, and the principal block ensued at the landing where the pit entrance is situated. The depositions of persons who escaped are apparently contradictory as to whether an iron gate at this point was left open or closed. The dead and the injured wee taken to the Royal Infirmary and the Central Police Office. The police made strenuous efforts to rescue the struggling multitude, and had it not been for their promptitude and energy there is no doubt the death list would have been increased. A " checker " recently at the theatre, named Turner, 639 been arrested on the charge cf calling out fire, and remitted by the magistrates to the sheriff. His motive is alleged to have been to warn a trapeze performer that he was too near a gas jet. One ac- count says that the prisoner had recently been discharged frem the theatre owing to the reduction of the staff. What- ever his motive for crying out "Fire," the false alarm was taken up by a fall house, and, while some leaped from the gallery into the athlete's swinging net, others rushed to self. destruction on the stairs. A similar panic happened at the Old Theatre Royal, Glasgow, in 1847, when from 5010 60

persons pens e . The fiillowing telegram was received on Monday-from her Majesty by the Loid Provost of Glasgow :—"The Queen is much shocked at the news of the terrible accident at the Star Theatre. Please express her Majesty's deep sympathy with the mourners and injured. Kindly report as to the state of the latter." The Lord Provost replied, thankirg her Majesty on behalf of the citizens. The man James Turner, who is charged with having raised the false alarm of fir o at the Star Theatre, Glasgow. on Saturday night, was, on Monday, ex 'mined by the Mae- gow Stipendiary, and remitted to the Sheriff. The authori- ties again inspected the theatre on Monday, especially the gallery iron gate, and several depositions were taken, some Of the witneases averring that the gate was open, and othei that it was shut-. The inquiry was private. The injured in the hospital are doing well, with the exception of the boy Cassidy. At a meeting of the Glasgown Town Council, on Monday, the Lord Provost, on behalf of the citizens, ex. pressed:deep sympathy with the relatives of those killed in the panic. Doctors Dunlop and Moore, the official surgeons, on Tues- day formally examined the bodies of seven of the victims of the Glasgow theatre panic, which were afterwards re- moved by relatives for interment. The expenses of the funerals are being borne by Mr. M•Kay, lessee of the theatre. All the wounded are doing well.

tious, ind anxious that, in whatever we do as a nation, we should move " from precedent to precedent." In addressing the meeting on Monday night, he pointed to the singular fact that, while both parties were agreed as to the necessity of extending the franchise. no pr.o- gress was being made with the Franchise Bill, though, he said, there was progress enough on one side in starting new methods of " how not to do it," Fle hinted that we had had enough of words, and what we wanted now was deeds. It was not sufficient to condemn the House of Lords—indeed, Mr. RIGBY is rather tender towards that institution—for "if the minority in the House of Commons would only add their voice to the majority of its members the opposition of the Upper House would fly like the mist of the morning before the rising sun." But the minority in the Commons have no such intention ; they look to the House of Lords as their great Caucus; to them it is a Conservative organisation t.O be worked for Conservative ends, and .it IS just because it has repeatedly allowed itself to be meanly used as an instrument to thwart the will of the nation that the nation is at present determined either to lessen its power or set it entirely aside. Mr. RIGBY was, of course, quite at home in dealing with agricul- tural topics, and he did well in urging the need of giving "real security of tenure," sp that the farmer in the investment of his capital will have full confidence that, so far as the law is concerned, he will be able to reap where he sows. There are no less than 277 landowners in the House of Common?, and five farmers only. What are they, it may be asked, amongst so many? Too little, it must be confessed, to leaven the whole lump, and hence the need of farmers , bestirring themselves, and seeing to it that they are not " jerrymandered " any longer. , It is inevitable, under such conditions of mis.- , representation as at present exist, that their interests should be neglected, and that agri- cultural labourers should be treated as of little more moment than the hedges and , ditches upon which they are employed. Talk about the farmers and their labourers being "swamped !" It is a normal condition of , things with them, and no change in repre- ' sentation can be made which will not be an improvement to them, least of all such change as that proposed by the Franchise Bill which is again before Parliament.. This feature of the case against the landed aris- tocracy was one to which Mr. LEADHArd, , directed himself with especial effect. He ' exposed, with the masterly skill which he in- variably displays, the hollowness of the pre- tence that farm labourers had anything to - fear from the action of their fellow workers ; in towns. This suggestion of the Tories Is t absurd on the face of it, in view of the great ; fact that at this very hour, when the Reform agitation may be said to be at white heat, • the enfranchised workers in city and town are the foremost and most earnest in de- manding that their brethren in the counties. shall enjoy the rights which they themselves- ' have exercised for sixteen years If they had any thought of "swamping," they must be what Mr. GLADSToNE spoke of as "dolts and idiots " not to see that, if they have any such game to play, they had better play it whilst they have the field to themselves. The Tories should say nothing about "swamping ; " they do pro- test too much. Mr. LEADHAM struck tha right note when he said that _armers, like manufacturers, will never get their interests adequately represented until they have the labourers at their backs to support them. As an instance of what can be do e by united action on the part of masters and men, we may point to the course which Mr. W. E. BRIGGS, M.P., took in compelling the late Government to remit a portion ot the tax upon cotton goods going into India. He could have done little or nothing as a manu- facturer, supported by manufacturers solely, but, backed by the operatives of Lancashire, who entered into an organisation on the question, he was successful in getting one and then another Government to deal with the matter until now that great grievance has , been removed. And so it will be when, with an extended franchise, farmers and agricul- tural labourers can unite and insist that their ?wrongs shall be remedied. They will never I get anything for their good from the EGERTONS and the WARBuRTOIVS, who show by their votes on questions affecting land that they stick by the traditions in looking to themselves. They must turn to men of their own class, like Mr. RIGBY, who know what they want and mean to have it; or men like Mr. LEADHAM, who, with powerful voice and not less powerful pen, are able, and are as willing are they are able, to instruct their fellow-men, and aid in redeeming them from the oppression of class legislation, and the bondage of bad laws.

IT seems that, after all, the burgesses of Warrington are to be polled on the question of levying a rate of Twopence in the pound in aid of the promotion of the Manchester Ship Canal Bill, In our last issue we placed before our readers a letter from Mr. THOMAS MORRIS announcing his withdrawal of the demand for a poP. On the acceptance of that withdrawal by the MAYOR, it was con- eluded that there would be an end of all idea of a poll. But there are wheels within wheels; as one difficulty is disposed of another crops up. It appears that Mr. MORRIS was not the only one to make a legal demand that the opinion of the burgesses should be put to a test; and now that Mr, MORRIS has stepped aside Mr. WILLIAM DIGGLE has come to the front. Others may shrink from a contest, but DIGGLE is pre_ pared to do or die. Like FITZJAMES, he can say

Come one, come all, this rock shall fly From its firm base as soon as I. And so arrangements are being made for a poll. It will cost something, but under the new phase which is presented it will not be a costly proceeding. There is no intention on the part of anyone, so far as we can gather, to make a fight of it, always of course excepting Mr. DIGGLE, and DIGGLE is,well, it is suffi- cient to say that he is DIGGLE. We are in- formed that in the favourable circumstances under which the poll is likely to be taken the expenses will be less than Lroo ; and it is certainly wo• th so much to ascertain beyond doubt what the ratepayers as a whole think as to the proposal to tax themselves in order to help on the Ship Canal movement. If BARKIS is willin,' who shall say nay? Not the Town Council, we should think, unless it be found that there is a legal obstacle in the way. As to this point, the promoters have made a change of front since the last Bill was brought before Parliament. It will be remembercd that when counsel's opinion was taken a few months ago, it was to the effect that Warrington as a Corporation could not legally contribute to the promotion of the bill. Warrington, however, in the new bill I?ecomes party, along with Manchester and Salford, to its promotion, and in this way it is hoped that, as two Corporations have decided to levy the Twopenny rate, there will be no diffi- culty as to the third. There is, we should point out, the possibility of further complica- tion through the interposition of the Local Government Board whose authority can be appealed to in matters of this kind —that is in certain contingencies. Opponents in Man- chester of the Ship Canal rate have, we understand, appealed to the Board on the question of the refusal of the MAYOR of Man- chester to proceed with a poll, notwithstand- ing that the gentleman who made the demand afterwards formally withdrew. The point raised is that it is unfair to opposing ratepayers to accept a withdrawal—that the ratepayers ought not to be deprived of their rights because one of their number happens to change his mind. No such issue can, of course, be raised in Warrington if a poll is proceeded with, and, looking, as the poet has it, "before and after," we are inclined to think the MAyort has acted discreetly in de- ciding that the opinion of the whole town shall be taken before the question of levying the rate is again brought before the fathers of the Corporation.

THE CITORCH BAZAAR AT WIDNES.—TIIO of St. Patin Church isalised the sum of £583. ALBERT-ROAD WESLEYAN (JHAPEL, WIDNES.—The an- niversary sermons were preached on Sunday by the Rev. S. P. Harvard, of Ormskirk. The collections realised £563 2d. THE FINANCES OF RUNCORN IMPROVEMENT COMMISSION- ERS,—Mr. John Dolby, district auditor, has just completed his audit of the accounts of the Runcorn Improvement Com- missioners, and a statement of the receipts and expenditure for the past year will be found in our advertising columns. A LARGE STEAMER AT RUNCORN.—The steamer Rosalind of Chester, left Runcorn on Monday for Nantes with about 600 tons of pitch shipped by Messrs. Simpson. Davies, and Sons. 'This is oar, of the largest steamers which has entered Runcorn, and shows that the port is able to accommodate vessels of considerable size and depth of draught. RECITAL AT WIDNES.—MISS Ba:kin on Monday evening gave a" recital" in Lacy-street Sunday School on behalf of that institution, and there was a moderate audience present. Mr. Eustace Carey presided. Miss Baskin is an accomplished elocutionist of great power, and cleverly interpreted several of the writings of G. R Sims, H. J. Field, and Will Carle- tom. Miss Poole sang W. M. Hutchinson's charming song 4' Pierrot" in a tasteful and accomplished manner, and Mrs. Robinson gave "The three fishers" with good effect ACCIDENT ON RUNCORN FAIR GROUND. -- A sailor mimed Robert Hughes, belonging to the vessel Catherine Williams, on Monday night fell from a fly-boat on the fair ground, end was picked up in an unconscious state, suffer- ing from a amained wriat, a never* scalp wound, and internal injuries. Hughes was standing up in the boat when he missed his foot-hold, and was thrown from a great height to the ground, and in fallmg struck the shaft of a cart so vice lently that it was smashed. He is progressing favourably under the care of Dr. A. McLennan. RUNCORN FREE LIBRARY COMMITTEE.—The monthly meeting was he'd on Wednesday, under the presidency of of Mr. F. A. Lake. Present: Messrs. J. Simpson, W. Handley, It. Briscoe, and J. D. Jones (librarian.) The monthly report showed that there had been 1,258 issues irom the lending department, representing an increase of 141 over the corresponding month of last year. Presented during the month:—By Mr. John Hoskins author) 1 vol. .of poems and drama; Mr. J. Faulkner, 2 Vole.; Runcorn ' Conservative Association, 13 pamphlets. FATAL ACCIDENT LT DIITON.-0n Tuesday morning, a an who was employed at Ditton Station as a painter, whilst crossing the railway at the station was caught by the Chester express, which was rushing past at a high rate a speed on its way to Liverpool. The unfortunate man was carried along the line a distance of abost f orty yards, 2nd when the people in connection with the station went to his assistance it was found that be had been dreadfully in- jured and mutilated. He was afterwards taken to the Royal Infirmary at Liverpool, but when he arrived there, it was, found that life was extinct. LIVERPOJL, SOUTHPORT, LED PRESTON .IUNOT/ON RAIL- WAY—In advertising columns there will be found the psospectus of this raway which is likely to prove a special attracion to investors—a maximum of profit promising it- self along with a minimum of risk. "The railway will form the all-important I:nk, connecting tin Cheshire f.ines, the Manchester, Sheffield and Lincolnshire, the Midland, and the Great Northern re:lv/aye, with the West Lancashire Railway, and will through Slat system form a competitive :Bile from Burnley, Accrington, Blackburn, Preston, and the whole of East and South-West Lancashire and Yorkshire, to Liverpool and the Liverpool Docks." It is needless to say that a line of this character has an assured traffic, and as it is to be worked under agreement at 46 per cent of the gross re- ceipts from the day of opening, shareholders will be happily free from all troubles as to rolling stock, cost of manage- ment, and the maintenance and renewal of road, stations, and works. The terms throughout are so exceptional, and the prospects of the undertaking are altogether so bright, that we have n; bc,Ditation in commending it to the attsntion of our readers.

The ate was estimated to realise £414 Ps 63. LIEAVY SENTENCES ON WIDNES DRUNKARDS.— At Wil• nes Police Court on Monday, Mr. F. H. Gossage and Mr. H. Gaskell, junior sentenced Stephen Scalley, Catharine Lynch, Rose Kelly, and Catharine Carey, all old offenders. to a month's hard labour for being drunk and disorderly. : The following persons were fined for a like offence :—John Cassidy, Michael Tennon, Michael Grennon, John Beattie, Patrick Breen, Annie Conaford, James Mannion, Emmanuel Smith, Edward Whalin, and William McGloyne. STEILIN3 WHISKY AT FRODSHAM.—At the Occasional Court House, Frodsham, on Monday, before Mr. E. A. Wright, William Taylor, of Frodsham, was charged with stealing a noggin of whisky from the Golden Lion. The prosecutor (Mr. Baker) stated that on Saturday evening h bad occasion to leave the bar a short time, and on his re- turn he saw the prisoner fill a glass from the whisky keg and than attempt to conceal tha glass under his coat. Peter was also charged with assaulting P. C. Bowerbank whilst in the execution of his duty. Shortly after mid- night on Saturday, P. C. At once Peter threw himself ts the ground and savagely kicked the constable on the legs and body. P. C's. Ho:brook and Cummings came upon the scene and both prisoners were secured. music in-an efficient manner. FIRE AT RUNCORN.-9iortly before five o'clock on Tues- day afternoon a fire broke out in the oil store of Messrs. P. Smith and Co., chemists, Bridge-street, Runcorn. Fortuna- tely Mr. Smith was in the shop at the time and quickly raised an alarm, and the fire brigade, under the command of Mr. Robert Wright, the superintendent, was upon the scene in a few minutes. The hose was connected with a hydrant in Ridge-street, and carried through the shop of Mr. G. H. Kiarham in order to reach the burning store, which is at the rear of Mr. Smith's premises. By this time, however, the fire haleete. Leined-a good hold upon the store, and the highly infeetnmable oils sent forth a sheet of fire high above the sur- reunding houses. while dense volumnes of smoke rolled over the lower part of the town. The greatest excitement pre- vailed, and the inhabitants in the adjacent premises becom- ing alarmed for the safety of their property, commenced to remove the furniture to a place of safety. The bedroom win- dows of Mr. Kirkhatn's house were smashed and the beds thrown down into the street. Having a good supply of water, the flu omen, aided by Superintendent Leah, Inspector Roche, P.S. Walley, and several constebles, succeeded in confining the fire to the oil store, which was gutted, and the whole of the stock destroyed. The damage is estimated at between £3OO and £400; but only part of the stock WAS covered by inaurance. WESLEYAN FOREIGN MISSIONS MEETING AT RUNCORN. —The annual services at Runcorn in aid of the Wesleyan Foreign Missions were held on Sunday, The Rev. Massey, and in the evening by the Rev. T. Hackett. On Monday evening the annual missionary meeting was held in St. Paul's Chapel, and there was a large attendance. Mr. J. T. War- rington, of Liverpool, presided, and en the platform were the Revs. James Nicholson, missionary from Ceylon, and Simpson Johnson (deputations), and E. J. Robinson, S. Mee3, T. Hackett, and J. P. Thomas; Messrs. J. Simpson, R. Shaw, T. Simister, T. Norman, E. Taylor, and B. Knive- ton. Mr. T. Simister, secretary, read the report of the Run- corn branch, which showed there bad been collected by Mrs. Soulby, £9 33; by Miss Harrison, £6 193 6.1 • Miss Simister, £8 18s : Miss Norman and Miss Peacock, £l6 10.3 ; public collections, November 2 : at St. Paul's, £l4 14s 9d ; at Cam- den Chapel, £1 33 61 contributed and collected by scholars of Brunswick Sunday School, £66 63 3.1 d ; collected and contributed by scholars of Camden Sunday School, £l9se sd; Mr. and Mrs. Johnson, missionary box, 153' • total, £143 193 51,1; showing a decrease on last year of £l6 46 71c1. Addresses were delivered by the chairman and the deputation on missior.ary work, and subsequently a vote of thanks was accorded to the committee and collectors for their services. Similar compliments were paid to the 1 deputation end the chairman. The collections amounted to £43 123 ld, BoWeretn MATCH fIETY:F.EN SHAV7 AND G. BALL.—The weather being all that couhl be desired for outdoor amuse- ment on Saturday, about 300 persons surrounded the green attached to the King and Queen Hotel, Padgate, to witness a bowling match between James Shaw and George Ball, I both of Warriligtou, for £lO a side. Slight odds were laid j on Ball before play commenced, but, not showing his usual form, ths:odds reversed shortly afterwards. Ball, who is well known as a first class player, and has 'several times beaten both J, Green and T. Hart on the above green, suffered an easy defeat owing to not having bowls for the sides of the green, whilst Shaw, who is a promising young player, and has previously been unsuccessful when competing against professionals, viz, P. Green and W. Taylor, Was well pre. pared with bowls. Shaw was the first to score, and totalled 10 to 5, 17 to 7, 21 to 14, and 27 to 16, when Ball made a run of nine, and shortly after" 31 all" was called. Odds of oto 4 were now laid on Ball, but his opponent kept to the front, and at the close of the half.game was 11 to the good. Ball now commenced to make up his leeway, and reached 55 to Shaw's 54 ; but this was the only time he was in front during the game, as his opponent, be some short but telling runs, totalled 60 to 55, 66 to 57, 79 to 68, 85 to 74, and 91 to 77, when Ball got possession of the jack, and it was thought by many he was going to win, as he re- peatedly put his bowls against the jack, but, after compiling seven, Shaw ran out the winner by 17 points. Tne scores 'at the finish of the game were—Shaw, 101 ; Ball, 84. Mr. J. Heald acted as referee, and his duties were of an agree- able character. A SUCCESSFUL WARRINGTON PIGEON SHOOTER. A match which created no small amount of interest, and brought together a company numbering nearly 600 persons, was satisfactorily decided at the Borough Grounds, Oldham, on Monday afternoon. The competitors were James Welsby, of Warrington, and Samuel Cocker, of Oldham, who had agreed to shoot at 21 pigeons each, with loz of shot, 21 yards rise, and 60 fall, H and T traps. Welsby is an old practitioner, and has earned an excellent reputation, whilst ICocker has also, since his fi st debut at the Borough Grounds, proved that he is a capital shot. Not long since, In a similar match with " Cocker" Knott, he accomplished a meritorious performance, killing sixteen in succession, and ultimately won. Toe shooting of neither, however, in the present match was noteworthy ; indeed, quite the re- verse. This may be attributed te the hilly state of the ground and a high wall facing the marksmen, as the weather was in every way favourable. The betting opened at evens, but just prior to the commencement odds of 6 to 4 were laid on Welsby. Cocker, who went on first, missed his first three, which gave Weleby a lead of two, but at the tenth round Cocker was one in front, Weleby having missed five in succession. All through the pair kept closely together, but eventually Welsher got in front, and won by grassing twelve out of twenty, Cocker, who allowed his last bird to escape, killing eleven out of twenty-ene. One of Welsby's birds fell just two feet inside the boundary, and this was the only occasion during the match that the referee was put to any trouble. The match, however, was conducted through- out in the most friendly spirit by both parties. Mr. T. R. I Allison, of Manchester, officiated as referee. Baker and Son, of Chester, being of the best class. The usual loyal and Masonic toasts were proposed during the evening, and songs were given by Brothers Webster, Williams, J. C. Robinson, J. Humphrey, Jse. DEATH FROM AN OVERDOSE OF OPIUM AT RUNCORN.— Mr. J. E. Worsley, the deputy coroner, held an inquest at the Waterloo Hotel, High.street, Runcorn, yesterday, on the body of George Bankes, aged 74 years. From the evi- dence of Mrs. Sarah Roach, of 15, Crescent-row, and Alice Pollit, wife of Samuel Povey, Crescent-row, it appeared that Bankes was a tailor by trade, and had for many years lived in Regent-street. For some time past he lied been un- able to work, and he had, together with the woman with whom he had cohabited for 29 years, been dependent upon a payment from the Union, and the charity of the neigh- bours. He had become twelve months in arrears with his rent, but the landlord told him that if he would begin to pay rent he would forgive him the arrears. The deceased was determined not to do so, and the landlord gave him his furniture, which he (deceased) sold on Monday. On the afternoon of that day the deceased went to Mrs. Roach's house and said he could not get lodgings, and asked her to give him a cup of tea. She did so and allowed him to stay in the house on Monday and Tuesday nights. He was much distressed in his mind in consequence of having had to break up his home, and on both nights he coughed very badly and roamed about the house. On Wednesday morn- ing he left the heaso and did not return until four o'clock, when Mrs. Roach made him some tea, and left him for half an hour. On her return she found him asleep on the sofa, and as he could not be awakened, Dr. McDougall was sent for and was with him until death occurred. It then trans- pired OA Alice Pollitt had seen the deceased smashing a Ismail bottle in the garden, and it WAS surmised that it had contained laudanum, as the deceased acknowledged that he had been in the habit of taking laudanum to soothe his cough.—Dr. McDougall deposed that he had made a post mortem examination and Lc* was of opinion that the de- ceased bad died him narcotic poisoning. He had ascer- tained that the deceased on Wednesday purchased a pre- paration of opium equivilant to 12 grains of solid opium. Four grains of opium had been found sufficient to clue deetb.—The jury retuned a verdict to the effect that the 6 ceased accidentally took an overdose of opium.

Thomas and Mr. James . Handley, Alfred Haddock and George. Barnes, young men, were brought up in custody charged with poaching on land in the occupation of Sir Richard Brooke, Bart. About mid- night cn Saturday a labourer named John Hoffland was crossing the "Big" Field, Norton, when he saw two dogs. 1 Suspecting there were poachers in the neigl,bourhood, he walked to the "Cover Side," and found several nets. The prisoners and three other men were there. Hoffland in- formed George and Adam Rigby, sons of the gamekeeper, and they followed the prisoners along the canal bank to Messrs. Wigg, Brothers, and Steele's works. The prisoners sent down nets and pegs as they ran along. They were carrying bludgeons. The prisoners were given into the custody of P.S. FOWL ROBBERY AT RUNCORN.—SMART CAPTURE.—Be- fore Mr. A. Thomas and Mr. James Handley, at Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, Thomas Gayter and William Evans, Young men, were charged with having, on the 2nd November, stolen four hens and two tame rabbits, value 17s, the property of Mr. John Meadowcroft, manager to the Bridgewater Navigation Company, Runcorn.—ln the exe- cution of his duty Arthur Povey, canal constable for the Bridgewater Navigation Company, about six o'clock on Saturday examined Mr. Meadowcroft's house, and found everything secured. At nine o'clock he discovered that the hencote had beea broken into, and three hens and a pullet taken, while two fine rabbits had also been conveyed away. The police were informed of the robbery, and about three o'clock on Sunday morning Sergeant Walley and Constable Bryan went to Gayter's house, in Heath-road. In the cup- board were found two of the stolen fowl dead, and a live rabbit. The officers then went to Evan's house. in Sewell- street, where a couple of dressed fowls and a rabbit cut to pieces were discovered. The skin of the rabbit was like that of one of the missing rabbits.—Both prisoners pleaded guilty. Gavter stated that he had a wife and two little children' and there was nothing whatever to eat in the house at all. He committed the robbery through hunger and nothing else. —Evans made a statement to the same Affect —Superinten- dent Leah said the prisoners were loitering about the street month after month, and never worked.—The Bench sen- tenced each prisoner to two months' hard labour.

BIRRELL'S GREAT DIORAMA. OF' SCOTLAND AND GRAND SCOTTISEI CONCERT.—" Bonnie Scotland" is to be brought to our very doors, and in such a manner that the most phlegmatic and unappreciative will have his soul stirred by the graphic delineation of Birrell's 50,000 feet of canvas, portraying with marvellous vividness the charm of "Bon- nie Scotland." It has lately been exhibited for six months at the Royal Agricultural Hall, London and it is within our I knowledge that everything in connection with the enter- I tainment is of the very highest character. Without the in- convenience (and danger) of a long raiiway ride, every one should go and see this magnificent entertainment, and, as if by magic, be transported to Scotia's loveliest scenery, and learn in two hdllirs what it costs months of travel to acquire, and at the same time be charmed with real Scottish music and song and dance. A glance at the list of the artistes will satisfy the most sceptical on this point, and if any- thing more were necessary to prove the high stand of the corps iszusicale, we have only to add that it will include a lady and gentleman who, a short time ago, had the honour of being summoned to Covent Garden to sing in M. Riviere'e concert, and when we state that Miss Griselda Wess and Mr. Thomas Birrell drew enthusiastic applause from a London audience, who on the same evening listened to Mdlle. Car- lotta Patti, we have said enough to warrant tke expectation of something out of the common in the rendering of the songs of Scotland. Mr. Bissell is one of those gentlemen who place absolute faith in liberal catering for the pubic, and would admit of nothing in his entertainment but first- °lade talent, cost what it may, This is evident from his en- gagement ot the numerous talented artists announced in his advertisements. On looking over recent numbers of our con- temporaries the idea strikes one of a rivalry as to which could give the best eulogium of the diorama and the con- cert. The critiques are a nesentient in the fact that the en- tertainment is in every respect the most complete of the kind extant. As the stay is necessarily limited, an early visit is necessary to prevent disappoint- ment.

SHOCKING SUICIDE NF,AR WIDNES.—A. melancholy occur- rence took place at the Pexhill reservoir, which is the pro- perty of the Widnes Local Board, on Wednesday afternoon, when Elizabeth Bradshaw, 48 years of age, daughter of Richard Bradshaw, caretaker of the reservoir, committed suicide. Bradshaw, who is very old, has recently been ill, and his daughter has had to perform his duties for him. About noon on Wednesday the deceased, after inquiring of her father if be was all right, went from the house, and as she had no reason for doing so, and did not retura when an hour had elapsed, the old man became anxious, and went in search of her. He found her lying at the bottom of the reservoir in 14 feet of water, and he obtained the assistance of James Houghton, who got the body out. The deceased had been twice confined in Reinhill Asylum for attempts of self-destruction, and she was only liberated in March last. Her sister, Mrs. Margaret Gore, some months ago drowned herself and child in the canal, near Penketh. Her elder daughter, whom she also dragged into the water, escaped after a severe struggle.—The inquest on the body was held yesterday at Crouton, before Mr. W. T. Husband.—R chard Bradshaw, the father of the deceased, deposed that he did not know any reason why his daughter should commit sech a rash act. It was not possible to fall into the reservoir if a person missed her footing in any way.—James Houghton, who had eecovered the body, thought it possible a person going down the steps might get into the position in which the deceased Was found.—Mr. Isaac Carr, engineer to the Widnes Local Board, did not think anyone could fall into the water and get into the position where the deceasel was found. The deceased had no right there—The jury returned a verdict of found drowned.—Mr. Midwood, in reply to the Deputy Coroner, said that immediately after the std occurrence became known at the Local Board offices a meet- ing of the Gas and Water Committee was held, and instructions were given to Mr. Carr to run the water in the reservoir off, and this was immediately done.—The Deputy Coroner said it would be satisfactory to the ratepayers to know that he had heard that there had been a great deal of beer consumed in preference to water since the occur- rence. THE SUFFOCATION CASE AT RUNCORN. In the House of Commons, on Tuesday evening, Mr. Warburton asked the Secretary of the Local Government Board whether his attention had been called to the death of two children from suffoc ition by chlorine gas at the soap and alkali works near Runcorn; whether he was aware that noxious vapours, destructive to vegetation and life, were constantly allowed to escape from these works; and whether he would take steps to compel the owners of these works to adopt measures for the prevention of this danger in the neighbourhood in future. Mr. George Russell said he had telegraphed for in- fetrnation on this matter, but up to the pr,sent moment he had received none. He would not forget the matter, and. perhaps the hon. member would put the question this day week or farther on, The Runcorn Soap and Alkali Com- pany, it should be stated, have done their utmost to miti- gate the sorrow of the parents of the two children suffocated by an escape of chlorine from their works, and have given them the sum of £5O as compensation for their loss. They are also allowing Mrs. Spencer, the mother, whom it will be recollected nearly lost her life by the effects of the chlorine, a weekly amount cf II for extra nourishment until she is able to leave the town for Soathport, where she will remain until fully convalescent. During her illness Mr. Wigg has caused every attention to be paid to Mrs. Spencer, and has forwarded supplies of grapes from his conservatories at Halton Lodge. Mrs. Spencer is now progressing very favourably. On Thursday evening the matter was again referred to in the House of Commons. Mr. George Russ;ll, in reply to Mr. Warburton, said he regretted to say it WAS true that the death of two children had been caused by chlorine gas at the soap and alkali works near Runcorn The verdict of the jury was that the deaths were due to error of judgment and misadventure on the part of the men in charge of the doors by which the gas could escape. Hitherto the reports of the inspectors appointed under the Alkali Acts had been very satisfactory, and the department were unaware that a case of this kind had ever occurred before. The depositions in this case received that day would be considered with a view of determininz whether the case ought to be made the subject of a prosecution under the Alkali Act.

THE SHIP CANAL IX PENSES : A FERIOOS .ELTMOUR.

When the deputations went to London last year in connectioa with th 3 Ship Canal, a stone of £lO or £BO was voted The rumour was that this sum did not represent the teal amount received by that Com- mittee for their expenses, but that over and above the amount valued by tee Board they received £l2 out of the law-clerk's bill. This was a very serious rumour to get about the town, and he thought some explanation or denial should be given.—The law clerk replied that when the de- putation came to his sffice to settle up accounts, the chair- man of the then committee said he thought that per sorrel expenses or money spent upon themselves, should not fall upon the Beard. He (Mr. Linaker) considered it .uofeir that the committee should put their hands in their own pockets, and he said that as he had done well out of the Ship Canal work, having represented several other authoritiee, he would take upon himself to set is a portion of the extra expenses. The Chairman : At the same time the committee took off what they coneidered person it expenses.—The Lew Cle:k : First of all it was sug- gested that 101 per day should be allowed. It was thought too much to corns out of the public purse, and that 5s for that kind of thing woreld do. I said, "Wall, I will pay the extra cost. I can afford it."—The Chairman seid he be- lieved what hod given rise to tee rumour was this. It was felt that if the Lew Clerk reduced his own expenses it would pave the way of some of the members who were erosions to reduce their expenses, and that they would be able to say that the Low Clerk had been willing to take so mach off his bill and members must take so much off theirs. Tnet was the true explanation of what took place—Mr. Lake said he did not understand the chairman's remarks. Not only did the Lew Clerk reduce the bill, but he actuaaly paid over to the deputation s) much out of his bill.—The Chairman: He actually took so much less, and the committee's expenses were reduced in the same way.—The Law Clerk said the expenses of the deputation were passed in a cheque te hirn, lie had to pay hotel bills, railway fares, and thing, of to at kind. Then came the question of what should he allowed to each monster of the committee for his expenses whilst in London.
