The Commissioners would have to pay the same amount of money.—Mr. Like : Do I understand you charged three guineas a day, and then out of that allowed- the deputation something —rile Law Clerk : No, it was not that way at all.—lbe Chairmen said Mr. Lake's as- eumption was that the Law Clerk had 3 separate account, and that after paying the hotel ex .renses he handed some- thing over to the committee.--Mr. Lakr : if the law clerk Raid more than his own person a 1 share it is just the same as lif be handed money over to the deputation.—The Law Clerk: Th. t - is a met:et- icr the law clerk.—Mr. LigLthurn said the practice was very different to that followed last year. Then they kept an account separate from the law clerk, and the whole cost only amounted to about £33 103, while the expenses this year amounted to £7o.—Mr. Nor- man : There is a difference, bo.cause the expenses the year you were off wete surcharged, and the others are not.—The Chairman said against that £33 Eh Mr. Lightburn should put the whole cost of the legal proceedings, and the law clerk pointed out that the extra cost would be represented by the railway fares alone.—The subject shortly afterwards diopped.

LIBERAL LECTURE AT RUNCORN. The first of a series of lectures on political top.cs to be de- livered during the present winter under the auspices of the Runcorn Liberal Aesocietion was given on Thursday even- ing in Bethesda Lecture Hall. Mr. B. B. Hackney, of the National Lioeral Association, had been announced to give a lecture on the House of Lords, but he was unable to be present, and Be. Langford, of Birmingham, took his place. Mr. R. Shaw, president of the Association, took the chair, and he was supported on the platform by Messrs W. Hand- ley, B. Kniveton, George Moss, F. J. Norm en, J. Bridge- water, F. J. Adams, and 0. Leak (secretary) Amongst the audience were the Rev. J. D. Thomas, the Rev. W. Vause, and Messrs F. Fairhurst, G. Bellamy, J. Bowyer, S. Coven- ' try, C. Littler, J. Faulkner, W. Faulkner. and T. Hand- ley. The Ceairman, in ietroducing the lee' urer, referred to the conduct of the House of Lords in rej dine the Fran- I chise Bill, and said whether the people of th.s country would continue to allow that extraordinary body to so mani- pulate measures that the people might be prevented from having their just rights, was a question which would soon be brought prominently before them. Be was satisfied the verdict would be clear and distinct. He did not suppose there would be any objection to that assembly sitting in comfort and ease in the gilded chamber so long as they did not interfere with what the people believed were their rights. —(applaus..)—but when they stood in the way of what clearly belonged te the peoole they were only bringing ruin upon themselves. (Applause.) The country would not be worse off if there was no upper chamber. (Applause)— Too Lecturer, who received quite an ovation on rising, sa- ted that within the past 50 years there bad scarcely been a measure introduced and passed in the House of Commons for the benefit of the great body of the nation, that had not been rejected two or three times, and then when passed, emasculated and weakened by that irresponsible chamber, the House of Lords. (Applause.) He described the peers as a body of men banded together for what they called" pri- vilege and property " and who were altogether opposed to the people obtaining political power, because they knew that it was only as the people obtained that power that they became able to regulate what laws should be passed, bow they should ba governed, and under what system they should be served. (Applause.) Speaking of the hereditary principle, he pointed out how rarely the genius of statesmanship, or of poetry, or art, or science des- cended to the sons of great men, and asked how was it likely that the peers should make great statesmen when their education and modes of life altogether unfitted them to appreciate the wants of the people. They were never bronght in contact with the people, and knew nothing of the wants, the desires, and the aspirations of the people. (Applause.) In every human society, except the House of Lords, if any member disgraced himself by any criminal act or any immoral act of great turpitude, they had the power to exclude such a man from the community until he re- formed, and brought forth fruits fit for repentance. Was it not monstrous that any man born in the purple, and by the right of his birth as a peer, no matter what conduct he might be guilty of, he did not cease to be a peer and to have power over the destinies of this great nation. ("Fear- ful.") He repeated the statement of Mr. C. S. Reid, the Tory member for West Suffolk, that if many of the members of the House of Lords had their deserts they would be in the pillory, and not a few in penal servitude. (Applause.) Such a house as that required a radical reform. Applause.) The lecturer instituted a comparison between the Colonial legislatures and the British, and ridiculed the idea that the abolition of the hereditary principle of. the House of Lords would endanger the Crown. He pointed out that while the constitution of the House of Lords depended upon a resolution passed by themselves, the succession to the Crown WAS fixed by an Act of Parlia- ment passed in the House of Commons. The Queen was a woman who had endeared herself to every heart an the 1 country even those who entertained theoretically Republican views of Government held Her Majesty I in honour as the head of the nation. (Loud applause.) Dealing with the question what was to be done, the lecturer propounded various schemes far the reform of the "Upper House," and said if they were to have such a house, abolish altogether the hereditary principle. (Ap- plause.) Its existence was an anomaly and an anachronism, and the House of Lords was hindering and not helping the progress of the people. (Loud applause.) When that was the case it was time for the health and strength and pros- perity of the nation that another system should he devised, and another scheme of government introduced which would work in harmony with the highest aspirations and the most bountiful hopes of the people themselves. (Applause.) Mr. B. Kniveton moved the following resolution:—" That this meeting hails with satisfaction the expressed intention of the Government to pass the Franchise Bill during the present session of Parliament, and strongly urges the Government to accept trocempromise—(applause)—which will deny to the two millions unenfranchised their right of voting at the next general election." (Applause) He supported :he resolution in an appropriate speech, a refer- ence to Mr. Chamberlain being received with the greatest -entLusiasm.—Mr. G. Mess, who had a very hearty recep- tion, seconded the motion, remarking upon the iniquitous proceedings of the House of Lords during the last fifty years.—The resolution was passed unanimously.—On the motion of Mr. W. Headley, seconded by Mr. F. Fairhurst, a cordial vote of thanks was passed to Dr. Langford for his men! lecture.

The statements made regarding the negotiations with the Government which have resulted in a removal of the shipowner,' objections to the personnd of the Royal Commission on Merchant Shipping were accep- ted as satisfactory, although there was still some faint op- position to the presence on the Commission of Mr. Chainberlain. The latter right hon. gentleman in a letter to Mr. Gourley, M.P., says there is no ground for supposing that he distrusts the shipping represenmtives either in or out of Parliament, and adds that he is only anxious to obtain is thoroughly fair and Oielent Commission.

div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.
LONDON, THURSDAY. A fortnight ago to-day the House of Commons met "for
the despatch of business." '.:l-o -day it for the first time ap-
proached business near enbugh to take it in hand. The

interval has been spent in wrangling and verbosity—as completely wasted as if members had been playing chuck- farthing ore the floor of the House, or leap-frog through the lobcie. The peculiar difficulty which those interested in the progress of public business find in these times is the new form obstruction lrus taken. As compared with its.develop- ment in 1881 and 1882, obstruction is now a fine art. Then members used to go the length of sitting up all night; there were frequent rows, and aiiseries of excitingscenes. Now mat- ters are managed vary differently. The lriss members have discovered that there lens necessity for putting themselves

_ out, or getting themselves put out. Their simple object being to waste time and prevent legislation, they can do it in (pie little ways not less effectively than when it was ac;wmpl:shed by regular fie d nights. Instead of defying the Speaker, and keeping the Hons.! sittirg all night, they make their speeches in unimpeachable Parliamentary form, one succeeding the other, and so talking the hours away. - - •• •

That this is more successful than the earlier manner, is proved by the simple fact of the waked fortnight. Ca Wednesday Mr. O'Donnell, losing his temper, recurred to the old style and was suspended with a business like promp- titude impossible to excel'. What was noticeable about the scene was the absolute apathy with which it was regarded. Once upon a tune the suspension of an Irish member was an event that shook Ch.? House to itsifoundatiun and brought about a state of excitement fa'al to business. On Wednes- day the affair was got through in a few minutes auclowith- out a hitch, just as lilt had been perfected by rehearsal. Mr. Justin McCarthy has produced in his "History of the Four Georges " one of those charming works which possr:sses a double merit. For those fond of historical studies the way is made pleasant. For those not attracted by the study irresistible attraction is provided. Croher wishing to say something particularly spiteful of Lord Macmlay, wroteishen reviewing his history "Us is a great, a very great, historical novelist." Mr. McCarthy's latest work, as was the case in respect of his " History of Our Own "limes," has all the charm of a novel with all the accuracy of a history. There is no more reason why history should not have the charm of a novel than there is why the Devil should have all the good tunes. itecognition of and action upon this principle is the secret of the remarkable success which Mr. McCarthy's appearance in the field c,f history has wet with. He writes history as a scholar pos- sessed of lively conversational powers and a sense of humour would talk history. But, as already Listed, it must not be supposed thit because the first instalment of the "History of the Four Georges" is fascinaring reading dill., therefore, it is not instructive. Mr. McCarthy has evidently steeped himself in the history and life of the times of which he discourses, and out of the fullness of his know- ledge his pen writeth. We have as yet only the first volume, a stout oue, set forth in srductively large print, which com- pletes the charm of the book. Mears. Chatto and Winds promise three more volumes, which will CCAlls the sooner if we have no more autumn sessions.

At the risk 61 contradicting Mr. O'Donnell, I am bound to siy that the Speaker is not "playing the part expected of him." We have so long been accustomed to see the chair successfully flouted by persons like Mr. O'Donnell, Mr. Biggar, and Mr. Healy, that the recent waking up of the Speaker is a matter of agreeable surprise. Mr. Peel has evidently made up his mind to enforce rules laboriously ar- rived at by the House, but which have been allowed to re- main a dead letter. This is the one bright spot in the Par. liamentary hintory of the week. If the Speaker is going forward as he has commenced, we shall soon see a change in the manners of the House.

There is a tine story current just now which finds much favour with the Conservatives, and will probably be cited in debate on the Franchise Bill. A gentleman, the son of a Liberal member, was the other day riding near Stratford-on- Avon when he overtook an agricultural labourer driving an empty cart. He thought the opportunity favourable for as- certaining the man's views on the political questions of the day, but found little encouragement. "Don't you go in for pelitics about here?" he asked in despair. "No," said the man, "I be goin' for drain-pipes." The Psychical Society are still diligently pursuing phan- toms through the land. The latest evidence of activity is the distribution of a kind of shorter catechism. Young en. thuslastic collectors have been appointed to distribute these papers, and return the replies to M. Edmund Gurney, high priest of the association. The catechism is divided under two heads 6. Hallucinations and Dreams." They are a T..Ct, series of conundrums suitable for discussion in the family circle in the season when, as the late Mr. Justice Keogh is reported to have said, "the nights are long and the days are short."

_ Mr. and Mrs. Bar croft are retiring from business for the most satisfactory reason imaginable. They have made a fortune, and desire quietly to enjoy it. How fortunes are mode in the theatrical profession may be illustrated by many references. The most familiar is the case of " Our Boys," at which Messrs. James and Thorne made sufficient to keep them in affluence for the rest of their lives.. Mr. James took the obviously wise course of retiring when the run of the piece came to an end. Mr. Thorne went on with the thea- tre, and, though he is doing well enough now, had (en a year or two occasion to regret that he had not followed his colleague's example. Burnand made a big sum out of "The Oolonql," though nothing by comparison with the profits of "Our Boys." The latest example of swift and sudden fortune coming to a nem previously unknown, is to be found in "The Pri- vate Secretary." The private history of this piece should be encouraging to young dramatists. The author, Charles Ilawtrey, took it round to nearly every manager in London, meeting a monotonous refusal. Edgar Bruoe, who bed just taken the Prince's, aod was in adventurous spirits, tried it, largely owing to the acting of Mr. Tree it was fairly Suc- cessful. But it was not good enough to stand in the way of " Called. Back," and. when that piece was ready the "Pri- vate Secretary" disappeared. Thence it went to the Globe where it suddenly blazed forth into irresistible attractive- ness. I hear of one going to engage stalls who was told that be "could have them in February." Mr. Hawtrey's gains up to the present time are estimated at between 5.,30,000 and £40,000. Miss Anderson's success is still the topic in all theatrical circles, and yet I fancy that the critics have said at once more or less thin they meant. In the two great revivals of Seakespeare noes' crowded by theatre goers, the frame counts for more than the picture, and this is best illustrated by the poorness of the general cast. The setting of the Lyceum play is exquisite. We have the beauty of Italian thsiers, cunningly copied fro:n pictures in the Academy at Vence, from Carpaccio and from Boaifazio, we have draperies and tapestries. and armour, and accessory, as in one of Makart's pictures and then great mediocrity in giving effect to poor Shaliespere's verses, or interpreting his play. It is the apotheosis of supers and some painters. Miss Anderson looes very lovely, and almost perfectly succeeds In ehat she attempts. But all the time she is Miss Anderson, the beautiful American actress, whose approval of Pears' soap so largely contributes to its sale. Wherever study or pose or the brute force of beauty can win us, her triumph is absolute. But she never forgets herself, and we never forget her. Now "Juliet " is the one character in all Sbakespere that needs the abandon- ment that comes of passion. The actress who shalt give us at all An acceptable " Juliet " must rely more on heart than mind, and never be self-conscious. The two revivals have singularly enough one thing in common. The poetry of each play is sacrificed, and somehow the play—as a play—seems to run smoother for the sacrifice. Everyone will go and see this " Juliet," and should do so. Bat what will remain in the memory will be not the cruel fate of these lovers of Verona, bnt the prettiness of Miss Anderson and the gorgeousness of the scenery. The nineteenth cen- tory comes in for all the praise.

THE DuirE OF AEGTLL ON THE POLITICAL Onis-s.—The following letter from the Duke of Argyll appehred in the Liverpool Daily Post on Saturday last:—" Sir,—An ex- tract has been sent to me from one of your recent numbers commenting en an expression attributed to me in a recent Veen to the effect that the difference between the two parties in the presmt crisis is only Difference of proce.; dare. lam not sorry for an opportunity of explaining that this report was an error. I did not use the expression, never have used it, and always object to it. The me7e dif- ference in the mode of procedure covers a real sebstantial difference, but this difference is to a large degree unavew ed. Both parties profess te desire it. The Redistribution BM should be settled by the present Parliament as now consti- tuted. If this profession is sincere on both sides, it ounit to be easy to adopt some mode of procedure practically securing it. This is what I said.—Your, , s am,. ARGYLL.— Inverary, Oct. 30th, 1884."

He raid that he deserted because he was refused permission to go on foreien service. He was remanded to Walton. The defendants were members of a crowd who took part in a disturbance in Silver-street on the night of the 20th ult., during which stones and bricks were used, and they were identified as having conduced to the damage at the house, wl/4ich was estimated at £2. They were each fined is and coat., and ordered to pay 10a each towards the damage, or go to prison for a month in default. John White.

MrscEniestiors.—Tiro-m-as- -o-allaghan, who pleaded guilty to being a deserter from R.M. Royal Irish Regiment in 1850, when en route from Manchester to Clonmel, was remanded to Walton.—Joseph Horton, charged with being drunk and disorderly, was dismissed.—Mary Flannery was fined 53 and costs, or seven days, for being drunk the same morning.—John Watkinson was charged with fraudulently enlisting in the South Lancashire Regiment, and was sen- tenced to three months' imprisonment; he had stated that he had not been in the army before, whereas he had been discharged from the 103rd Regiment. • FBAUDIILENT REMOVAL OF GOOD9.—John Fryer, a colour- sergeant stationed at Orford Barracks, who did not appear, was summoned to show cause why he should not be com- mitted for disobeying an order made upon him for the pay- ment of £7 15s as rent due, he having fraudulently removed his goods.—The Bench at first committed the defen- dant for a month, but afterwards withdrew the de- cision on the advice of the Clerk, there being a conflict of legal opinion as to whether that course could be adopted in regard to a soldier, and whether his offence was a criminal one, or should be considered as a civil debt.—The case was therefore adjourned.

The match created a great amount of local interest, and the result was a surprise to the partisans of the home team. Runcorn were defeated for the first time this season by one goal, one try, and two minor points to one try and one minor point. For the win- ners Walsh played a safe game, but had very little to do. Hough tackled well, but Massey was net in his St. Helens form. T. Barne's tackling was good. All round play was very fine, and H. Speakman and Gilbert were unselfish, but out of form. Sr. THOMAS'S (Sr. HELENS).— These team.' met at Haydock on Saturday, when there was a fair number of spectators. The visitors arrived late, which prevented the game being played the usual length of time. The Temperance captain won the toss, and elected to play with the wind in his favour for the first half, the ball being set in snotioa at 3-40. The game had only just com- menced when the home forwards traversea on to the Saints' territory, which necessitated Peachy using his hands in de- fence. This only relieved the pressure for a time, for from a beautiful pass the Temperance men succeeded in scor- ing their first point. The leather was again put in motion, and the visitors' forwards broke loose, taking the sphere down the field, and scored their first and only goal. The home team again commenced the attack, and succeeded in scoring their second goal, Peachy being called into requisi- tion, to which he responded admirably. At change of ends St. Thomas's had the wind in their favour, but the Temper- ance men scored three more points, the Saints choosing to leave the ground ten minutes before the time was up in con- sequence of the growing darkness, the game standing at five games for Temperance, to St. Thomas's one. EARLESTOWN V LIVERPOOL STANLEY.—The Earlestown team achieved their most brilliant victory this season, on Satur- day afternoon, when they met and defeated the Liverpool Stanley Club at Earlestown. The visitors mustered their strongest eleven, and as Earlestown also turned out its full strength a good game was witnessed. The weather was favourable, and some 500 or 600 spectators assembled and displayed enthusiasm at the success of the Earlestown Club, The teams appeared on the field at four o'clock, and the visitors WAR the toss. They chose to play with the sun at their backs, and Degnall accordingly started the ball for Earlestown, the latter team playing with the ground in their favour. For the first few tninntes the Earlestonians hell a decided advantage, but Allow and 113vey played splendidly and repelled the assaults of their opponents. The Stanley forwards were held in check by the Earlestown hacks and half-hack 4, v h 3 were repeatedly cheered for their Play throughout the entire game. The home team had hard lines in their attempts to score, and up to half-time no score bad been made; and when ends were changed it was ex- pected the visitors would win, as they had the ground in their favour. The Earlestonians played up with dash and energy, and the game became of the fastest possible character, the spectators manifesting considerable excite- ment. After both goals had been endangered Rich and Ellison ran the ball up the right wing, and the latter splen- didly centreing the ball, Dagnall rushed up and headed it through amid great cheering, ten minutes after the change of ends. The visitors put forth every cifort to secure an

The fund to indemnify Mr. O'Brien. editor of United Ireland, closed on Saturday at nearly £7,000 an amount which does not cover his expenditure. Mr. Hirrington, M.P., speaking at the National League meeting at Dublin, on Tuesday, charged the Dublin Castle officials, from Earl Spencer downwards, with murd7r and conspiracy to murder.

THE SKYE CROFTERS.—The land agitation in Skye has assumed such a serious aspect that it has been decided to largely reinforce the police in tie island, and it is stated that the police will be furnished with arms. ARSON BY A CO-OPERATIVE MANAGER—At Leicester Assiz,s, on Monday, Alfred Reeve, formerly manager of the Loughborough Co-operative Store, was brought before the Lord Chief Justice to receive sentence for having set fire to the premises on September Bth, thus doing considerable damage. The prisoner was sentenc3d to five years' penal servitude. THE PLYMOUTH TRAGEDY.—At the Exeter ASSIZE'S on Wednesday, Edward Bath Edwards, cabinet maker, was tried for the murder of his two children, the eldest aged eight years, at Plymouth, by cutting their throats whilst his wife was absent. The accused and his family were in great poverty at the time. The jury found the prisoner guilty, and Mr. Baron Huddleston passed sentence of death. Lord RANDOLPH CHURCHILL was the principal speaker at a Conservative demonstration at Huntington on Wednesday. He described the accusation that the Tory party was res- ponsible for wasting time in Parliament as one of the habi- tual Radical misrepresentations If there had been waste of time the fault lay with Mr. Gladstone, who ought to have adjourned Parliament last August and not prorogued it. OPERATIVES WAGES AT OLDHAM.—A large number of re- turns have been received in answer to circulars sent by the Employers' Association as to the proposed reduction of 5 per cent in the cotton operatives' wages. Many firms are in favour of the reduction, but some limited companies are against it. The feeling is that the contemplated reduc- tion will fall through, as the spinning business is improv- ing slowly. DEATH OF VISCOUNTESS SHERBROOICE.—ViSCOMIteSS Sherbrooke died at 34, Lansdowne-square, en Monday. The deceased, Georgina, was the second daughter of Mr. George Orred, of Aigburth House, Liverpool, and married, in 1816, the Right Hon. Robert Lowe, formerly Chancellor of the Exchequer, who was raised to the peerage by the style and title of Viscount Sherbrooke. Her ladyship had been in der:lining health for several weeks. A PASSENGER SHIP ON FIRE.—NARROW ESCAPE OF EMI- GRANTS.—The passengers and crew by the steamer Maas- dam, of Rotterdam, which was sighted on fire on the 25th October, have arrived at New York on board the North German Lloyd steamer Rhein from Bremen. The Rhein reports that on the 24th in lat. 4938, and long. 27.41, she fell in with the Maasdam, which was enveloped in flames. The passengers and crew, numbering 186 persons, bad taken to the ship's boats, and they were all picked up by the Rhein.

DASTARDLY OUTRAGE ON A MINER.—At Wakefield, on Monday, Thomas Smith, a miner, was committed for trial charged with having perpetrated a dastardly outrage in Wakefield. The prisoner had lately been on strike, and it was alleged that about midnight he left his house and threw a cartridge with a lighted fuse into the house of Benjamin Wilson, miner, who had refused to strike. The cartridge exploded in Wilson's hand when he was about to throw it out. The prisoner then threw a cartridge into the house of another miner.

A Commorr STREET DANGER.—On Saturday night, while two flute bands were marching through Cathcart-square, Greenock, a horse yoked to a baker's van took fright at the noise made, and became unmanageable. The driver attempted to draw the horse up, with the result that the van capsizd. The square being much crowded at the time, a number of persons were knocked down. One man named Hugh Hill was killed outright, two others had their legs broken and were removed to the insrmary, and four or Ave others had their injuries attended to at the police office.

EMPLOYMENT FOR THE GREAT -EASTERN.-Mr. E. W. Pine. special commissioner of the New Orleans Exhibition, on Monday night signed a contract chartering the steamship Great Eastern for twelve months. The great vessel will proceed from Milford Haven, it is hoped, during the last week in November for New Orleans direct, with English art and collective educational exhibits. which will be conveyed and returned to England freight free. She will be moored in the Mississippi river, and utilised as a floating hotel and place of public entertainment for evening fetes, Lto., for which purpose a large sum will be spent in fitting her up. COLLISIONS IN PLYMOUTH SOUND.-A collision occurred off Plymouth breakwater early on Tuesday. The steam tug Trefry, of Par, was towing three schooners out of the Sound when she crossed the bows of the steamer Hastings, of Lon- don,which was coming in. The three schooners struck her on the port side, sweeping her upper works, carrying out davits, smashing the beats, and damaging the bridge. The schooners all sustained serious injuries. Another collision occurred in the Sound shortly afterwards, the steam tug Ryhope being cut to the water's edge by the trawler Beatrice. The weather was dirty, and the Ryhope lying at anchor.

THE CO-OPERATIVE BANE FRAUDS—ACTION BY Mn. R. BANNER OAKLEY.—In the Queen's Bench Division, on Tues- day, Mr. Richard Banner Oakley, who was sent to penal servitude in connection with the Co-operative Bank frauds, sued Messrs. Boyle. sanitary engineers, for £2OO commis- sion. The plaintiff, after his imprisonment, became tho defendants' traveller, and subsequently manager. The de- fendants argued that the plaintiff entered their employ by fralut, only giving the name of R. Oakley,"and surpressing the word " Banner," so that he could not recover. His Lordship held there was no defence, and gave judgment for the plaintiff.

SODDEN DEATH OF A BOLTON ALDEBMAN.—Mr. Charles Wolfenden has died very suddenly at his residence, Ash- leigh, Heaton, near Bolton. He attended a meeting at the Conservative Club on Monday, to consider the question of the Mayoralty, and left with Alderman Myles. On the way home he complained of a pain in his chest. Alderman Miles accompanied him to his residence. They reached the kitchen, where the latter expired in ten minutes, the cause of death being rapture of one of the small vessels of the heart. Alderman Wolfenden was Mayor for the borough in 1875,1876, and 1877. He was a sharebroker in business at Bolton and Manchester. His age was 59 years. Tim RIBBLE Wonas AT PREsrorr.—The contractor is proceeding very rapidly with the, works of the Ribble Navi- gation and Dock Improvement. Already extensive tram lines have been laid, and two locomotive engines are in ac- tive use for carrying purposes. Considerable progress has been made in the initiatory stages of the excavations, on which a heavy staff under the superintendence of Mr. Nott, is engaged. Substantial brick offices and other out- buildings have been constructed in a remarkably short space of time, and the Penwortham side of the river has under- gone quite a transformation. Vessels have during the week brought up extra loads of plant. A stationery engine has also been laid down in connection with the works. All the departments seem to have got into a good working groove, and there are not wanting signs that the undertaking is being pushed on energetically and with thoroughness. Maxtor Pat Etncnotes.—An analysis of the results of the municipal elections on Saturday shows that the Liberals had slightly the advantage. The principal gain was at Stockport, where they wrested seven seats from their opponents, and at York and Hertford, where they claim gains of four seats. They also gained three seats at Shef- field and at Luton ; two each at Boston' Blackpool, Barn- staple, Bury (Lancashire), Maidstone, Neath, Oswestry, Heywood, and Windsor; and one at Liverpool. Ashton- under-Lyne, Birkenhead, Bangor, Bodmin, Bootle, Derby, Devizes, Denbigh, Dudley, Rochdale, West Bremer:eh, Gravesend, Conway, Oldham, Bristol, Bolton, Chorley, Huddersfield, Lancaster, Launceston, South Shields, St. Ives, Haute, Stockton, Truro, Stamford, St. Helens, War- wick, Wells, Yeovil, and Newport, Isle of Wight. The principal Conservative gain was at Gloucester' where they won four seats. They also won three each at Colchester, Leamington, Newark, Norwich, and Shrewsbury; two each at Caine, Burnley, Exeter, Preston, Rotherham, and Scar- borough; and one at Accrington, Bewdley, Bedford, Beverley, Evesham, Plymouth, Falmouth, Reading, Tor- rington, Croydon, Dover, Grantham, Chard, Grimsby, Hun- tingdon, Louth, Rochester, Tynemoutb, Sandwich, Salis- bury, Southport, Yarmouth, Newcastle-under-Lyne, Poole, Oxford, Wigan, and Wakefield. At Macclesfield two Trades Unions replaced two Liberals and at Burslem a working. man's candidate won a seat. In this country the Liberals , gained 71 seats against 58 by the Conservatives.

SCARBOROUGH ELECTION: INCREASED LIBERAL MAJOR- ITY.—The election to fill the vac incy caused by Mr. Dod- son's elevation to the Peerage, took place on Monday. A telegram from a private source reached Sir George Sitwell on Sunday to the effect that General Gordon had been cap- tured. This was speedily promulgated and a general feel- ing of sorrow overspread the town. The poll opened at 8 a.m. on Monday, and shortly afterwards Liberal placards were issued entitled "Sunday lies," which they confronted with "Monday's truth," in the shape of a telegram from Mr. E. H. Hamilton, Downing-street to Mr. W. S. Caine, M.P , stating, "In reply to your telegram to Lord Richard Grosvenor, the news about Gordon's capture, which is put in circulation by a Paris journal, there has been no confir- mation whatever of it, and you may certainly discredit it." This and a more emphatic distinct denial of the previous Conservative telegram elicited another in reply to this effect, "Rowland Winn, M.P., to Sir Charles Legard, Bart. The Khedive on Saturday night telegraphed to the Queen that Gordon was prisoner and Khartoum is taken. He repeated it yesterday." Two or three hours later there appearea the following, issued from the Liberal Committee rooms.— "Foreign Office, 1-5 p.m. From Grosvenor to W. S. Caine, M.P. Statement in Times of this morning that the Khe- dive telegraphed to the Prince of Wales that Khartoum had fallen is absolutely untrue." During the afternoon Lady Londesborough telegraphed that she had heard privately from London that Khartoum had fallen, that Gordon was a i Prisoner, and that the Government was keeping the infor- mation back till after the Scarborough election. Blue (Con- servative) favours predominated the whole of the day, es- pecially about the harbour, where the fishermen polled in largo numbers for Sir George Sitwell on account Of the part taken by the Government in the passing of the Fishing Beat Act. The result of the poll was declared at 9-45 as follows :

Lieut.-Colorrel Steble (L) Sir George Sitwell (C) Liberal majority 289 While the Conservative figures are exactly the same ss at the last election, the Liberals show a gain of 67, so the Tory efforts in circulating false intelligences for party purpcses appear to have failed miserably,.

IifISCELLANBOUS EirrzeTatearEerr.—The first of a' series of weekly entertainments under the auspices of the Hope of Earlestown Lodge of Good Ternplars was held in the Lodge-room, Bridge-steeet, on Saturday evening. There was a very large attendance, and the chair was occupied by Brother E. Newman. After an address by the Chairman songs were nicely rendered by Sister Whitty, and Brothers McDonald, Kenning, and Walker; recitations by Brothers Gr:Warberton, Cob, and Mr. D. B. Griffiths, and Sister Barnard; and readings by Brothers Newman, Clarke, Ken- yon, and Barnard. The proceedings were interspersed with a selection of hymns, which were sung by the meeting. BLYLESTOWN CO-OPERATIVE SOGIETY—The quarterly meeting of the members and shareholders of the Earlestown Co-operative Society was held in the Co-operative Hall, Earle-street, on Wednesday evening, when there was a good attendance. The chair was occupied by Mr. Win. Davies, president. The retiring committee-men were Mr. J. Latham and Mr. J. Seddon, the former being re-elected, and Mr. William Pearson appointed in the place of Mr. Seddon. The quarterly report and balance sheet showed a profit of £IB3 Os 40, from which the society proposed to pay a dividend of 23 44 in the £ to members, and is 24 in the £ to non- members, which would leave a balance of .£1 Is OL-1 to be carried to the contingent fund.

GOOD TEMPLARY AT EARLESTOWN.—The quarterly session of the mending of the Hope of Earlestown Lodge of Good Templars was held in the lodge-room, Bridge-street, on Monday evening, when there was a full attendance. Brother John Taylor, W.C.T., presided. Soveral items of business were gone through, including the initiation of a new member, after which the quarterly reports of the officers were received. Brother Edward Newman, W.S., reported on the work of the lodge and coming arrangements, and said that there were 70 members inn good standing on the books, a slight decrease since last quarter. The Worthy Marshall (Brother W. Kenning) reported as to the state of the lodge property, and the Worthy Superintendent (Brother New- man) on the Juvenile Temple. The nomination and election of officers for the ensuing quarter was then proceeded with, the following being appointed :—Brother John Taylor, W.C.T., Sister E. Clarke, W.V.T., Brother E. Newman, W.S., Brother W. Hemmings, W.F.S., Brother George War- burton, sen., W.T., Brother A. W. Kenyon, W.Ch., Sister E. Whitty, W.M., Brother George E. Warburton, P.W.C.T. The officers were afterwards installed by Brother John War- burton, L D., assisted by Brother G. Clarke, D.M. Commit- tees for visiting the sick and absentees, and a finance com- mittee were appointed. A committee was also appointed to draw up the quarterly programme. The lodge closed about ten o'clock.

ORGAN RECITAL BY MR. H. J. DIIRDIAN.—In aid of the fund for clearing off the debt on the organ at the Congregational Church, Crow-lane, Newton, Mr. H. J. Darman, the late organist of St. John the Baptist's Church, gave an organ recital in that place of worship on Thursday evening. Notwithstanding the unfavourable character of the weather, there was a large congregation. Mr. Darman's abilities as an organist are well known, and his performance was greatly appreciated. At an interval in the proceedings the Bev. James Allett, pastor, stepped forward, and said that when the organ was opened their liabilities amounted to about £220, but since then the deficiency had been considerably reduced by contributions from both within and without the congregation, so that that night the whole of their responsibilities could be covered with £lOO. They pro- posed to raise that amount by organ recitals through the winter months, and in asking Mr. Durman to inau- gurate that series the committee were influenced by their strong desire to begin at home, and it had been a source of gratification to the members of the congregation gen- erally that the invitation had been so cordially accepted by Mr. Durman. A collection was made, and while this was being done Mr. Durman, by request, gave "In native worth" (Creation). At the close of the performance the Rev. James Allatt announced that the next recital would be by Mr. W. H. Jude, of Liverpool. TENANTS'DINNER AT NEWTON. The annual rent dinner to the tenant farmers on the es ate of Mr. W. J. Legh, M.P., in the Newton district was held:at the Pied Bull Hotel, Newton, on Monday evening About 70 persons par- took of dinner, there being also present—Mr. J. E Pardev, Mr. J. Fairclough (Warrington), Mr. G. Hilton, Mr. ter, Balharry, and others.—After the tables had been cleared Mr Pardey presided, and the usual loyal toasts were proposed and duly honoured.—ln response to the toast of "Mr. and Mrs. Legh," Mr. Pardey said on behalf of Mr. and Mrs. Legh and family he thanked them very much for the hearty way in which they had drank their health. Mr. Lrgh was always gratified when his health was drank, and he would be more ss when be knew it had been proposed by a very old tenant, one who had attended the 40th rent dinner. (Ap. plause )—ln proposing the toast of 'Success to Agriculture and Commerce," the Chairman observed that when they wished for success he was afraid they did not al ways get it. They all knew that if agriculture was not good commerce was not good.—Mr. Balharry responded for agriculture, and Mr. G. Airey, Lowton, for commerce, remarking that they all knew what a depressed state the country was in, and had been for some time past. At Wigan, which was his native place, the coal, iron, and cotton trade had not been flourish- ing for some years, but it seemed now to be reviving. Men were making more time, and when this occurred it was a. precursor o! better times, and he hoped it would continue.— Other toasts followed, the proceedings being enlivened by songs from several of the farmers.
NEWTON COMMISSIONERS. MONTHLY MEETING.

The monthly meeting of the Newton Improvement Corn. missioners was held at the Town Hall on Monday afternoon, when there were present—Messrs W. F. Gooch (chairman),. James Fairclough, B. B Glover, Thomas Hunt, T. J• Gillespie T. W. Emmett, J. E. Pardey, J. E. Woreley (law clerk), and R. Brierley (surveyor). The minute/I.a the last meeting were read and confirmed. HIGHWAY AND SANITARY COMMITTEE. - A meeting of the Highways, Public Works, and Sanitary Committee was held on the 6th October, at which Mr. Brierley submitted tenders fer the supply of trees and shrubs for the Cemetery;. Messrs Pardey, Stone, Hunt, and Fairclough were re-appoin- ted a special committee to consider the same and it was re- solved that Mr. Edward Green, of Warrington, be called in to advise upon the planting of the cemetery and the trees- most suitable for the purpose. At another meting of the Committee, held on the 20th tilt., Dr. Watkins attended to read his quarterly report and to announce the spread of scarlet fever.—The Surveyor haying certified the sum of £4OO due to Mr. John Bothwell on the cemetery buildings contract, a cheque for the amount was passed. It was re- commended that a person to act as cemetery keeper, gar- dener, and attendant, be at once advertised for at a salary of 25s per week, with house and coals free. The follow- ing plans were submitted and approved : William Mills and Thomas Ellison, 14 cottages in Wargrave-road ; Thos Molyneux, 6 cottages in Wargrave-road ; and W. Elson ad- ditional storeroom in Legh-street.—The minutes were con- firmed.

IMPORTANT SEWERAGE ARRANGEMENTS FOR EAMES- rows.—At a meeting of the Highways, Public Works, and Sanitary Committee, on the 6th October, it was resolved that the plans of the Central and Earlestown outlet sewers, as altered by Mr. Brierley, be approved, and that copies of the plans be submitted by him to Mr. Legh'a agent. The committee having further considered the plan for dealing with the sewage from the west outlet sewer at Earlestown, it was ordered that Mr. Brierley be iastructed to survey and take levels with a view to carrying the sewer under the canal, north side of the common lock, into tanks to be erected between the canal and the brook. Another meeting of the committee was held on the 20th ult. The committee having considered the necessity for extending the main sewer and repairing Wargeave-road, south of the entrance to the church yard, the Law Clerk advised that inasmuch as that portion of the road had never been repaired by the township, that in his opinion the expense of so doing was chargeable to the property owners abutting. Further con- sideration of the subject was adjourned.—Mr. Brierley read his communication of the 7th Oct. to Mr. Legh's agent respecting the land and easements for sewers and works, and reported that he had just received the following terms:— Land required for sewage works and easements for all sewers as shown upon ths plan, "a perpetual annual" rent of £5O, with the usual reaervation of mines, the Commissioners to indemnify Mr. Legh against any nuisance or damage by their sewage operations, and subject to arrangement for tenants' interest. rite offer was without prejudice, and not to be used in any negotiation in the event of its not beiag accepted by the Commissioners. It was resolved that the foregoing teems and conditions be accepted. It was ordered that the special committee be instructed to negotiate with the tenant of Newton Hall Farm for immediate possassion of the lead required for sewage works and Park-rd. improve- nient.—A letter was read from Mr. Worthington, dated 18th Oct., asking what steps the Commissioners were taki-Ig to pre- vent the sewage from flowing into the canal, west of Enke- town. It was ordered that Mr. Worthington he informed that an amended plan will be submitted as soon as possible. Tenders for the sewering of Wargrave, and south west end of Park-road, together with the improvement of Park-read near to Wargrave schools, were submitted, and it was resolved that the tender of Mr. J. Pennington, of Earlestown, amounting to 089, be accepted, and that the usual contract agreement be prepared.—On the motion of Mr. Fairclough, seconded by Mr. Gillespie, the minutes were passed. THE STREAD OF SCARLET FEVER AT EARLESTOML— Mr. Emmett said he had a word or two to say with regard to the spread of scarlet fever at Earlestown, mentioned in the minutes of the Highway aucl Publiq Work e CoMmittee. Ho

thought it was desirable that the Commissioners should placard the town cautioning or giving advice to the inhabit- ants, the danger they were incurring by going into houses where fever existed. He had good reason to believe that that had been done to a very considerable extent, and he was told that the fever had been much spread by that means. —Mr. Brierly said be could endorse what Mr. Emmett bad said with regard to the spread of that infection. It had been b nspread by neighboure going into each other's houses, believed every ease during the last month had been traced to have been carried from one house to another ia that manner. Mr. Pardy remarked that so doubt Mr. Enemett's suggestion was is very valuable one, but there might be some difficulty in getting the inhabitants to carry out the instructions.—The Chairman : That would be the difficulty, I believe.—Mr. Pardy said the medical elect bacl found one case that had been conveyed through attending a sort of tea party in the next bottee.—The Chairman said the people must know very well the dknger of visiting &autos where the fever was; and if their awn judgment did net tie" ter them they had only themselves :10 blame. He did not think the placards would have much effect beyond giving advice.—Mr. Gillespie said the placard might open their eyes to the danger, and would do no harm.—Mr. Emmett If it was placarded they would not be able to say that thel* were not aware 0 it. He would then move that placards be posted in the town, in terms drawn up, by the medical officer, the surveyor, and Mr. Wesley,—Mr, Gillespie had great pleasure in seconding the motion, which was passed. THE GAS QUESTION AGAIN.-At a meeting of the Gas and Water Committee, on the 20th October,the carbonizing' account for the first month was read, giving fuel used 149 tons, gas made 1,506,200 cubic feet, averaging 10,013 feet per ton of fuel used, the illuminating quality orthe gas be- ing equal to 20 candles at the works. It was ordered that the Law Clerk be instructed to enforce payment of arrears due from Messrs. W. Meadows and Son for tar and am- moniacal liquors,according to contract.—After the minutes had been passed, the Chairman alluded to the complaints made as to the quality of the gas at the last meeting, and asked if there had been any improvement in the quality. Mr. Brierley: No sir. The cause of the complaints have been local, and the gas is the same.—Mr. Pardey said the com- plaints had come from each end of the town —Mr. Brie:ley Nevertheless it was local. It bad been proved to the-com- mittee that it was local.—Mr. Gillespie remarked that un- fortunately the complaint emanated from different parts of the town, and it could hardy be exp'cted that all the pip!' were defective.—Mr,Brierley : We don't find complaints in other owls of the town.—Mr. : I beg you pardon. —The Surveyor: With regard to Mr. Gillespie, he has en" larged his house and not enlarged his pipes.—Mr. Gillespie It is only Mr. Brierley's statement that is the proof then.- -Mr. Brierley There is the test of the gas in the office. Mr. Glover stated that that was a qtaestion which was gone into at the last meeting. when Mr. Brierley said 20-candle' gas was made,which was a fair quality, and that the com- plaints were local. He (Mr. Glover) then joined in com- plaining upon the inferior quality of the gas, but since then he had gone into the question and at his house had found out sufficient explanation.—Mr. Emmett, after considerable discussion said in order to meet all wishes he would move that Mr. discussion, test the gas from day to day during next month, and that at the next meeting he produce the results. —Mr. Fairclougla added that at the same time he would like Mr. Brierley to go to the houses where complaints had been made and examine the service pipes.—Mr. Gillespie seconded the proposition, remarking that he should be glad to carry out any recommendation that could be made to improve the lights.—Mr. Brierley stated that a resolution had been passed that they had to supply 20-candle gas, and they did so. He challenged anyone to prove to the con- trary.—Mr. Gillespie asked if they always had the same pressure at the works.—Mr. Brierley said- they had except en Sunday nights, when the pressure was lowered a little on account of the various works in the town being stopped.-- The motion of Mr. Emmett was then passel. FINANCES.-At a meeting of the Finance Committee, on the 20th ult, accounts amounting to £1,105 4s 9d were examined and passed for payment.—The minutes were confirmed.

div.head: NOTES BY THE WAY.
div.p: NOTES BY THE WAY.

On Saturday Notts Association-b-ei ilesr.idon, at Notting- ham, by six gcals to two; at Cambridge, Lincolnshire and Cambridgeshire played a drawn game—one goal each ; Notts beat Sheffield Wednesday by one goal to none; in the Association Cup Competition', Old Westminsters beat the Bournemouth Rovers by six to none, St. George's (Birming- ham) beat Aston Unity by five to one, and Rornford beat Clanton by three to two; in the Dumbartonshire Cup Corn. petition, Dumbarton beat Renton by four be none and Vale of Leven beat Jamestown by four to one; in the Essex Cap Competition, the Old Foresters beat Excelsior by four to two; in the Staffordshire Cup Competition, the Wolverhampton Wanderers beat Stourbridge S,andard by five to one ; at Reading. Berks and Bucks beat Oxfordshire by four to one; at Oxford, the University beat Old Wyke- hamists by five to one; at Cambridge, the University beat the Swifts (a weak team) by 13 goals to none; Partick Thistle beat Our Boys (Dundee) by five to two; Hamilton Academicals beat Partick by four to two; Abercorn beat Lugar Boswell by three to two; Cowlairs beat Northern by five to none; at Chiswick, Upton Park beat Guy's Hospital by six to two ; in the Staffordshire Cup Competition, Wal- sall beat Burton S:rollers by ten to one; at Edinburgh, St. Bernard's beat Heart of Midlothian by one to none; Hiber- nians beat Cambuslanp; by two to one; at Bolton, the Wan- derers beat Halliwell by three to one; and Astley Bridge beat Eagley by five to three. The analysis of the scoring in the second round of the County Competition shows a good majority of points in favour of the victorious clubs, but the average (3.2 to 1) is less than half the record in the previous round (671 to 1.) Fifty-two clubs were drawn for the round, makiog 26 ties. One club (Accrington) has withdrawn, and 22 have been de- feated, while three pairs have not succeeded in settling their differences. There have been played 27 matches, in which 123 goals to 40 have been scored. Dividing the clubs into sections, as does in this column in connection with the first ,round, it appears that six teams of the Accrington, Church, and Rossendale districts scored 35 goals to 11 in seven matches; five Bolton clubs, 23 goals to 10 in six matches ; three clubs of the Preston district, 15 to 4; three Damen -clubs, 17 to 3; three Blackburn clubs, In two matches (one tie not being played), Bto 2; two Clitheroe teams, sto 3; Great Harwood 10 to nil; and four teams of other districts, 6 to 3.

On Saturday Warrington defeated Runcorn at the latter place, while the second teams met at Warrington, the re- su,t being a draw in favour of the visitors. The defeat of the Runcorn first team is the first that they have sustained this season.

The victory of Earlestown over Liverpool Stanley on Saturday was a popular one with the supporters of the first-named club. The defeat of the strong team sent to represent Stanley by two goals to none was a creditable performance for the local eleven. A d'spute as to one of the points scored by Earlestown brought the game to a conclusion some five or six minutes before the proper time.

The St. Helena Recreation Ist met Haigh Ist on the ground of the first-named club on Saturday, and the home team wone by one try and two minor points to nil. The play of Tickle and Seddon at three-quarter back was good, but the feature of the match was the game Green played on the wing, while the forward play of Parr, Gregor', Dean. and Rankin was prominent. The Bullough -brothers and Bootle for Haigh were repeatedly applauded for their dashing runs and the clever and neat passes they made. The Re- creation half backs ought to take a lesson flora them, and try to desist from holding the oval so long. The game throughout was a magnificent one, there being an absence of any wranglinz,. The St. Heleners have made a great improvement on their lastyear's form, and from the way the captain (Mr. Parr) at present handles its men it would seem as if the team will again rise to its old standard.

WARRINGTON BAND OF ROPE UNION CHILDREN'S FESTIVAL. On Monday evening a very successful children's festival was held in connection with the Warrington Pond of Hope Union. The festival was held in the Public Hall, which was crowded, the audience evidently largely consisting of parents of Band of Hope children. The platform, and also several rows of seats immediately in front, were filled with a specially trained choir of children, consisting in all of about 350 voices. This juvenile choir was further strength- ened by a select number of vocalists from Manchester Glee Union, who greatly contributed to the success of the even- ing. The choir WAS under the very efficient conductorship of Mr. C. H. Pigot, whose efforts were ably seconded by Mr. F. Booth at the organ. The Mayor had intended to preside on the occasion of this festival, but unfortunately, as was announced by Mr.W. Roberts, his worship found himself un- able to attend owing to his suffering from a severe cold. In consequence of this the chair was oecupied by the Rev. S. Wilkinson. The proceedings of the evening were opened by a hymn, "Toiling on," which was sung by the choir and audience, after which a prayer was offered up by the Rev. J. Yonge. A part song having been sung by the children and choir, The Cerairtatew in a few introductory remarks, said that while regretting the absence of the Mayor he was sure everyone connected with the Warrington Band of Hope Union would rejoice to see so many people present, not only children, but also parents of children, and tak- ing so much interest in that their first concert. The so- ciety they were met to support that night was called the Warrington Band ef Hope Union. It was an expressive title, and one which would speak home to the heart of everyone present. In the first place it was a Warrington Band of Hope Union; it was not a London, a Liverpool, or a Manchester, but a Warrington Band of Hone—some- thing which had to do with themselves, something which he hoped would influence the future of this town for good for ever and ever. Then again it was a Band of Hope Union, which was for the purpose of joining together the Christian people of Warrington, whatever might be their creed, and to teach the young temperance virtue and godli- ness. It had been said that II one could only get hold of the children, they might go or do what they liked after, bat they would be influenced by their first teachers. So he believed that it they could only instil into the minds of their children the great duty of temperance, the great duty , of abstaining from what might in future years do them , harm, and certainly would never do them any good, very ; much good would be effected. (Applause.) He urged the children to be very regular in their attendance at the Band of Hope meetings, for when there was a good atten- dance it was a great encouragement to those who worked for the cause, while on the other hand when the attendance was not good it was a discouragement. He hoped everyone I connected with that Band of Hope Union would try to do their duty in furthering the cause, because he believed it was a great and noble work in which they were engaged. If they only worked and strove hard then he believed the cause would advance amongst them. (Loud applause.) A part song was next sung by the choir after which the solo in the song," Angels are waiting" was so well rendered by a little girl named Polly Jane that she was enthusiastic- ally recalled. A glee, "Strike the Lyre," Was well rendered by the choir, as was also "A musical dialogue " by Lois Booth (Buttermarket-street). The next solo singer was Miss Eulalie M. Pigot, who gave "Where's my little Nellie" in a very happy manner, and was warmly applauded. In the second part, besides several pieces by the choir, "A Maiden and her bonnet" was prettily sung by Annie Murrell, who won quite an ovation, and a recitation by a boy named Peers, a member of Howley-lane Beind of Hope, was very successful. Mr. BEALES, of Manchester, also gave an inspiriting ad- dress, attending as a deputation from the Lancashire and Cheshire Band of Hope Union. He was there, he said, a Band of Hope boy who had been faithful to his pledge. (Applause.) Many years ago when he signed the pledge it was not a mere matter of experience; it was a matter of experiment as to whether a man could safely sign the pledge and live through it. It was now his experience that the Band of Hope boys and girls of 20 years ago had risen up and felt stronger without the assistance of alcoholic liquor, and would be able to live on to their old age. (Hear hear.) He then alluded to the fact that Joseph Livesey having attained the ripe age of 80 years, though he had been born of consumptive parents and been engaged in unwhole- some employments in his youth. The papers bad landed Joseph Livesy to the skies, and then they were warned, more especially by one notable paper, which said that cer- tainly great and good and lasting blessings had followed the life of Joseph Livesey, but it would caution his followers not to go to extremes in advocating their cause ; let it be done in moderation, this paper said, and then let the lower and illiterate classes of society take an example of modera- tion of the higher and educated classes of society. The ques- tion which occurred to him was which were the higher classes. (Laughter.) Another thought which occurred to him was that it was not a question of class and education and social position, but a question of the cursed drink itself. He asked them all that night, boys and girls and men and womee,if that alcohol they were fighting with was not the same cursed alcohol which the Bible condemned. He said it was the same alchol, and in many instances a ten times worse alchol. It was not a question of class but a question of the drink itself, which brought down the educated and highly elevated as well as illiterate artisan. They were there that night resolving that by the help of God, by precept and example, they would lead them to the bright and better times that were to come. (applause.) Dr. Thompson, the venerable ex-president of the Congregational Union, said he had now three times the influence over his scholars and Sunday school that he had before signing the pledge. He (Mr. Beales) asked Dr. Thompson if he felt anything prejudicial to his health through signing the pledge, to which Dr. Thompson replied "My dear sir, look at me; I assure you lam better in health and body." (Ap- plause.) Mr Beales then gave figures to show the larger number of children who joined the church from Sunday schools in connection with which there were Bands of

div.head: GREAT SANKEY SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: GREAT SANKEY SCHOOL BOARD.

The monthly meeting of this Board was held in the School-room, bankey, on Tuesday afternoon. There were present Messrs Turner (chairman), Ridgway, Cook, her. foot, and S. Sutton (clerk). FINANCE.—The Clerk reported that there was now placed to the credit of the Board in the bank £lOB 4s dd.—Cheques amounting to £34 4s 104 were signed. FEES.—A letter was read from the Education Department sanctioning the scale of fees fixed upon by the Board to be charged at the schools.

REPAIRING TIIE SCHOOLS.—The Chairman stated that the repairs to the schools, decided upon by the Board, had been executed, and the accounts sent in was as follows : Bricklayers, LI 17e 3d; joiners, £3 Os 3d. These accounts were ordered to be paid. APPLICATIONS.—AD application was read from Miss S. J. Gregory, 168, Liverpool-road, Sankey ' • and another from Miss M. H. Hobson, the Square, Penketh, for the two va- cant situations of assistant teachers.—After a short conver- sation Mr. Ridgway proposed, and Mr. Kerfoot seconded, that Miss Hobson be appointed at a salary of £35 per an. ' • and it was also agreed that Miss Gregory should be asked for further particulars as to her qualifications. THE ATTENDANCE OFFICER.—The Clerk said that it would not be ntcessary for the Board to proceed to the ap• pointment of an attendance officer as Mr. Shearer, who had hitherto done duty as attendance officer, said he would be willing to continue to do that duty providing the Guar- dians had no objections, and would expect no remuneration. —The Chairman said they were greatly obliged to Mr. Shearer for his offer, and it was agreed that it should be accepted. This was all the business of interest.

div.head: DEATH OF THE POSTMASTERGENER AL.
div.p: DEATH OF THE POSTMASTER- GENER AL.

News of the death on Thursday of Mr. Fawcett, the Postmaster-General, will be received throughout the king- dom with unfeigned regret. The hon, gentleman was seized a few days ago, at Cambridge, with an affection of the chest, which only became serious on Tuesday night. On Thursday morning the symptoms became severe, and in the afternoon he died. The sad news was received with great surprise and regret in the House of Commons. The right honourable gentleman was in the prime of life, having only completed his fifty-first year, but the severe illness from which he suffered a year ago had greatly weak- ened him, and a few days since it became known that he was again very unwell, though no more serious results were anticipated than absence from the House of Commons dur- ing the autumn session. The four years during which he has held the Postmaster-Generalship have been marked by reforms and improvements in the postal and telegraph de- partments that have borne abundant testimony to the en- lightened vigeur of his administration, and his numerous works on economic subjects, relative to both England and. India, have given him a high place amongst the first thinkers of the age. He has sat in Parliament over nine- teen years, the first nine as member for Brighton, and the last ten for Hackney. The Daily News says :—Mr. Fawcett had been laid up at Cambridge since Sunday last with an attack of pleurisy accompanied by inflammation of the lungs. Dr. Paget and Dr. Latham, who were in attendance, issued at 10-30 on Wednesday morning the following bulletin :—" Mr. Faw- cett has been suffering since Sunday last from a sharp at- tack of pleurisy with inflammation of the right lung. During the last twelve hours be has been free from pain, and his strength is maintained." On Thursday morning the following bulletin was issued at 10-30 :—" Mr. Faw- cett has had a restless night. In addition to the pleura- pneumonia there is increased bronchial irritation. The gen- eral condition gives ground for anxiety." Dr. Paget visited Mr. Fawcett at a quarter to three o'clock yesterday after- noon, and remained with him some time. In answer to questions, Dr. Paget said, "Mr. Fawcett is a little better than be was this morning. He feel himself better, and is better. There are decided signs of improvement." Between six and seven o'clock on Thursday evening the report of his death at about half-past five arrived ire London, and was shortly afterwards an- nounced in both Houses of Parliament. Lord Richard Grosvenor handed the telegram to Mr. Gladstone on the Treasury B-nch, and it was subsequently passed over to Mr. W. H. Smith, who made the fact known on the Con- servative side. The death of Mr. Fawcett 01010 as a great shock upon the House of Commons. It was known that he was ill, but it was not supposed that there were any danger- ous symptoms. Expressions of regret and sympathy found utterance not less on the Conservative side than amongst Mr. Fawcett's political friends.

div.head: _.•___. BRUTAL ASSAULT AT SANKEY
div.p: _.•___. BRUTAL ASSAULT AT SANKEY
BRIDGES.

On Wednesday afternoon Messrs. J. Rylands and J. Tins- ley, county magistrates, eat for a considerable time at the Session House, in Irlara-mtreet, IVarrington, engaged in hearing a case in which a married man named Enos Woods, of Sankey Bridges, was charged with assaulting Mary Stevens, wife of John Stevens, butler in the employ of the Rev. Sandys Jackson, the Vicarage, Sankey Bridges, and residing in Barnard-street, Sankey Bridges.—Mr. P. Davies, solicitor, Warrington, prosecuted, and Mr. A. Browne, soli- citor, Warrington, defended.—Mr. Davies applied that the Information, which charged the defendant with a common assault, should be altered to a charge of unlawfully and maliciously wounding and inflicting grievous bodily harm. —Mr. Browne opposed the application, but the Bench granted it, and the information was amended, and the more eerious charge was preferred against the defendant.—Mr. Davies, in stating the case, submitted that if the evidence he should call was true, the case was as bad a one as they could possibly hear, and the defendant might consider him- self fortunate that he was not charged with manslaughter. On Saturday, the B,h of October, Mrs. Stevens was in her house at about 8 30 in the evening, and bad occasion to go out to make some purchases at a shop at a corner of the street. On proceeding out of the house she saw defendant sitting underneath the window, and he said, " What have you been saying about my wife ?" She denied having said anything about his wife, and advised him to take no notice of idle tattle, and he °ailed her an " Irish cat." She replied, 0 Mr. Woods, do have sense, and do not take any notice of women's jars." She then went into the shop, and the de- fendant, after looking through the window, also went into the shop, and exclaiming" I'll do for you," struck her a violent blow on the back of the head. Mrs. Stevens imme- diately became insensible, and fell on the floor as though dead. She received a severe cut on the back of the head and bled profunsely.—The complainant then bore out the statement of her solicitor, and stated that she was taken to the Infirmary te have her wounds dre.sed. Cross-examined: Complainant denied that she had for three or four months past insulted both the defendant and his wife.—Dr. Starkey Smith said that he saw the complainant on the morning of the 19th ult. She was suffering from a vertical wound at the back of the head, about 1/ in. in length ; it was a scalp wound, and went to the bone, the skin being com- pletely severed. In his opinion a Sharp knuckle might pro- duce such a wound, because it was jagged, and not clean cut, as would have been the case with a knife. The wound, however, from its position, was more likely to have been caused by a blow from a blunt instrument than from a fall. He had attended her ever since, and she had been in very great danger through it. Cross-examined: The wound might have been caused by the woman falling backwards with her head against the blunt corner of a tile.—Sarah Ellen Gough, Howard-street, a little girl, spoke to seeing defendant strike complainant, and said that the blow was given at the side of the face, and the complainaet then fell. —Sarah Ann Bracegirdle also corroborated.—Mrs.William- son, in whose shop the affair took place, was called for the defence. She said there were five or six loose tiles placed one on the top of the other in a corner of the shop. Mrs. Stevens fell close by the tiles, and blood was found on the floor and alto on the tiles.—Mr. Browne admitted that tech- nically his client had been guilty of an assault, but said that he only hit the woman on the face and she fell, sus- taining the wound by falling on the tiles.—The Bench thought that the defendant had been guilty of a brutal as- sault ; even admitting that the wound was caused by fall- ing on the tiles, the woman.would not have fallen had the defendant not struck her. He would be fined .f.. 3 and the costs of the case.
Serious floods continue in the eastern provinces of Spain causing great damage to property, but only slight loss of life.

BOILER EXPLOSION: FOUR MEN KILLED AND 20 INJURED. —A boiler explosion occurred on Wednesday night at the Staffordshire Steel and Ingot Iron Works, Easton, killing four men and injuring about 20 others. It appears that three out of a range of ten large boilers, which generated steam for 33 engines, burst, and the engine-houses and basic shed were shattered. Two men were thrown into an ad- joining can 1, while two women, who had taken their hus- bands' supper, were severely scalded in addition to those killed and injured mentioned above:

Jardine's Acrostic; Fazikerley Plate, Sir G. Chetwynd's Chibbv ; Alt Welter Handicap, Captain Machel I's Canzoni ; Grand Sefton Steeplechase, Mr. Fitzgerald's New Meadow ; Wednesday. Plate, Mr. A. B. Sadler's Round Shot. On Thursday, Mr. Manton's Thebais won the Liverpool Autumn Cup, Mr. Leigh's Goggles being second, and Lord Zetland's Amalfi third.

THE " MIGNONETTE " Casn.—The Grand Jury at Exeter Assizes, on Monday, found a true bill against the captain and mate of the unfortunate yacht Mignonette for murder- ing the boy Parker in order to prolong their own lives. Baron Haddleston, in his charge, said the taking of the I.oy's life , was a case of deliberate homicide in regard to which there was no saving clause in law. Dudley and Stephens, captain and mate of the Mignonette, were tried at Exeter Assizes, on Thursday, on the charge of having murdered Richard Parker, on the high seas. The jury, acting on the sugges- tion of Baron Iluddlestone, returned a special verdict on the facts of the case, and the Supreme Court is left to decide the point of law as to whether the act was mutder, The men have been admitted, to bail,

78}, Carr sirionding quarter last year Mr. Pardey remarked that the school attendance ofGcer had complained of the want of school accommodation at Earles- town, and there was no doubt many children ia Earlestown did not attend school. That was owing to a want of assist- ance at Vie Eariestown District Infants' school. It had got abroad that complains had been made against the mistress, but there had not been the slightest imputation against her, and everyone felt she had done everything sine could. He did not know whether that Beard would feel it to tee its duty to take any action to meet present requirements. They had of course to consider the pockets of the ratepayers, but unless so.nething was done soon they would have a school board stepping in, and it would mean an addition to the rates.—Mr. Eunnett stated that there was a want of teachers at the infants school, and that being so, scholars who for- merly attended were wandering about the streets.—The Chairman asked under what management the school was carried on.—Mr. Pardey stated that it was under the man- agement of a body of trustees, and he thought it was a matter that ought to be looked into. There were originally ten trustees—the vicar of the parish and the Chairman for the time being of the London and North-Western Railway' Company being ex officio trustees. He believed that most of the trustees had allowed their qualifications to lapse, and some steps ought to be taken to fill up the trust—The Chairman thought the matter should be brought before the managers of the school as far as they knew them.—Mr. Par- dey said there was a necessity for enlarging the school, and there was land to enlarge it upon. It could .be done at com- paratively little cost, and it would save the the township a considerable sum in rates.—On the motion of Mr. Glover, seconded by Mr. Gillespie, it was resolved that the law clerk should communicate with the managers of the school upon the subject. This was the principal business of interest.

DARING BURGLARIES AT EARLESTOWN. During the present week two burglaries of a most daring character have been committed in Earleatown. In both cases the unfortunate sufferers have been tradesmen of long standing, and the fact that their premisea are situated in the principal streets of the town, and that rsarties were sleep. lug there at the time of the robbery tends to show the daring nature of the burglars. The first robbery was com- mitted at the shop of Mr. Siddeley, grocer and previson dealer, Earle.street,on Sunday night or early on Monday ' morning. Mr. Siddeley and his wife retired to bed on the Sunday night after seeing that everything was safe and securely fastened, and nothing disturbed their slumbers until about two o'clock on Monday morning, when Mr. Sid- delay heard a small dog, which had been brought into the house on the previous day, making a noise though not barking. The dog being new to the house M. Siddeley thought nothing of the circumstance,, but when he went down stairs about seven o'clock in the morning, , he ascertained that BOMB person or persons had forcibly en- tered the house and shop. The stairs door had been propped" from the outside by the burglars, so that they would have little to fear from anyone coming down the stairs. Ultimately Mr. Siddeley forced open the door, when he at once saw that the shop had been thoroughly ran- sacked from top to bottom. Every drawer had been pulled open and their contents scatterectabout ; the money drawer and desk were prized open, and papens, &1., thrown over the counter and floor, but luckily the burglars secured no money, for Mr. Siddeley, as an act of precaution, had re-- moved all the cash on. the previous evening. The robbers evidently detexmined not to return empty handed, then seized a number of shirts and stockings, with which they de- camped. It was afterwards ascertained that the house- breakers had gained admission by taking out a pane of glass from the kitchen window and then unfastening the window catch. In their 11,ght they left open the back door. The affair was duly reported to the police, who are actively be- stirring themselves in the matter, but as yet no apprehen- sion has been made.

The second and most serious burglary was committed at the shop of Mr. Thomas Cooper, watchmaker and jeweller, Market-street, late on Wednesday night, and here the rolrbers secured considerable " booty." Mr. Cooper was away from home that night,. and the house and shop were left b charge of Mrs. Cooper and a daughter, 15 years of age. After locking up the shop and fastening all the doors and windows Mrs. Gooper and her daughter went to be. about ten o'clock. An hour and a half 'atm Mrs. Cooper was disturbed by The barking of their dog wEch was chained_ at he bottom of the stairs, and near to tte door leading' from the house to the shop. She called to the dog, which. continued to bark, however, and from othezmoises she heard gee was convinced that some person or parsons had broker. into the shop. She thereupon shot up the bedroom window 4 and immediately afterwards heard the steps of some persons 'running away. She and her daughter shortly afterwards went downstairs and,saw evidences that a burglary ban been com— mitted. Mrs. Cooper got the assietance of several neighbours and information of the robbery was given to the police, but in this balance the man or men got clear away. Entrance had been efte' cted by the breaking of one of the kitchen win- dows and unfastening the "catch.".ln doing this the person would seem to have cut his hand, for the gl ies was stained with blood, while the poker, which had evidently been seized as a weapon In case of a "surprise," was also stained with blood. The poker was thrown down in the yard by the robber In hi, flight. Oa an examination of the shop being made it was found that a large quantity of gold earrings, gold and silver rings, brooches, bracelets, breast pins, and studs bad been extracted, and with those the thief ' made off. The total value of the missing articles is about £3O, and there is no doubt that but for the discovery, br Mrs. Cooper, of the robbery, a large number of other goods would have been stolen. W 3 may add that, fortunately, all the watches and other articles left with Mr. Cooper for re- pair were untouched. It is to be hoped that the offender or offenders will be brought to justice.
