Fine" Fellows—Magistrates. A Pillar of the Church—A pious apothecary. ART OF CONVERSATION.—You convince a man, you pe - suade a woman. Why are pawnbrokers like pioneers of progress ?—Because they are always ready to make an advance. "Every man is born with a Mentor," says a henpecked husband. "That's his conscience. When he gets older, he often gets a tormenter. That's his wife." "Major, I see two cocktails carried to your room every morning, as if you had some one to drink with." "Yes, sir; one cocktail makes me feel like another man; and, of course, I'm bound to treat the other man." A lion-tamer quarrelled with his wife, a virago, and was chased by her round his tent. Sorely pressed, he took refuge in the cage among the lions. Oh, you contemptible coward," she shouted, "come out if you dare !" Meissonier, since the opening of the exhibition of his pic- tures, has apparently a dislike to paint women; his reply to a critic who asked him for his reason was merely, "They can paint themselves better than I can." Scene—Scotch grocer's. Apprentice has spent half an hour looking for a missing brush. Highland master: " Whaat for are you spending the whole day for the last half-hour looking for a sing when you know quite well that you'll never find a sing but where waas it?" "I have concluded not to go to the play to-night," said Fixton to Mrs. F.; "I want to see a friend; and, besides, you know, it's a little damp, and you might catch cold, dear." Mrs. F.: "Catch cold! You humbug, your first thoughts are always for yourself !" Fixton : "Yes, dear, and my second are for you; and second thoughts, you know, are always the best!" Hearing a noise at night, Jones descends with a lighted candle, and discovers a burglar escaping with a full sack. "Hallo," he cries, " come back, you 1" "Eh, what ?" re- turns the burglar. " Ah, yes, the silver candlestick Per- mit me." He takes it from the hand of the astonished Jones, and puts it into his bag. "Ten thousand thanks. Have I forgotten anything else ?" "What caused your little boy's illness ? " asked an in- genuous mother of a mother whose little son was very ill. " He was climbing a ladder," said the lady," and lost his equilibrium." "Poor little fellow !" said the sympathetic listener. Do buy him another; he'll be more careful next time !" COURAGE.—" Charles A. Dana married when he was re- ceiving sdols. per week for literary work," said Captain Gray, putting aside a newspaper which contained a picture and biographical sketch of the great journalist. "By George, he must have had a courage !" "Not necessarily,' replied Mr. Balkins. "I was never regarded as a man of extra- ordinary courage, yet I married when I had only &lois. in money and no income at all." "I should regard that a very courageous act." "No," replied Mr. Balkins, "for you see the girl I marricd was worth 50,000dols." ASSOCIATIONS.—The Press Association—pen, ink, and paper; the Medical Association—pills, powders, and plas- ters; a musical association—wood, string, and brass ; Asso- ciation for the Promotion of the Fine Arts—brush, palette, and colour; a literary association—books pamphlets, and periodicals.; a sanitary association—cleanliness, wholesome dietary, and sobriety; the Supply Association—victuals, liquors, and condiments; a legal association—wig and gown, and "black cap ;" the Liberal Association—s s. d.; the Licensed Victuallers' Association—pewter-measures, beer- pumps, and whisk-Casks; the Association of the Virtues— faith, hope, and charity.—Bailie. In olden tilme, before Maine laws were invented, one Wing kept the hotel at Middle Granville, and from his well- stocked bar furnished " accommodation for man or beast." He was a good landlord, but terribly deaf. Fish, the village painter, was afaicted in the same way. One day they were sitting 'by themselves in the bar. A traveller from the South, on his way to Brandon, stepped in to inquire the distance. Going up to the counter, he said, "Can you tell me, sir, how f.r it is to Brandon ?" "Brandy ?" said the ready landlord, jumping up." "Y, sir, I have some "—at the same time handing down a decanter of the precious liquid. "You misunderstand me," said the stranger; "I asked how far it was to Brandon." "They call it pretty good brandy," said Wing. "Will you take sugar with it r—reaching, as be spoke, for the bowl and toddy-stick. The despairing traveller tamed to Fish. "The landlord," said he, "seems to be deaf. Will you tell me how far it is to Brandon ?" .Thank you," said Fish, "I don't care if I do." The stranger treated, and fled.

The Bank rate was again advanced 1 per cent. on Thurs- day. It is now 5 per cent. The Oldhatn magistrates on Wednesday committed to the Liverpool Assizes Edward Abraham, the solicitor's clerk who is charged with forging the endorsements upon a cheque for £1,500 sent by an insurance society to his employers, and stealing the money which he obtained from

the bank. " TICHBORNITEISM." The " Claimant " has recently addressed three meetings at Leeds. Each were great failures in point of attendance, and as a last resort to attract public attention one of his few friends suggested that the Claim- ant's supportcrs should find the capital for an independent newspaper to advocate Tichborniteisrn. THE AGNEW LIBEL CASE: SEVERE SENTENCE.—At the Manchester Assizes, on Wednesday, Mr. Edward Brooke, of Pabo Hall, Conway, was indicted for libelling Mr. Agnew, M.P. for South-East Lancashire, and Mr. W. Lockett Agnew, his nephew. Mr. Brooke pleaded guilty, and the Solicitor-General addressed the Court in mitigation of punishment. The Judge described the libel as a most cruel one, and fined the defendant £5OO for the libel on Mr. Agnew, M.P., and £5 for the libel on Mr. W. L. Agnew; and ordered him to pay the whole costs of the prosecution. CONVERSATIONAL ENGLISK.—What Interesting and impor- tant information often passes as word currency, and converse upon topics In which no great differences of opinion are likely to arise. Precise rules cannot be established to trace the origi- nal calves cf a prevalent idea. or the various seasons why we are content to sink our prejudices when approaching what, nolens voices, has become the vogue. Amongst the many we are content to take one illustration of the rapidity with which the public appreciate being well served. The Bradford Manu- facturing Company, having made a new departure, resolved to deal only with consumers direct, as previously the public generally had little option but to pay the regulation high prices, which it is reasonable to suppose must be put upon dress goods which pass through the hands of merchants and shopkeepers before reaching the final purchaser. The Company had a keen eye to the requirements of the pub lc, and had evi- dently carefully weighed the matter and the soundness of the principle of direct trading. Few cared to interest them- selves in the matter when the first offers were made through the Press to the public, but those that did avail themselves were not sissy to make their friends duly acquainted with the advantages of buying direct; and so, almost imperceptibly, the system has gained ground until thousands of ladies now pur- chase direct from the looms of the Bradford Manufacturing Company, at Bradford, Yorkshire. div.head: OF THE PEOPLE.
div.p: OF THE PEOPLE.

Sir.—lt often seems an-37;U; ;fine-jet; perplexity to some of our parsons to account for the apathy and indifference exhibited by the large majority of the working people towards the established Church and her services. Our clergy attempt to solve this by attributing such to the levity and wickedness of the age, and in viewing the matter from such a standpoint they allow themselves to become perfectly blind to any fault connected with themselves or foe Church. But to my mind to this alone is the unpopularity of our Church and her ministers to be attributed. Allow me to ask at whet period of her.history have her actions been found directed on the side of the people and in support of their liberty ? I doubt if we should be able to find one instance of it. But, in opposing and crushing the cause of liberty, and in aiding the strong against the weak have her actions chi-tly been directed. As an instance of this, whenever a Bill has ben brought forward (as in the case of the Fran- chise measure) extending our liberties, the bishops' actions have been, with few exceptions, directed in endeavouring to destroy it, and, I believe, so long as our Church is joined to the State will this be so. But I Arn not going to enter into the question of disestablishment. All I have to say upon this matter is this—if the Church cannot exist and support itself without the aid of a temporal prop like the State, such goes to prove that she is rotten and lifeless, but Ido not for a moment credit this. Now I admire the Church's service as much as any one, and I do not object to whet some may style "High Church." I lik3 to Ibten to good singing, and to listen to an eloquent sermon; but I must, as far as my experience goes, confess the latter is a treat to the congregations of most of our churches, cbuntry ones in particular. The sermons we are compelled to listen to are for the most part doll and insipid, and this often rendered more so when it has to be read word for word from manuscript. In such churches, and where the sermons are of this klrad, need our parsons be disturbed at the apathy, and perhaps undevotional aspect of his congregation, which perhaps feels a wholesome relief when the words of the Benediction are pronounced? The minister is often grieved ti find his listeners growing beautifully less under his preaching ; while perhaps he sees his less educated brethren, the Dissenters, are drawing large congregations. I believe the established Church does not represent the re- ligious opinions of one•half of our country, and although the Establishment costs us hard upon Ten Millions per annum, she is no more the Church of the Nation than the Irish Church was before its disestablishmmt.—l am, Sir, etc., POPULI. November Oth, 1884.
THE WARRINGTON CORPORATION AND THE SHIP
CANAL.

That it will pay us to contribute for if we don't thc promoters will not grant the clauses without putting the town to the expense of a petition. 5. That if we have to petition it will probably cost us a rate of 41 in the Z.—Yours truly, OBSERVER. Sir,—The comparison I made in your issue of the 25th ultimo, between the amounts which the chief supporters of the rate in promotion of the fillip Canal scheme and its chief opponents would respectively have to pay in the un- likely event of the rate being levied, has received more attention than I anticipated it would, and has been some- what misunderstood by one or two of your correspondents ; kindly, therefore, permit me a word or two by way of re- joinder. Let me inform " Clifford Dix" that the opposing firms Oppose as firms, and that the full force of their votes will follow their signatures; whereas I cannot without authority consider Dr. Mackie as representing Mackie and Co., Limited. Hence my figures on both sides are as fair as I can possibly make them. However, taking it that Dr. Mackie represents Mackie and Co. (who are assessed on 1.392 10s.), and that Mr. George Woods represents the Longford Wire Co (whose works are outside the borough, and are not rated to the extent of a single penny within it), the four supporters of the rate at the Public II 11 would re- present a total assessment of £789 lOs , as against the £10,941 of four of the opponents. I may add that the in- dividual proportion which at least two gentlemen would be called upon to contribute of their firm's rate represents a much larger sure than that represented by the contributions of the four supporters referred to and their firms all added together. If "Clifford Dix" otnnot see that there is a great prin- ciple involved; if he cannot see that the question before the ratepayers is pre-eminently one upon which no majority however large cm legitimately claim to force a minority however small, I have no more to say to him. To Mr. George Woods, not a single line of whose letter is fairly warranted by anything I have written, and scarcely a statement in whose letter is correct, I think it best on the whole not to reply. And for two reasons: The publ.c can- not be at all interested in my personality ; and I could not well follow my friend's advice to avoid personalities in dealing with a letter containing nothing but person dities.— Yo crs, Ltc., LIBRA.

div.head: SHIP CANAL RATE.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL RATE.

Sir,—l have been challenged to defend my attendance and action at the town's meeting., and my opposition to the proposed rata in promotion of the Ship Canal. I accept the Challenge. Considering my connection with tha largest manufacturing and ratepaying firm in the borough, I hold 'that although debarred from taking part in the proceedings of the formal meeting. and from holding up my hand against the elayor'e resolution, I was, nevertheless, entitled to attend the meeting and watch the proceedings. Further, I had at least as much right at the meeting as Mr. Adameon, Mr. Leader Williams, and other members of the Ship Cereal Committee from Manchester, whom the Guardian, in a leader issued the day before the meeting, intimated would attend it. _ My position was ex- plained to the Deputy-Town' Clerk. I did not vote on the resolution, or take any part whatever in the meting until the proceedings udder the Act governing the meeting were at an end. I refer to the moment when the demand for a poll was mile. With that demand (as the Mayor quite correctly intimated at the time, and as pro- bel;ly everybody except Alderman Burgess knows) the form 11 ratepayers' meeting was at an end. Thenceforth the meeting was open to anyone. Knowine this, and regretting as I did the action of the Mayor in haying apparently per- sisted i king the vote whiles a ratepayer was standing up claiming in loud tones to be heard ageinet the resolution oon of C wage resulting in such confusion that a lar: e p sense of duty, the persons in the Hall did not grasp the issue put and did net vote at all upon it), I Was impelled by in the interests of fair play and in order to afferd the Meyer the opportunity he subsequently had of explaining his otherwise incomprehensible action, to rise and cell attention to so unfortunate an incident. The qeestion of the relative numbers for and against the resolution is not now worth pursuing, inasmuch as from what I hear there ewe several ratepiyers prepared to demani a poll under any circum- stances. With respect to the treatment I received at the hands of the meetieg, I have no complaint to make. I know how irritating the expression of an adverse opinion is to any mejority in any meeting, and, compared with the manner in which opponents to the rate in Manchester were received, my reception was most courteous. The proceedings at the Manchester town's meeting are thus summarised is the Manchester Guardian of October 11th :—" Speakers in favour of the Ship Canal were listened to, and others shouted "down. The resolution was put by the Chairman, and a vast majority of hands held up in favour of it. A poll was demanded in the midst of such yells and execra- tions as rarely fall to the lot of a murderer."

div.head: CHURCH CHOIR.
div.p: CHURCH CHOIR.

Sir,—As, I regret to s-air7my-n—arne—has come before the public in connection with the above, I should be glad Lobe allowed space for a few lines of facts, and that without being considered egotiatica% Briefly, then, the history of nay connection with the Parish Church is as follows: Five years ago, in reply to an advertisement, I offered my ser- vices as organist and choirmaster to the Parish Church, and, as requested, named my terms, i e, £lOO a year stipend. The Rector invited an interview, and in the course of con- versation stated that the choir had memorialised him, unanimously, to appeiat Mr.Pattison, but as that gentleman had insulted Mrs. Qnekett he would never have him in the church again; and, further, that some few members of the choir then asked him to appoint Mr. W. S. Woods, but as that gentleman's father had behaved very badly to him, the Rector would on no account have any membtr of the Wood family officially connected with the church. Then the Rector stated that there would be another advertisement different to the flrs', but I tired net mind it, and he would write me again. The second advertisement drily appeared, and to my astonishment £5O was now named (for the first time) as the fixed stipend. The Rector kept his word and wrote me again ; but on the second in'erview I told him that the second advertisement was so different from the first that I could no longer censider the app-intment worth baying. The Rector relied that if I thought only of the £5O stipend I was making a great mistake, as, by his influ- ence as former clerical secretary, and now a mernbsr of the committee, he felt quite jastffiei in saying that he could ensure my appointment (if I became his organist) to the Clergy Daughters' School, the music mastership of which was then vacant, and no doubt the Training College would also BEIOI3 be vacant, as they had also got tired of having the same music master as the Clergy Daughters formerly bad. Etch appointment WdS worth 100 guineas a year; and then, besides, there was an excellent teaching connection in the town, simply wa'ting for the new man to take no. How could I withstand this Warringtonian El Dorado? I knew absolutely no one in the town, and so could not inquire. Besides, why should I not trust the Rector? Well, I did trust him, and there alas! as I found to my cost, I grieviously erred. The Clergy Daughters' School has no music master to this day ; and only last Christmas the Training College appointment became vacant, and I was not appointed because (as I have every reason to know) I wa3 officially connected with the Rector!

- During my five years apprenticeship in learning to fairly estimate and appreciate the Rector's stability of character, I bad several offers of much more lucrative appointments, but I refused them one by one in deference to the rectorial beguilements, until the event of last Christmas referred to above, and then, somehow, my eyes, which so far I had been able to keep shut, refused any longer to perform that blind- ing Office, and, sir, I was wide awake! I determined to re- sign, but how could Ido so just then? The Rector had re- signed to the bishop; his two curates were leaving " be- cause" (as the Rector told me) "be could not saddle his successor with his nitrates"; so when he had got rid of them he would "hang up his harp." (Parenthetically, I thought at the time, that there was another and more ancient instrument of the harp family which the revd. gentleman might have hung up once for all, with advantaee to the community at large, and myself in particular.) Well, with a new rector things might be better; they couldn't be worse, I thought, so I decided to wait and see. Lo! what did I see? The curates went loaded with testimonials not of the Rector's pramoting. Than the resignation was withdrawn, as there was no valid resig9ation till the Rector resigned to the Patron who is not the bishop! After all was quietened down, on the 20th Jane last I asked the Rector to increase my stipend. On the 22nd, in presence of his warden, he told me it could not be done, the offertory having gone down considerably since the two curates (Nos. 68 and 67!) went, &e., &re On the 23rd I accordingly gave three months' notice of resignation. The choir then memorialised the Rector and wardens to retain me. Both the latter repeatedly expressed themselves in reply that they were most anxious to do so. But no reply cams from the Rector until Sunday, September 14th, when the choir were invited to the rectory—not, however, to hear a reply to their memorial as to myself, but about another matter. They pressed the subject of the memorial, when the Rector expressed himself as eager to retain me, and said finally that he would fall in with whatever the wardens ar- ranged. The latter had prey ioasly aecertained from me the terms on which I would cmient to remain, and the Rector's warden said "it could ba done—it only depended on the Rector." After the interview the choir informed me that it was all arranged and that I was to stay. General jubilation! But alas for Rectorial promisee! On the 29th September, at 5.30 pm, I received an intimation signed by the Rector and wardens "that they had come to the conclu- sion te accept my resignation as tendered on the 23rd June last, and with many thanke for my past services, &c., &c.," they "begged to subscribe themselves"—what they were— " Rector and Wardens." Of course I mid say much more as to the incidentals of my appointment and connection with the Parish Church, but I refrain and shake the Rectorial duet from my feet, "a sadder and a wiser man." Apologising for so far trespassing on your space—Yours, C. E. ROWLEY. 14, St. Ann's-square, Manchester.

div.head: TEIE VACCINATION CONTROVERSY.
div.p: TEIE VACCINATION CONTROVERSY.

Sir,—You very kindly published my last letter to you, in which I promised to notice the conduct of the Local Government Board, in relation to the late prosecutions at New-ton, also the merits of vaccination, but as many events relating to these prosecutions including distraints and im- prisonment, are still pending, it woullonly be wise to say the Local (London) Government Board have ever been known to screen vaccination from reproach, to secure this object ;as at Norwich and Blackburn, no pains or expense are usually spared. As regards vaccinnation itself, it is un- defined and totally undefinable. The lymph operation and marks vary in almost every district, the doctor alone defin- ing his operation and. punctures, and wha' ever these may be and how performed it as gospel vaccination, the merits or demerits being largely determined thereby. When man was first created, and. was fresh from the hands of his Maker, there was given to him every herb bearing seed for the sustenance of his bxly a natural portal was also

div.head: EXAMINER SATURDAY, NOVEAMER 8, 1884.
div.p: THE EXAMINER SATURDAY, NOVEAMER 8, 1884.

given. The practice of inserting beneath the skin WU not thought of then. Are we wiser than our Maker now? The blood, which is the life, has ever had a network of critics to preserve it from contamination ; first the stomach, the digestive organs, and the various processes of assimilation, etc. Vaccination at once ignores all these, hence I must here suggest to your readers that which enters not by the stomach to the blood:, but climbeth in some other way, the same is a thief and a robber. In the vegetable world it is the rotten or decayed parts that live upon their sounder and purer neighbours, as instance the rotted apple may soon contaminate a host of its sounder kind. The onion, potatoa, &3, have the same attributes, and the greater 1 the rottenness, toe greater its proficiencies; "ill weeds will up." The rotted apple can never act on that which is equally rotten with itself; it can only pollute that which is superior to itself, and the more superior the more and better food it is, and hence an easier prey. Now what is true in the vegetable world must.be true in the animal world, for the same God of the vegetable is also God of the animal, and can never contradict himself. The lymph (disease) then Can never act on any supposed smallpox within the body, but must act only on those parts healthier and sounder than itself, the purest, and noblest, because better food, being the easiest prey. Hence females, because finer and superior in texture and sentiments (like Miss Ellen Terry), suffer con- siderably, and were it not for the wonderful recuperative powers of living nature soon not one of the vaccinated would be left to tell the tale. Of the wisdom of thus tax- ing children in their earliest infant days your readers can judge, for if only say 10, 20, or 40 of their healthiest days I be usurped in resisting imported disease, how much force will remain to battle with the natural ills a child is heir to? If it be such a task for some of us to cut our wisdom tooth, what must it be for a child to cut twenty ? Farther, assuming vaccination to be the greatest godsend or blessing humanity ever had, what then about compulsion? Intemperance is a canker worm, eating up the very vitals of the nation, yet none of us ever even think of making total abstinence compulsory. Infidelity is the twin sister of in- temperance; but we don't make church and chapel going compulsory, and where'Would be the Christianity of Christ were it compulsory; and where would be man's free will ? If all of us made our likes,dislikes, and beliefs compulsory on our neighbours, would this not substitute the law of force for the law of love, and usher in the time when "those may take who have the power, and those may keep who can." Again, if any neighbour being injured by (and claim com- pensation for) my four yet unpolluted children, lam open to consider the claim. Your kind insertion will bo a great favonr.—Yours, &c., ALEXANDER FORSTER. 19, Regeat-street, Etriestown, Nov. 3rd, 1884.

RUNCORN AND WIDNES, RUNCORN LIBERAL ASSOCIATION.—ANNUAL MEETING. A special and annual general meeting of the Runcorn Liberal Association was held in Bethesda School-room, Runcorn, on Tuesday evening. Mr. R. Shaw, president, oc- cupied the chair, and amongst those present were Messrs. B. Kmveton, T. Handley, J. Bridgewater' F. J. Adams, F. J. Norman, C. Littler, J. Faulkner, J. Clarke, Lunt, J. Cur- zone, W. Reedier, W. Marsh, R. Boyle, B. Bisbrown, and 0. Leak (secretary).—On the motion of Mr. B. Kniveton, 3ecoaded by Mr. Bridgewater, it was unanimously decided that the annual general meeting should be held in the month of November. This resolution was necessary in order that the names of the members elected to salve upon the Central Liberal Council for Mid-Cheshire could be forwarded at the proper time.—The minutes of last meeting having been read and confirmed, Mr. 0. Leak read the annual report, and also a report from the revision agent with refer- ence to Runcorn, which rend as follows :—" The result of the revision in 1884 leaves the position very much as before. Many claims and objections made by either side being found invalid were mutually withdrawn. It is to be regretted that these objections have to be made, but owing to the policy of the Tory agent we are obliged to defend ourselves by similar tactics. Liberal property claims Conservative do. Conservative gain l. Liberal objections to old register and overseers' Hate Comervative objections to old re- gister and overseers' lists ..... Liberal gain Liberal £l2 occupiers' claims Conservative do. Liberal gain • Nett Liberal gain 9 The Revising Barrister refused this year to allow any claim where the rateable value of the property as assessed by the committee was under the sum of £l2 instead of as previously accepting the letting value."— Mr. Whinyates moved, and the Chairman seconded the adoption of the report.—The motion was carried.—The next business was the election of president, and the Chair- man remarked that last year he told them be hoped they would exercise their privileges of making a change. It would not make the slialatest difference to him whoever was elected. He should support the Association in every pos- sible way he could. (Applause.) He did not think it wise always to have the same president, the some treasurer, and The same secretary.—Mr. T. Handley proposed the re-elec- tion of Mr. Shaw as president of the Association for the en- suing year. (Loud applause.) He did not think it wise at this time to replace a gentleman who had been president for several years, because before another year had passed there would prObably have been an extension of the fran- chise, and may be a general election, and additional work would be thrown on the Association. Under these circum- stances it was well to have old officers when great changes were about to take place. Mr. Shaw had served them well In the past, and he had no doubt would serve them well in the future.—(Applasse )—Mr. F. J. Adims seconded the proposition with great pleasure.—Mr. B. Kniveton sup- ported the resolution, which was carried with loud acclama- tion.—The Chairman, who was cordially received, said he was snitch obliged to them for again appointing him to the position of president, but, as he had said before, nothing could affect his views upon political matters. They did not depend upon any office he might hold; he loved the cause. As long as there were inequali• ties which he censidered ought to be put right, and put right at a very much quicker rate than they had done for a long time past. (Hear, hear.) No small thing would pre- vent him from being a staunch Liberal. (Hear, hear.) When they oonsidered how good tempered the people were in waiting for reforms which they ought to have had years ago, and which would have been a blessing to the masses of this country, he thoueht they ought not to be thin- skinned in a matter of this kind. (Hear, hear.) They in Runcorn had done the best they could for Liberalism, and he was sure that if Runcorn at the next election did what was done at the last election they would not stand badly off. He could assure them from facts that they knew, although no one could tell how any person voted, that there was a considerable majority for the Liberal candidate in the Runcorn district, and it was owing to the votes in the country districts, where there were not the means of gather- ing the population together, and placing before them the exec' position in which the two political parties stood with regard to the people. He had never been able to talk to a Conservative long without finding that he was a Liberal. It was strange, but it was so. Cn the surface they appeared strong Conservatives, but he had not come in contact with one who would say that the present land system was right. The other day he was speaking to a Conservative, and seid "Suppose you managed to save a few hundred pounds and wished to leave it to your children; do you think you onght to pay con- siderable more duty to the Government of this country for the transfer of that money to your children than the Duke of IVestmiester could transfer the sime value of land for?,' He added Now, supposing there should be any favour given ought it not to be given in favour of the man who has worked hard to try and live respectably and to leave some- thing that may be a kind of nucleus for his children rather than the man who did not used any favour and considera- tion ? ' The man was quite as Liberal as he (the speaker) was on that question and a number of others. and it was al- most difficult to find where the Conservatives differed from the Liberals. They had been brought up Conservatives— they had not beceme so through studying the various ques- tions, and he (Mr. Shaw) thought the more meetings they had such as were held last winter, and placed before the work- ing classes the various important questions of the day in their true light, the more Liberal would they become. He could Only say that if he were 'spared he should do his best to secure for the working-man what he believed he was en- titled to. (Applause.) Referring to the result of the revi- sion court, tee Chairman said that showed them that they must have the franchise extended, so that any person who paid his poor rate should have a tote. (Rear, hear.) his was not surprised at the difficulty the Government had in introducing the Franchise Bill into the House of Commons, because the landed aristocracy knew that two millions more cltizens were admitted to the franchise, men woul I be sent to Parliament who would legislate for the benefit ot the country and mankind. (Applause.) He was sure the audience were quite as well satisfied as he was that the Liberal party did not need any urgiog on with the redistri- bution scheme. The Liberals were far more anxious fee re- distribution than the Conservatives were. (Hear, hear.) It was not something they were afraid of. (Hear, hear.) He however, supported the Government in the coarse they' had adopted with regard to the franchise and redistribution. Supposing the Government had to ap- peal to the country on the present franchise, it was for every one of them to do the best they could to return again to power a Liberal Government, but to do more than pain a Franchise Bill and a Redistribution Bill—to prevent the Upper House from having any control over matters affect- ing the repressntation of the people.—On the motion of Mr. Leak, seconded by Mr. Whinyates, and supported by the Chairman, Mr. I'. Handley was re-elected vice-president. —Mr. T. Norman was re-appointed hon. treasurer, on the motion of Mr. W. Handley, seconded by Mr. Bridgewater. —The Chairman, in moving the re-appointment of Mr. 0. Leak to the hon. srcretare ship, said they knew how very well Mr. Leak had managed the business of the Association as well as the regletration business. In the past times Con- servatives were allowed to remain on the register long after they had left the town, and he dare say long after they had left the country altogether, but Mr. Leak had remedied all this, and no longer were persens allowed lobe on the register who had no right to be there.—Mr. Biebrown seconded the motion, which was unanimously carried, and Mr. Leak suit- ably acknowledged the appointment.—At the suggestion of he secretary a resolution was passed having the effect of making all subscribers to the Association members of the Committee. The following appointments were then made :—Mid-district—Chairmen, Mr. W. Handley and Mr. George Moss; vice-chairmen, Mr. P. Speakman and Mr. John Pritchard; secretaries, Meesrs. F. J. Adams and B. Kniveton. East district—Chairman, Mr. J. R. Frith ; vice- chairman. Mr. F. Fairhurst; secretary, Mr. J. Bridgewater. West district—Chairman, Mr. S. C. Beckett ; vice-chair- man, Mr. W. R. Chadwick; secretary, Mr. F. J. Norman. Halton diatrict—Chairman, Mr. S. Taylor; vice-chairman, Mr. J. N. Lolls; secretary, Mr, H. Ford. Weston district —Chairman, Mr. James Handley; vica-chairman, Mr. John Kirkham; secretaries, Messrs. James and John Bill. Executive Committee—Messrs. J. D. Jones, W. Marsh, J. A. emith, E. Taylor, George Bellamy, R. Wright, F. Fair- burst, J. Whinyates, S. Pope, T. Faulkner, John Wilson, C. Littler, and Lea. A vote of thanks to the officers for their services during the past year, and to the chairmae for presiding, brought the proceedings to a close. per lb.

RUNCORN COUNTY COURT. TUESDAY—Before Mr. W. Wynne Ffoulkee, judge. THE CAUSE LIST. There were 84 original plaints, one adjourned plaint, and 12 judgment suoamonses set down for hearing. A BANKRUPT COMMITTED.—WiIIiam Lightfoot, formerly a wheelwright, appeared before hie Honour under the follows ing circumstances :—On the 11th March in the present year, Lightfoot applied for an administration order under the new Bankruptcy Act, and an order was made upon him to pay his debts amounting to £lB in full at the rate of £1 16s per month. He failed to obey this order, and in August he was again brought before the Court, and as his Honour was not satisfied that he had the means to pay, the acting creditor Mr. Henry White, through Mr. F. A. Lake, solicitor, con- sented that the order should be reduced to a .61 a month. He, however, had not complied with this order, and he was I now £3 in arrear in his payments. He excused I;is neglect on the ground that he was not in regular employment, and had had a great deal of sickness amongst his children. Mr: Lake said the defendant had only been one week out ef em- ployment during the past three months, and he should leave the matter entirely in the hands of his Honour.—hlis Hon- our pointed out to the defendant that as long as the admin- istration order was in force nobody could take any proceed- ings against him, and it was his bounden duty in return for this protection to make a great effort to obey the order of the Court. He must pay the arrears in three weeks or go to gael for 42 days. 'ACTION AGAINST A RUNCORN SOLICITOR-A LEGACY WANTEP. Charlotte Helms, widow, Helsby, sued Mr. W. H. Linaker, •solicitor, Runcorn, for the sum of £5O, the amount of a legacy bequeathed to the plaintiff by the will of Winifred Mary Salt, late of Runcorn, deceased, of which will the defendant is sole executor.—Mr. Tibbits (Messrs. Tibbits and Son, Chester) appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. F. A. Lake for the defendant.—Mr. Lake at the outset admitted that a legacy of £5O had been bequeathed to the plaintiff

by Mrs. Salt.—ln the course of discussion, his Honour said it was for the plaintiff to prove that after the payment of all the debts of the estate there were assets sufficient to pay the leeacy.—Mr. Tibbits said the residue was sworn under £5OO, and he should prove that the testatrix had the sum of £5OO on mortgage of property in Runcorn, certain gas shares which had been sold for £l6O, and he believed other pro- perty. Application had been made to Mr. Linaker for the legacy, but they were unable to get it. He should be able to show that the defendant instead of paying the legacy had paid upwards of £lOO to the residuary legatee, which showed that there had been assets and that those assets had been misapplied, as the plaintiff's legacy should have been paid in the first instance. The plaintiff was unaware of the legacy having been left her until twelve months • after the death of Mrs. Salt. There was £5OO upon good security in Runcorn, but that sum WAS called in, and £4OO of it was invested upon property the bnildlnee society had a charge of £9OO over.—His Hon- our said the only question was what money was left behind, how was it invested, and how had it been expended,. No residue could be realised until all the debts of the estate were paid.—Mr. Tibbits said he was informed that the testa- trix owed nothing at her death.—Mrs. Charlotte Hulme, the plaintiff, deposed that the legacy had been left her by Mrs. Salt, whe died at Sutton on the 26th March, 1880. —Thomas Howe, bricksetter, Hapsford, said Mrs. Salt was his sister. She was an invalid, and lived with him and his wife. After her death Mr. Linaker told him there would be £3OO or better for him, and he had since then received from Mr. Linaker upwards of £lOO by instalments of £2 per month towards keeping him. The other Saturday he went to draw £2 and only rectived 10s., as Mr. Linaker said he could not get the money off the man who had it.—By His Honour: He did not know where Mr. Linaker got the £2 per month from.—By Mr, Lake: Mrs. Salt had ceased to live with him two years before her death, and he did not know anything about her affairs afterwards. He saw Mr. Linaker shortly after he death and told him that he should have to go to the workhouse if he did not get something. Mr. Linaker offered to lend him come money by weekly instalments.—Mr. Lake : Were not theee peymente loans to you until such time as your share of the estate should come to you ? Yes, sir.—This was the case for the plaintiff.—Mr. Lake submitted that there was no case, but Mr. Linaker Was desirous that the case should be gene into thoroughly, and he would at once call upon him.—Mr. Linaker said in 1875 Mrs. Salt had £5OO mortgaged on property in Runcorn, and she had also £lOO in the Frodsham Gas Co. She came to him and said she wanted £lOO ready money, and the £5OO was called in at her request. On the 20th October, 1876, she advanced £lOO on a second mortgage on twelve houses in Runcorn for a term of seven years. The term expired in October, 1833. In April, 1877, he commenced receiving the interest on this £4OO, and he received it until April 1880, when the testatrix died. That interest, at the rate of five per cent., amounted to £7O altoge'her. In June, 1880, he sold the gas shares for £167 7s 65 ; and he also received about the same time a year's dividend, amounting to about £7 10s. These sums made altogether £244 17s 65,and this was all the money he received on Mrs. Salt's accennt during her lifetime or since her death. In June, 1876, Mrs. Salt had a stroke, and at her request he commenced to pay for her board and lodg- ing, and Is manage her affairs, for which he was to receive £5 5s a year. His disbursements on her account, from June 27th, 1876, to March, 1880, including the sum of £2 2s, his own professional charge for attending at Sutton and making the will came to £233 17s 3d. He produced receipts and vouchers. Since then he had paid various expenses for funerals, sale of shares, &c., which brought the total disbursements to £2BB lie. That left the estate, outside the £4OO mortgage, indebted to him £l3 13s 6d. He had since received by way of interest on the £4OO the sum of £4O. Prior to October, 1883 the building society had taken charge of this preperty in cons quence of the mortgagor's personal position having become a great deal worse, and -akin-lately the society sold the property. He understood that the arrears of interest, the fines, and costs of sale were barely covered by the amount realised. In October of last year, when the time for which the money was lent expired, he wrote to the mortgagor, requesting him to pay off the mortgage. He replied, stating that from the position in which he then was he could not pay any money, and he (Mr. Linaker) instructed Messrs. Day and Lake to sue the mortgagor under his covenant. The action was brought, and defendant instructed Messrs. Fletcher, of Northwich, to defend, but ultimately judgment was obtained for the £4OO and the arrears of interest. The solicitors conferred to- gether, and Mr. Lake came to the conclusion that if he issued execution he would barely obtain the costs of the execution, and he advised him (Mr. Linaker) to wait that he might be able to bring about such an arrangement as would pay a consiaerable portion of the £4OO Judgment had been signed, but no execution had been issued. With re- ference to the payments to the man Howe, these were not ir eluded in the particulars at all. They were advanc,d by himself, and he would explain why he made them. After Mrs. Salt's death Howe, who was in very ill health, came to him and said that if he could not get some money he would have to go into the workhouse. He told him there would not be any money for him for several years, but added that he did not mind taking the responsibility of paying him 103 per week, and he would reimburse himself when the money of the estate was paid in. He never made the payment as execu- tor to the estate. He anticipated that Howe would be in a position to refund. Although he was entitled by the will to charge for hie professional services, he had not done so. He had explained all these circumstances to Mrs. Hul me, and be went over to Cheater on Saturday, but Mr. Tib- bits would not hear anything about the matter, or ex- amine the accuunts.—Mr. Tibbits : I applied to you for an , account long ago, and you promised me one, but I could not get it. Ho asked his Honour to look at the receipts of the payments to the man Howe, and said they were all made on I behalf of the estate.—His Honour : They are evidence of admission of asaets But sow the accounts are before you what assets are there ?—Mr, Tibbits : I have had no op- portunity of looking at the accounts.—His Honour: There are assets no doubt, but they den't seem to be realised —Mr. Tibbits cross-examined Mr. Linaker at some length, and asked him if the £lOO advanced on the 12 cottages, on which a building society bed already a mortgage, was good security.—Mr. Linaker : 41 per cent. Were you not the mortgagor of that property to the Banding Society 7—No I was not.—Did not the cottages belong to you F—They had done some time before but I had sold them. When Mrs. Salt advanced this money she WAS in perfect health, and went herself to inspect the property.—la answer to further iltustioos, Mr. Linaker said he sold the property to Mr. J. J. Speakman for £1,300, and there was duo to the building society a little over £BOO. The houses were mortgaged to the building society two or three years before he purchased them. He sold them subject to the mortgage. When he called in the £5OO there was no contemplated sale of the Iproperty to Mr. Speakman. It was celled in simply to give Mrs. Salt £lOO ready money she wanted. Mr. Tibbits said on Monday be received a telegram from Nir.Linaker which read as follows :—" Speakman cannot come to Chester to- day. Have arranged for the payment of the full legacy. It you call to-morrow will settle."—Mr. Linaker acknow- ledged that he sent that telegram and explained that he had seen Mr. Speakinan, his brother, and one or two of his friends and they agreed that as it would be an expensive thing if execution was issued, they would try to arrange for £5O of the mortgage money to pay off the legacy. He had done all he could to get the legacy. He should not pull it out of his own pocket, he could not afford it..—His Honour said there must be judgment for the legacy. The only matter was how soon it could be paid. He assumed that Mr. Lake had given good advice as to not proceeding with the execution, etherwise he should not keep these people waiting until these things Cattle in. Still there was a certain amount of discretion to be used to make the most of the estate that the executor ought to be allowed to exer- cise, but at the same time thee's people should not be kept waling an unreasonable time. He did not know what others there were to be paid under the will ; or whether there was anybody besides the legatee.—Mr. Linaker : No one else, sir. —His Honour: Clearly the legacy is due, and I must enter up judgment for the plaintiff, no execution to issue without leave of the court.—Mr. Tibbits: Will your honour limit the time for payment. we have waited four years and a half now.—Mr. Linaker: I could not touch the money un- til 1883.—Mr. Lake said Mr. Speakman and himself were in conference and would be able to make some arrangement shortly.—His Honour said there must be judgment in the usual way, no execution to take place without leave.

At the Dablin Commission, on Tuesday, the second trial of James Ellis French terminated in another disagreement of the jury. The Austrian anarchist Theilmann, for whose arrest on the charge of high treason a warrant was issued several months ago, has been apprehended at Reichenberg, in Bohemia.

George Townend, collector of rates for the Heywood Cot, poration, was reminded on Wednesday on a charge of em- bezzling £5 which he had received in payment of a street improvement rate. It is stated that there are other charges of a similar character to be preferred.

- NEW PEERS.—The Gazette announces the granting of , letters patent to Mr. Dodson, by the title of Baron Monk Bretton, of Conyboro and Hurstpierpoint, Sussex ; and to Sir Water JAMS, as Baron Northbaurne, of Betteshanger Kent, and Jarrow Grange, Durham. A STABLE BORNEO Dower.—On Thursday morning a fire was discovered to have broken out at a stable belonging to Mr. Henry Howell, provision dealer and carter, residing at 87, Hoyle-street, Warrington. The stable is situated in Lilford-street, and an alarm was given as soon as the dis- covery was made. The manual engine was taken to the spot, but was not used, the stable being bruned down before its arrival. Damage was done to the amount of £5O, a horse, valued at £2O, beteg burned to death, and the building, a wooden structure, being destroyed. The origin of the fire has not been ascertained, but it may have been caused by two youths, one of them the son of Mr. Howell, who had previously been in the stable with a lighted candle. There is no doubt that it was accidental. None of the property was insured.

div.head: SHIP CANAL POLL.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL POLL.

Contrary to what was generally expected on its becoming known that Mr. T. Morris intenM to withdraw his demand for a poll, it has been decided that the decision as to the levying of the twop. nny rate should be left to the whole body of ratepayers. Mr. Morris, in accordance with his announcement in our columns last week, gave the Mayor of Warrington notice of his wish to withdraw his demand, but there were some doubts as to whether the Mayor could legally allow the demand to be withdrawn. The necessity of a solution of this problem has, however, been obviated by Mr. Diggle's persistence in the demand for a poll he made at the recent ratepayers' meeting, and which be has renewed in a declaration to the Mayor. It is therefore understood that the poll will now be taken on Mr. Diggle's demand, Mr. Morris being thus ex- onerated from any responsibility in forcing a poll and with regard to the consequent expenditure. Those opposed to the levying of a rate in aid of the Canal are still as resolute as ever in their opposition, and we believe a number of them have petitioned the Local Government Board with regard to the subject. They have laid before the Local Government Board their views as to the private and speculative nature of the Canal enterprise, and have asked for the opinion of the Board with regard to the pro- posed action of the Corporation. Those in favour of the rate are also active in promoting their views, and have, we believe, received numerous promises of support, proxies being very readily given. It may be added that the action of the Mayor of Manchester in allowing the poll to be with- drawn in that city has been brought under the notice of the Loc 11 Government Board. as several gentlemen of legal standing are of opinion that when once a poll has been de- manded at a public meeting it cannot ha withdrawn.
The sth of November celebrations passed off generally Without serious disturbance. In Sheffield, by an accidental o:splosion of fireworks, damage to the extent of abeat £3OO was done.

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.

• ---,a" Vice-Chancellor Bacon on Vtiday afternoon granted an injunction restraining Miss Davey from publishing or part- ing with the late Lord Lytton's letters. A MATLOCK HOTEL BURNT DOWN.— A fire broke out on Friday morning in the Old English Hotel, Matlock Bridge. Despite the exertions of the firemen the building was gutted, only the outside walls remaining. The damage is estimated at from £lO,OOO to £12,000. SUPPOSED INFANTICIDE AT PRESTON. The body of a newly-born child has been found in St. Paul's churchyard, Preston. A man passing the church saw what be thought was a bundle of rags, but which proved on examination to be a piece of old bedding, containing the body of a child which had apparently lived. The parcel had evidently been ' thrown over the rails. The police are making inquiries. HORRIBLE CHILD MURDER AND MUTILATION.—At Ath- lone, a man named Lyons and his daughter are in custody for the murder of the latter's child. The body was horribly mutilated; the head had been cut off and thrown into a lane, and the trunk, with only one arm attacked, was found in a garden. The police searched the room occupied by the prisoners and found the missing arm hidden behind a picture hanging on the wall.

SiTOCHING COLLIERY ACCIDENT: Two MEN KILLED.— On Friday morning, about nine o'clock. two men named John Beaumont and :John Walker were killed by a large fall at New Oaks Colliery, near Barnsley. Beaumont and his hurrier, Walker, were at work when they were both buried by the fall, and killed on the spot. Walker's body was ex- tricated about an hour afterwards, but Beaumont'i remains were not got out until later. Both men were unmar- ried.

AFFAIRS IN SOUTH AFRICA. The War Office authorities were busily engaged on Friday in selecting from a large number of volunteers the officers who are to accompany Sir Charles Warren to South Africa. Orders were cabled to Bombay instructing the troopship Serapis, which leaves for Portsmouth about the 11th inst. With the 13th Hussars on board, to proceed via the Cape. She will call at Capetown and there land the Hussars in the event of Sir Charles Warren deeming it necessary to requisition their services. The Union Company's steamer Trogan, which leaves for South Africa aboutt he 20th inst., is being prepared to accommodate 300 military pas- sengers.__ _

THE DEATH OF MR. FAWCETT. M.P. The remains of the late Postmaster-General will be in- terred in Trurnpington Churchyard, near Cambridge, on Monday next, about noon. A special train will be des- pitched from St. Pancras at tea o'clock, arriving in time for the funeral.

Mrs. Fawcett on Friday received a large number of telegrams and letters of condolence. They included addresses from the staffs of the General Post Office and the principal provincial postal estahlishments. The vacant Postmaster-Generalship will not be filled up until after the funeral, but it is understood in the best in- formed circles that Mr. Shaw-Lefevre will have the refusal of the office. In the event of that gentleman's acceptance, Mr. Courtney is expected to become First Commissioner of Works, being succeeded in the Secretaryship of the Treasury by Mr. Henry Fowler. The Liberal Association of Hackney have not decided upon the selection of a candidate, but several names have been under their consideration for some time past. On Friday afternoon a deputation from the various work- ing class associations in the East end of London waited on Captain T. S. Lemon, a well-known Radical and labour advocate, to request him to become a candidate in the inter- est of the working classes for the representation of Hack- ney. Captain Lemon accepted the Invitation subject to the concurrence of the Radical and other working men's clubs In the borough.
THE PRESIDENTIAL ELECTION.-RETURN OF MR CLEVELAND. •

The New York -C-Wree-p—on.cle;t7;iil;e Daily News tele- graphs that Mr. Cleveland has been elected. He has car- ried all the doubtful States and many of the States hitherto invariably Republican. Mr. Blaine's defeat is regarded "as the overthrow of the most ingenious and powerful combina- tion for securing a corrupt Government ever organised in America." The Herald says that the candidacy of Mr. Blaine was a humiliating disgrace to the country, and that his return would have been a national justification of public dishonesty and trickery of every kind. The Evening Post says that since the fall of Richmond there has been no such triumph in the country. The complete official returns give Mr. Cleveland about 1,500 majority in New York State and ensure his election. The National Republican Committee has issued an address denying the accuracy of the counting, and declaring that Mr. Blaine is returned. NEW YORE, FRIDAY, 2 m.—The latest official returns show that the Democratic gains exceed the preaious esti- mates, thus giving Governor Cleveland a plurality in New York State and ensuring his election as President. The Re- publicans concede Indiana to the Democrats. The latter have elected nine members of Congress and the Republi- cans three, leaving one district in doubt.
A Central News New York telegram says :—There have been many disturbances throughout the night, but quiet has been restored by the announcement of Cleveland's election.
NEW YORE, FRIDAY NOON.—Mr. J. Gould has congrat- ulated Governor Cleveland upon his election to the Presi- dency. This disposes of any doubts as to the republican defeat.
THE CHOLEBA.-SERIOUS OUTBREAK IN PARIS.

Pants, FRIDAY.—The outbreak of cholera in Paris is fully confirmed. This tnorning 20 Cases were registered, four of which ended fatally. The epidemic is at present chiefly confined to the working quarter Jf St. Antoine. The Prefect of Police has already visited the infected houses.

div.head: FRANCHISE BILL.
div.p: THE FRANCHISE BILL.

The adjourned debate on Mr. Stanhope's amendment to the second reading of the Franchise Bill was resumed. Sir R. Cuoss said no per.on could find fault with the tone of the Prime Minister's speech on moving the second reading. But there compliment must end, as he felt certain that great disappointment existed that he had thrown ne new light on the present situation or shown them any way out of the difficulty In which they were now placed. They strongly objected to the question before them being dealt with as the Premier proposed. The Conservatives bad no desire to op- pose the extension of the franchise. They had no wish to cover the paper with amendments to the bill on its going into Committee, and under such circumstances he thought the Premier ought to meet them half way and give some guarantee that the same Parliament should deal with redis- tribution as well as an extension of the Fran- chise. If there was wilful determination on the part of the Government not to allow them to see his redistribution scheme and disturbances took place, and diffi- culties arose, the country would know whom te, blame, and if an appeal to the constituencies took piano the great mass of the people would, he thought, be of opinion that the Op- position had asked for nothing else but what was wise, nec- essary, and just.—Sir C. DILIIR said he was quite prepred to admit that the principle of the bill was accepted on both sides, but notwithstanding that several speeches from the Conservative side clearly showed that some were opposed to any extension of the Franchise, the Liberal side adopted the bill absolutely while the Conservatives only accepted conditionally upon effect being given to their own party's views. The Premier had promised to give the fullest infor- mation with regard to the redistribution scheme provided it could be given without jeopardising the Franchise Bill, and if it could be made clear that the fullest information could be supported with- out endangering the enfranchisement of two millions of the people he could assure the right hon. baronet that the fullest information would be at once supplied. (Cheers.) He ex- pressed hope that means might yet be found of arriving at a satisfactory conclusion.—Lord R. CHURCHILL took excep- tion to the speech delivered by Mr. Gorst last night. He accused Mt. Gorst of prostrating himself before the Prime Minister, and advising his friends to make an ignominious surrender.—Mr. C. RUSSELL supported the Bill, although he did not approve the whole of its provisions.—Mr. FiNcir HATTON supported the amendment if the Prime Minister would insert a clause in the Bill stating it should not come into operation until the Redistribution Bill passed, the dif- ficulty would be removed.—Sir F. MILNER supported, and Mr. D. GRANT opposed the amendment. [LEFT SITTING

THE SWINDLER AND THE POLICEMAN.—A man giving his name as James Stafford, with several aliases, who stated that he was a pensioner, was on Monday sent to gaol for a month by the Warrington magistrates for pursuing a sys- tem of fraud by false pretences. He went to the house of James Sixstnith, labourer, John-street, and engaged lodg- ings, remaining there ter a night and having two or three meals. He also succeeded in borrowing Ts from Mr. and Mrs. Sizsmith, and a pair of shoes, and then left, ostensibly to fetch his luggage, but did not return. He, however, wett to another house, and, credulity favouring him, borrowed 28 in a like manner. Not satisfied, he made a third attempt, this time walking unsuspectingly into the bands of a swind- ler's natural enemy, the police. He proceeded to the house of Mr. Wheatley, one of the borough constables, and made his usual inquiry for lodgings, and while negotiations were being made with Mrs. Wheatley, the husband, with charac- teristic euspicion, "smelt a rat," and went to the police station, where information of the swindles already Perim- trated having been handed in, he recognised the description of his would-be-lodger, and returned home. Stafford was still there, and Wheatley, remarking to him that he ap- peared to have been having a glass or two, invited him out, saying that "he Would take him somewhere where he could have it a bit stronger." With this touch of pleasant sar- casm the intended victim conducted his companion to the ' police station, where he again had the benefit of cheap lodgings, and for a tenger period than he bargained for,

GOOD TEMPLAIIY AT BATCIIFORD.—A public meeting WEIS held on Monday evening in connection with the Bonehill Branch Lodge, in the Temperance Hall. The chair was- taken by Brother Harrison, who, after expressing his plea- sure at seeing so many present, proceeded with the pre- grarnme. which consisted of readings, recitations songs, trios, all being very well gone through by the children, as- sisted by members of the lodge. Mr. Adams was present and made a short speech. After a very enjoyable meeting the proceedings were brought to a close about 9-30. WIFE BESTING AT BGETONWOOD.—At the Warrington County Petty Sessions on Wednesday, a middled-aged man named Thomas Club, a collier, was summoned by his wife, &Aber, for an aggravated assault on the 31st Oct .ber.. Mr. P. Davies, solicitor, Warrington' appeartd foe the wife, and stated the facti of the ease. The parties had, he said, been married 25 years, and there were three children of the mar- riage. He should call evidence showing great cruelty on the part of defendant, and should ask the Bench to consider the advisability of gr,ntng a separation order. On the day that the assault for which he was summoned took place, the defendant came frmn his work in the afternoon and quar- relled with his wife about some insignificant matter, and without any provocatioe he knocked her down by a blow In the face. When she was on the ground he kicked her until she was insensible, and then left her ,vhere she lay, bleeding from the mouth. The defendant denied having committed the assault, but witnesses were called to prove that he had • been in the habit of systematically assaulting his wife, the son of the parties saying that his father had run him and his mother out of the house with the paker, and had threatened "what he would do if it was not for his own, neck." The Bench fined the defendant 5 and costs, and granted a separation order, ordering him to pay Si towards ' the maintenance of his wife.

THE LIVERPOOL, SOUTHPORT, AND PRESTON JUNCTION RAILWAY. Incorporated by Special Act of Parliament 47 Fs 48 Vic., Scasion 1881 (Royal Assent 7th August, 1884). to Oonnect LIVERPOOL with PRESTON. BLACKBURN, lc., anl EAS l LANCASHIRE?, Through the Cheshire 1 ines Extension and West Lancashire Railways, and under agreement with the W. at Lancashire Railway Company to wok, maintain, and manage the entire Railway in perpetuity at 40 per cent, of the gross receipts be- low £57 per mile per week, and 50 per cent of the grass re- ceipts over £57 per mile per week. Authorised Caplet consists of £200,000 in shares, with £66,610 borrowing powers. The Directors of the Liverpool, Southport, and Preston Juno- lion Railway Company have authorPed their Bankers the Manchester and Live- pool District Banking Company. Limited, to receive subsc.iptions for £200.00,, being the C unpany's Share Capital, in :0,,00 shares of £lO each at par, or £.O, per £lO share, to be converted Into stock when fully paid, payable as follows : . ' £1 on each elo share on application. 1 „ 10 „ allotment. i 2 ~ 10 „ January srd, 1885. 2 „ 10 ~ February 3rd, 1885. 2 „ 10 „ March 3rd, 1885. 2 ~ 10 ~ April 3rd, 1884. 210 - -- Interest at the rate of 5 per ems. per annum will be paid half-yearly, on the let January and Ist July, until the Ist January, 1887, upon all amounts paid up, from date of pay- ment, under the guarantee as hereinafter stated. Payments in full, or in advance, may be made on Allotment, or at any subsequent time. The Liverpool, Southport.. and Preston Junction Railway Company was incorporated by special Act of Parliament for the purpose of constructing a DOUBLE line of Railway, seven and a half miles in length, to connect Liverpool and the Liverpool and Gershon D cks with Preston, Blackburn, and East Lancashire, through the Cheshire Lines Exteosion and West Lancashire Hallways, and, by means of the Blackpool Railway, with B'ackpool. . The Railway will form the al-important link, connecting the Cheshire Lines, the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire, the Midland, and the Great Northern Railways, with the West Lancashire Railway, and will through that system form a com- petitive line from Burnley, Accrington, Blackburn, Preston, and the whole of East and South-West Lancashire and York- shire. to Liverpool and tire Liverpool Docks. The districts above referred to are at present served only by the London and North-Western and Lancashire and Yorkshire Railways, by whose lines all the immense Marna to and from Liverpool, and the Liverpool Docks, is monopolised. The traffic of the London and North-Western and Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway Companies amounts to an average of £l3O 6e. 2d. per mile per week, and the dividends on the ordi- nary stocks of these a rmpanies for the three years ending June 30th last, averaged £6 Os. sd. per cent. per annum. 1 A grosg traffic per nide per week, equal to either that of the London and North-Western or Lancashire and Yorkshire Rail- way Companies, averaging the receipts would, on the Liver- pool, Bouthnort, and Preston Junction Rahway Company, pro- duce £50,820 ss. per ann ' which sum, less the fixed working expenses, would ensure adividend little short of that paid by the most prosperous Railway in the kingdom. A gross revenue of only £56 19s 4d. per mile per week will be sufficieiot, after providing for the interest on the borrowing powers, to pay 5 per cent, interest on the whoie of the share capital of the Company. The Liverpool, Southport, and Preston Junction Railway Company has no preference capital whatever, the £200,000 slams, now for sabscription, forming its only share capital. The following are the quotations taken from tha St •ck Ex- change Official List of the stocks of the two railways, which this line, when completed, will compete with : London and North-Western Railway 165 per cent., or 65 percent. premium. Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway 114 per cent., or 14 per cent premium. The great source of traffic for which this line will compete, and for which the Company has been especially incorporated, Os that erlalng and terminating in the cotton, coal, and wool- len districts of Lancashire and Yorkshire and the Liverpool Docks respectively. The great advantages of the working Agreement are that the LIVERPOOL, SOUTHPORT, AND PRESTON JUNCTION RAILWAY COMPANY will be for ever free from the cost ot worki rg and management, the supply ef motive power and other rolling stick, the main' enance and renewal of the line, stations, and works, and liabilities arising from accidents and claims for compensation ; all these being covered by the per- rentage of the gross earnings retained under the worklag agreement. Moreover, the revenue of the Company will not be in any way affected by the cost of working, as the fixed propor- tion of gross, earnings above menrioned, must, under all cir- cumstances, be paid os er to the Liverpool, Southport, and Pres- ton Junction Railway Company, independently altogether of what it may cost for working. A contract, dated October 28th, 1884, has been entered into by the Company with Mr. Charles Brade Lek, of Wigan, who is now completing important w.,rks for the London and North- Western and Caledonian Railway Companies, and who under- takes to purchase the land and complete the railway and stations ready for public traffic, and to maintain the same for twelve months after opening. The terms of the contract guarantee that the capital of the Company shall Not be exceeded. The contractor agrees to complete the railway and works to the satisfaction o the Board of Trade and the Company, and, subject to the terms of the coutrsct, to open the same for pub. its traffic of every des viption, within 18 months from Novem- ber Ist, 1884, and to pay interest, as before stated, at 5 per cent, per annum, halt ye any. email amounts frr the time being paid up in raped of the shares now for subscription, viz., on January and July Ist in each year, until January Ist, 1887. teing 8 months beyond the contract time for the completion and ope ,ing of the railway and works, by depositing for that purpose with the Mar.chester and Liver pool District Banking Company, Limited, a sufficient sum in the names of John Eorshaw, Esq., Mayor of Preston, Lancashire. Edward Holden, Esq . Laurel Mount, fihipley, Yorkshire as trustees for the subscribers, to provide for the due and punc- tual payment thereof. The' interest will commence imme- diately, and will be payable half-yearly at the bankers of the Company, by dividend warrants, which will be forwarded by post to the registered address rf each subscriber. Should any application not be accepted, the deposit paid will be returned without deduction, and if the shares alloted to any subscriber be less than the number applied for, the surplus paid on application will be credited In reduction of the amount due on allotment. HAMM ON LICENSED PREMISES.—John Pickavance, of Ecdeaton, was summoned for being drunk on licensed pre- mises, the Rising Sun public-house, on the 28th ultimo, and was fined 10a. and costs, or, in default of payment, 14 days' imprisonment. TUESDAY—Before W. W. Pilkington and J. Mcßryde, Rags. DRUNK.—John Clarke, of Leyland, was lined 5s and costs for being drunk on the previous day. ALLEGED Tanyr.—Robert Dodd, of Bamfurlong, was brought up on suspicion of haring stolen a pair of boots. He was discharged. WEDNESDAY.— Before Mr. H. Baxter (Mayor) and Bfr. J. C. Gamble. DRUNK—Francis Maguire was charged with having been drunk and disorderly at Eccleston on the previous day. He pleaded guilty and was fined 5s and costs. PRESCOT PETTY SESSIONS. TEESDAY.—Before Mess's. Earle and Willis. NONPAYMENT OF RATES —Charles Robinson (Prescot) and Henry Fong (iVhiston) were summoned for the non- payment of water rate for the Prescot Local Board, and an order for payment was made in each case.—The following persons were also summoned, at the instance of Joseph Worrall, surveyor to the Huyton Local Board, for the non- payment of Local Board rates : Thomas Leather (Huyton Quarry), John Prescot (Huyton), Matilda Doris (Roby), J. E. Smith (Roby), Char:es Meredith (Huyton).—The Bench ordered each defendant to pay the rates. A ST. HELENS CARTER IN TROUBLE. James Grundy, carter, residing at St. Helens. was charged with an offence against the Highway Act. ASHTON. ASHTCN LOCAL 130ABLI.—The monthly meeting of this Board was held on Wednesday forenoon. Our report is held over until next week. UNLAWFULLY Usixo e NET.—On Monday, at the Wigan County Police Court, Thomas Rosbottom, a collier, was charged with unlawfully using a net for the purpose of tak- ing game at Billinge Chapel End, on the 23rd of February Oast. Defendant pleaded guilty. Mr. Clayton (Messrs. Peace and Ellis) prosecuted, and said on Saturday, the 23rd February, about eleven o'clock in the morning, defendant with another man. who had absconded, were together in a field at Billings Chapel End, in the occupation of Samuell Eteck. and over which Lord Gerard had the right of shoot- ing. There were hares in the field, and the men were seen drawing a net towatds one of them. The gamekeeper came up, and the men ran away. Defendant was fined 20s and Coats; in default, 14 days' imprisonment.
